sections.why: Most thesis disasters are topic failures decided in a ten-minute corridor conversation. Build feasibility into the decision from day one.
A literature review is only as good as the search behind it. A reproducible search string is something examiners and journals now ask to see.
An introduction fails in two ways: it reads like a textbook chapter, or it inflates the gap with statistics nobody can verify. Keep it tight, sourced and honest.
A literature review is not a summary of ten papers you happened to find. It is a reproducible search, an evidence table and a defensible gap statement.
Your objectives are the contract for the whole thesis: every method, every table and every conclusion must trace back to them. Get them precise now.
The methods chapter is the document you will be held to for three years. Every ambiguity here becomes an unanswerable viva question later.
Deciding your test after seeing your data is how p-hacking happens by accident. Plan the analysis before data collection, and verify every number AI gives you.
Results report what you found, in past tense, with no interpretation. Every number must match the output, and every table must earn its place.
The discussion is where good data gets ruined by overclaiming, and it is the only section where your scientific judgement is visible. Structure it deliberately.
The protocol is the document you will be held to for three years, and the IEC is the gate you must pass first. Decide everything in advance.
A thesis and a paper are different documents. Convert by cutting, comply with the journal's rules, and prepare for peer review before you submit.
Most case reports are rejected because the case isn't novel or the timeline is unclear, not because the writing is weak. Check publishability first, then write to CARE.
A conference presentation is often your research's first audience. Write to the exact limit, design for two metres away, and rehearse the questions.
A seminar is judged by what the audience remembers the next morning. Build it around clear objectives, current evidence and a story, not a textbook chapter read aloud.
A journal club is not a summary of a paper. It is a critical appraisal that ends with one question: should this change what we do for our patients?
Slides support the speaker; they are not the speech. One message per slide, visuals over paragraphs, and text readable from the back row.
CMEs, invited lectures, community talks and panel discussions: every talk needs one big idea, a story to carry it, and a close the audience remembers.
Ward protocol posters, infographics, patient leaflets, pocket cards and AI-generated illustrations: visuals teach faster than words, when they are accurate and simple.
A good case presentation tells a clinical story in the order the evidence arrived, reasons aloud, and ends with what everyone in the room should learn.
Content earns attention; delivery keeps it. Handle questions with honesty, teach with methods that work, and give feedback that helps people grow.
Understanding beats memorising. Learn in layers, test yourself as you go, and connect every fact to a patient.
A plan you can actually follow beats a perfect plan you abandon in week two. Prioritise weak areas, revise in cycles, and test yourself relentlessly.
Marks come from volume, analysis and strategy: practise daily, learn more from every wrong answer than from every right one, and manage time under pressure.
Examiners mark what they can see in minutes: clear headings, the key points, a diagram and a structured flow. Knowing isn't enough; practise writing it.
Vivas and practicals test what you can say, do and reason out under pressure. Practise aloud, one question at a time, with feedback.

Good diagnosticians don't know more diagnoses; they reason better. Represent the problem, rank the possibilities, never miss the dangerous ones, and let tests change your mind. (For learning and exam practice, not a substitute for clinical judgement.)
What you can recall on exam day matters more than what you once read. Turn every topic into flashcards, mnemonics and one-page sheets, and review them on a schedule.

prompts.t: Feasibility-first topic shortlist
prompts.use: Months 1 to 3 of your postgraduate course, before you commit to anything.
prompts.why: Most theses fail at the topic, not the analysis. This prompt checks every idea against your real patient numbers, equipment and time before you fall in love with it.
prompts.p:
You are a senior clinical research methodologist with over 20 years of experience supervising postgraduate theses in [YOUR SPECIALTY]. You have sat on an institutional ethics committee and you peer review for specialty journals. You are blunt about feasibility rather than encouraging.

MY CONTEXT:
Specialty: [e.g. Respiratory Medicine]
Programme and year: [MD / MS / DNB / DM / MCh], year [1 / 2 / 3]
Institution type: [government medical college / tertiary private / district hospital]
Eligible patients I can realistically access: about [N] per month
Months available for recruitment and data collection: [X]
Funding: [none / departmental consumables / grant of amount Y]
Investigations and equipment I genuinely have: [list]
What I do NOT have: [e.g. flow cytometry, PET-CT, research nurse]
Statistical support: [none / department statistician / paid]
Clinical interests: [2 to 4]
Diseases with high burden in my setting: [list]

TASK:
Generate 8 candidate research questions I could design, complete, defend and publish inside my timeline. For each, give exactly:
1. Working title as it would appear on a thesis cover page.
2. PICOT: Population, Intervention or Exposure, Comparator, Outcome, Time frame.
3. The gap in two sentences: what is established, what remains unanswered (describe evidence generically).
4. Study design, and one line on why not the obvious alternative.
5. Feasibility score out of 5, justified against my context above.
6. Indicative sample size with every assumption stated.
7. Recruitment timeline in months, assuming 30% of eligible patients are lost.
8. Primary outcome and the exact instrument, scale or cut-off.
9. The three most likely reasons it fails.
10. Honest publication ceiling: local, national indexed, or international.

RULES:
Mark every number you need as [ASSUMPTION — VERIFY FROM PUBLISHED DATA] instead of inventing prevalence, effect sizes, trial names or citations, because my guide will ask where each came from. Drop any question needing resources I said I do not have. At least 2 of the 8 must survive if recruitment halves.

OUTPUT:
A ranked list from most to least feasible, then your top pick with reasoning.

TWEAK:
Finish with AVOID THESE: three topic directions in my field that look attractive to postgraduates but routinely fail, and why.
tips: Run it twice, once with your real patient numbers and once with half. Any topic that survives both is the safe one.
Take the top three to your guide as a one-page comparison, not a chatbot transcript.
Read AVOID THESE before you fall in love with an idea.

prompts.t: Five Indian abstracts → six thesis topics
prompts.use: After you have saved 5 recent abstracts from Indian centres in your field (Semantic Scholar or PubMed, last 3 years).
prompts.why: Topics generated from memory repeat what already exists. Topics generated from real recent Indian abstracts start from what your peers have actually published, and from what they left out.
prompts.p:
You are a research mentor at an Indian medical college who has guided over 50 postgraduate theses to completion. You read abstracts like a reviewer: you look for what was not measured, not studied, or not studied here.

MY CONTEXT:
Specialty and programme: [e.g. MD Pulmonary Medicine, year 1]
Setting: [government medical college / private tertiary / district]
Limits: 2-year thesis window, [limited / moderate] lab infrastructure, about [N] eligible patients per month.
[PASTE ABSTRACT 1]
[PASTE ABSTRACT 2]
[PASTE ABSTRACT 3]
[PASTE ABSTRACT 4]
[PASTE ABSTRACT 5]

TASK:
1. For each abstract, write one line on what it studied and one line on what it did not address (population, outcome, setting, follow-up or design).
2. From these, identify 3 research gaps relevant to Indian patients.
3. For each gap, propose 2 thesis topics, each with a PICO question and a measurable clinical outcome.
4. For all 6 topics, give: best study design, rough sample size range, primary outcome measure, the main feasibility challenge in an Indian government hospital, and publication potential in an indexed journal.
5. Rank the 6 and recommend the top 3 to present to my guide.

RULES:
Work only from the abstracts I pasted. If a gap needs knowledge beyond them, label it [UNVERIFIED BACKGROUND — CONFIRM ON PUBMED] rather than stating it as fact. Name no additional papers unless you can give a verified PMID or DOI.

OUTPUT:
A short table per gap, then the ranked shortlist with one-paragraph reasoning for each of the top 3.

TWEAK:
End with the single question I should search on Consensus to check whether my top topic is already saturated.
tips: If an abstract is from a different population (Western, paediatric), say so in the context line. It changes which gaps are real.
Keep the 5 abstracts. They become the first five studies in your Review of Literature.
If fewer than 3 real gaps appear, your search was too narrow. Search the gap, not the disease name.

prompts.t: Socratic research-question workshop
prompts.use: When you have a vague idea ("something on sepsis in the ICU") but no question.
prompts.why: A good question is refined, not generated. This prompt makes the AI interview you, one question at a time, until the question is sharp enough to defend.
prompts.p:
You are a clinical epidemiologist who runs research-methods workshops for postgraduates. You never hand over answers early. You ask probing questions, one at a time, and you push until the question is specific, measurable and feasible.

MY CONTEXT:
My rough idea in one or two sentences: [e.g. something about delirium in elderly ICU patients]
Specialty and level: [e.g. MD Anaesthesiology, year 1]
Setting: [e.g. 20-bed mixed ICU, government medical college]
Time for data collection: [X months]

TASK:
Run a workshop with me in rounds:
1. Ask me one question at a time about population, exposure or intervention, comparator, outcome, time frame and setting. Wait for my answer before asking the next.
2. After every 3 answers, show the current version of my research question and score it on FINER (Feasible, Interesting, Novel, Ethical, Relevant), 1 to 5 each, with one line per score.
3. Point out the weakest FINER element and ask the question that fixes it.
4. Stop when every FINER score is 4 or more, or after 5 rounds.
5. Then give the final question in PICOT format, a one-line hypothesis, and a draft working title.

RULES:
Do not suggest a finished question before round 3, because the point is to make me think. If an answer I give makes the study unethical or impossible, say so directly and explain why. Keep every question you ask under 30 words.

OUTPUT:
Conversational, one question per turn. Use a short FINER scorecard table at each checkpoint.

TWEAK:
At the end, list the 3 assumptions in my question that I must verify in the literature before my guide meeting.
tips: Answer honestly, including "I don't know". The workshop is only as good as your answers.
Screenshot the final scorecard. It becomes slide 2 of your topic presentation.
Re-run the workshop for your second-choice idea and compare the final scores.

prompts.t: Guide-meeting pitch pack for your top 3 topics
prompts.use: The day before you meet your guide or research committee to choose a topic.
prompts.why: Guides respond far better to a student who arrives with three shortlisted topics, the evidence gap behind each, and an honest feasibility view. This prompt builds that one-page pitch.
prompts.p:
You are a head of department who has chaired thesis-topic committees for 15 years. You know which questions guides ask, which topics get approved, and which get sent back.

MY CONTEXT:
Specialty and year: [e.g. MS General Surgery, year 1]
My guide's known interests: [list, or "unknown"]
Department case load relevant to these topics: [numbers per month]
Topic 1: [title + PICOT + why it matters]
Topic 2: [title + PICOT + why it matters]
Topic 3: [title + PICOT + why it matters]
Evidence I have for each gap (searches, Consensus result, abstracts): [PASTE NOTES]

TASK:
1. Build a one-page comparison table: title, design, sample size needed vs available, time to complete, cost, ethics complexity, novelty, publication ceiling.
2. Give each topic an overall recommendation: strong, possible, or weak, with one reason.
3. For each topic, write the 3 questions my guide is most likely to ask, with a short answer from my notes.
4. Write a 60-second verbal pitch for my first-choice topic.
5. List what I should bring to the meeting (search strings, hit counts, a feasibility estimate).

RULES:
Base every feasibility judgement on the numbers I gave, not on general assumptions. Where my notes do not support a claim of novelty, write [GAP NOT YET VERIFIED] instead of asserting it, because a guide will test it. Keep my voice: a first-year resident, not a professor.

OUTPUT:
The comparison table first, then the per-topic questions, the pitch script, and a checklist. Fits on two printed pages.

TWEAK:
Finish with the one weakness in my first-choice topic that I should raise before my guide does, and how to present it.
tips: Print the table. A one-page comparison beats scrolling a phone in a guide's office.
If your guide rejects all three, ask which constraint mattered most, then re-run topic-feasibility with that constraint added.
Practise the 60-second pitch out loud twice.

prompts.t: India gap finder: 15 topics from scratch
prompts.use: When you have no abstracts or ideas yet and need a starting list today.
prompts.p:
You are a senior researcher in [SPECIALTY] at an Indian medical college, known for steering residents towards questions that matter to Indian patients rather than copying Western topics.

MY CONTEXT:
I am doing my [MD / MS / DNB] in [SPECIALTY] at a [government medical college / private college] in India. I have limited lab infrastructure and a 2-year thesis window.

TASK:
Generate 15 potential thesis topics that:
1. Address conditions with a high burden in India (e.g. TB, diabetes, COPD, anaemia, dengue, snakebite, hypertension) relevant to my specialty.
2. Have limited published data from Indian populations.
3. Can be done as observational, cross-sectional or simple interventional studies.
4. Need no advanced laboratory infrastructure.
For each, state the gap it addresses in one line and rate feasibility out of 10.

RULES:
Describe gaps generically. Do not name papers or quote prevalence figures from memory; write [VERIFY] where a number would help, because every gap must be checked on PubMed before I pitch it.

OUTPUT:
A numbered table: topic, gap, design, feasibility /10. Then the 3 you would pick and why.
tips: Paste your 3 favourites into Consensus as yes/no questions. Keep only the ones with mixed or insufficient evidence.
prompts.try: MD General Medicine, government medical college in Bihar.

prompts.t: Clinical hunch → PICOT question
prompts.use: When you have noticed something on the ward ("these patients seem to do worse") and want to turn it into a question.
prompts.p:
You are a clinical research mentor who helps residents turn bedside observations into answerable research questions.

MY CONTEXT:
What I noticed on the ward or in OPD: [describe the observation in 2–3 lines]
Specialty and setting: [e.g. Paediatrics, tertiary PICU]
Rough patient numbers per month: [N]

TASK:
1. Restate my observation as a clear clinical question.
2. Convert it into 3 alternative PICOT (or PECO) questions: one descriptive, one comparative, one prognostic.
3. For each, name the study design that answers it and the primary outcome.
4. Say which is most feasible for a postgraduate thesis and why.

RULES:
Keep each question to one sentence. If my observation is more likely explained by bias or chance (e.g. referral pattern), say so first, because that changes the question.

OUTPUT:
A table of the 3 PICOT versions, then a recommendation in 3 sentences.
tips: Write your observation down the day you notice it. Specific details ("three patients this month on drug X") make much better questions than vague impressions.
prompts.try: Elderly patients with hip fracture on our ward seem to develop delirium more often when surgery is delayed beyond 48 hours.

prompts.t: FINER stress-test of my research question
prompts.use: Before you submit your topic to the department or research committee.
prompts.p:
You are a research committee member at an Indian medical college who scores postgraduate topics every term. You are fair but you do not pass weak questions.

MY CONTEXT:
My research question: [paste in PICOT form]
Study design: [design]
Resources and patient numbers: [brief]
Time available: [months]

TASK:
1. Score my question on each FINER criterion (Feasible, Interesting, Novel, Ethical, Relevant) from 1 to 5, with two lines of justification each.
2. Identify the single weakest criterion.
3. Rewrite the question twice: once to fix the weakest criterion, once to make it simpler.
4. Say which of the three versions you would approve and why.

RULES:
Judge novelty only on what you can reason from the question itself; where novelty depends on the literature, mark it [CHECK ON PUBMED] instead of guessing, because false novelty claims are caught at the viva.

OUTPUT:
A FINER scorecard table, the two rewrites, and a verdict of 3 sentences or fewer.
tips: A score of 3 on "Novel" is fine for a thesis. A score below 3 on "Feasible" is not.
prompts.try: Is serum vitamin D level associated with exacerbation frequency in COPD patients at a tertiary hospital in north India?

prompts.t: Is this topic already done to death?
prompts.use: After shortlisting, when you suspect your topic may already be heavily studied.
prompts.p:
You are a systematic reviewer who can tell within minutes whether a research question is saturated, contested or open.

MY CONTEXT:
My proposed question: [PICOT]
Search results I found (titles or abstracts from PubMed, Consensus or Perplexity): [PASTE TITLES / ABSTRACTS HERE]

TASK:
1. Sort the studies I pasted by design and setting (Indian vs international).
2. Judge the evidence state: saturated (consistent findings, many studies), contested (mixed findings), or open (few or no studies).
3. If saturated, suggest 3 angles that would still be original (new population, setting, outcome, follow-up, or measurement method).
4. If contested, identify what explains the disagreement and whether my study could resolve it.

RULES:
Judge only from what I pasted. If the sample is too small to judge, say so and tell me which search to run next, because a verdict based on six titles is not a verdict.

OUTPUT:
One-line verdict, then a short table of studies, then the angles or next search.
tips: Consensus's meter is a quick first pass. This prompt is the second pass on what it returns.
prompts.try: Paste 10 PubMed titles for "neutrophil-lymphocyte ratio sepsis mortality".

prompts.t: Turn gaps into Consensus yes/no questions
prompts.use: Between gap-finding (Perplexity) and topic selection, before you check evidence density.
prompts.p:
You are a medical librarian who trains residents to query evidence engines such as Consensus effectively.

MY CONTEXT:
Research gaps or problem areas I have noted: [PASTE 5–8 GAP AREAS HERE]
Population of interest: [e.g. Indian adults with type 2 diabetes]

TASK:
1. Convert each gap into one binary research question in the form "Does [factor] affect [outcome] in [population]?"
2. Give a second, narrower version of each question.
3. Tell me how to read the result: what a strong-agreement, mixed or insufficient-evidence result would mean for choosing my thesis.

RULES:
Keep each question under 20 words and answerable with yes or no. Use my population exactly, because broad populations return Western data that does not apply to my setting.

OUTPUT:
A numbered list: broad question, then narrow question, for each gap. Then a 3-row interpretation guide.
tips: Keep only the questions whose result is mixed or insufficient. Strong agreement means that topic is done.
prompts.try: Gaps: sarcopenia in COPD, vitamin D in TB outcomes, early mobilisation in ICU.

prompts.t: Topics I can do from existing hospital records
prompts.use: When prospective recruitment looks slow, or your thesis window is short.
prompts.p:
You are a clinical researcher who has published multiple retrospective and record-based studies from Indian hospitals, and you know their pitfalls.

MY CONTEXT:
Specialty: [SPECIALTY]
Records available: [e.g. ICU admission registers 2019–2024, discharge summaries, lab information system, OPD registers]
How complete and reliable these records are, in my honest view: [brief]
Approximate number of records: [N]

TASK:
1. Suggest 8 thesis questions answerable from these records.
2. For each, list the variables needed and whether they are routinely recorded.
3. Flag the main bias for each (missing data, misclassification, selection).
4. Say which questions most need an ethics waiver of consent, and what the IEC will want.

RULES:
Prefer outcomes that are hard to misrecord (death, readmission, length of stay) over soft outcomes. Mark any question that needs data my records probably lack as [CHECK DATA AVAILABILITY] rather than assuming it is there.

OUTPUT:
A table: question, variables, bias risk (low / medium / high), IEC note.
tips: Pull 20 random files before committing. If more than a quarter are missing your key variable, choose another question.
prompts.try: Medicine ward records of acute kidney injury, 2020–2024, about 900 admissions.

prompts.t: Topics that fit a 12-month data window
prompts.use: When your approved data-collection window is 12 months or less.
prompts.p:
You are a thesis coordinator who has rescued many late-starting postgraduate theses by right-sizing the question.

MY CONTEXT:
Specialty: [SPECIALTY]
Months left for data collection: [X]
Eligible patients per month: [N]
Current (too ambitious) topic idea, if any: [describe]

TASK:
1. Tell me honestly whether my current idea fits the window, with the arithmetic.
2. Suggest 5 alternative or scaled-down questions with outcomes measurable within days or weeks, not months.
3. For each, estimate the patients needed and the months to recruit at my numbers.

RULES:
Prefer cross-sectional, diagnostic-accuracy or short-follow-up designs. Show every calculation with its assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION], because I will have to defend the timeline to my guide.

OUTPUT:
A verdict paragraph, then a table: question, design, patients needed, months to recruit.
tips: Build in a 2-month buffer. Theses almost never finish recruitment on schedule.
prompts.try: DNB Orthopaedics, 10 months left, about 15 eligible patients per month.

prompts.t: Topics needing only routine investigations
prompts.use: When there is no funding and you can only use tests the hospital already does free or routinely.
prompts.p:
You are a researcher who has built a publication record entirely on routine clinical data in low-resource Indian hospitals.

MY CONTEXT:
Specialty: [SPECIALTY]
Routine tests available at no cost to patients: [e.g. CBC, LFT, RFT, ABG, chest X-ray, ECG, bedside USG]
Tests I cannot afford: [list]
Patient groups I see often: [list]

TASK:
1. Suggest 10 thesis topics that use only the routine tests I listed.
2. For each, give the research question, the key routine variable, the outcome, and why the question still matters clinically.
3. Mark the 3 with the best publication potential.

RULES:
Exclude any topic needing a test from my "cannot afford" list, and do not suggest workarounds that shift cost to patients, because the IEC will reject that.

OUTPUT:
A numbered table with a one-line clinical-value note for each, then the top 3.
tips: Ratios and indices built from routine tests are popular but crowded. Pair them with a hard outcome to stand out.
prompts.try: MD Medicine; routine CBC, RFT, LFT, ABG, ECG, chest X-ray; lots of sepsis, CKD and snakebite.

prompts.t: Validate an existing clinical score in my population
prompts.use: When you want a solid, publishable design with a clear outcome, and a well-known score exists in your field.
prompts.p:
You are a clinical epidemiologist experienced in external validation of prognostic and diagnostic scores in Indian populations.

MY CONTEXT:
Candidate score or rule: [e.g. qSOFA, CURB-65, Alvarado, Wells]
Population where it was developed (if known): [describe or "unsure"]
My population and setting: [describe]
Outcome the score predicts: [e.g. 28-day mortality]

TASK:
1. Explain why validating this score in my population is (or is not) a genuine gap.
2. Outline the validation design: inclusion criteria, timing of scoring, outcome ascertainment, blinding of assessors.
3. Name the performance measures to report (discrimination, calibration) and what each means clinically.
4. Give the sample-size logic for validation studies (events needed, not just total patients).

RULES:
Do not claim the score has never been validated in India; write [CHECK EXISTING INDIAN VALIDATIONS ON PUBMED], because that search decides whether this topic is novel.

OUTPUT:
Four short headed sections, under 400 words in total.
tips: Validation studies are strongest when the score is calculated before the outcome is known. Build that into your protocol.
prompts.try: CURB-65 for 30-day mortality in community-acquired pneumonia at a district hospital.

prompts.t: Quality-improvement and audit thesis topics
prompts.use: When your department wants a thesis that also improves care, or clinical trials are impractical.
prompts.p:
You are a quality-improvement lead trained in PDSA cycles and clinical audit, who has supervised QI projects in Indian hospitals.

MY CONTEXT:
Specialty and unit: [e.g. Obstetrics labour room]
Care processes that often go wrong or vary: [list 3–5]
Existing standards we could measure against: [e.g. WHO, national guideline, hospital protocol, or "unsure"]

TASK:
1. Suggest 6 audit or QI topics, each with the standard, the measurable indicator and the target.
2. For the best one, outline a before-and-after design with one PDSA cycle.
3. Explain how to report it (SQUIRE 2.0 headings) and whether it counts as research needing full IEC review.

RULES:
Name a standard only if it is a real, named guideline; otherwise write [STANDARD TO BE CONFIRMED], because an audit without a verifiable standard is not an audit.

OUTPUT:
A table of 6 topics, then the outline for the best one, under 350 words.
tips: Ask your IEC early whether QI counts as research at your institution. The answer changes consent requirements.
prompts.try: Time from admission to first antibiotic in suspected sepsis in the medical emergency.

prompts.t: Questionnaire-based topics without the KAP trap
prompts.use: When your topic will rely on a questionnaire or scale.
prompts.p:
You are a psychometrics-trained researcher who reviews questionnaire studies and is tired of weak knowledge-attitude-practice (KAP) surveys.

MY CONTEXT:
Area of interest: [e.g. inhaler adherence, depression in dialysis patients]
Population: [describe]
Languages my patients speak: [list]

TASK:
1. Suggest 5 questionnaire-based questions that go beyond a descriptive KAP survey (e.g. linking a validated score to a clinical outcome).
2. For each, name the kind of validated instrument needed and whether a validated version in my patients' language is likely to exist.
3. Explain what translation and validation steps I need if it does not.

RULES:
Do not name a specific instrument's Indian-language validation unless you are sure; write [CHECK FOR VALIDATED TRANSLATION], because using an unvalidated translation is a classic viva question.

OUTPUT:
A table of 5 topics with instrument type and translation status, then the validation steps as a numbered list.
tips: A validated instrument plus a hard clinical outcome makes a questionnaire study publishable.
prompts.try: Adherence to inhaled therapy and exacerbations in asthma, Hindi-speaking OPD patients.

prompts.t: Head-to-head decision matrix for 2–3 topics
prompts.use: When you are stuck choosing between two or three final topics.
prompts.p:
You are a pragmatic research supervisor who helps residents decide with criteria, not gut feel.

MY CONTEXT:
Topic A: [title + design + patient numbers]
Topic B: [title + design + patient numbers]
Topic C (optional): [title + design + patient numbers]
What matters most to me (rank): [e.g. finishing on time, publication, learning a skill, guide's interest]

TASK:
1. Build a decision matrix with my priorities as weighted criteria.
2. Score each topic 1 to 5 per criterion, with one line of reasoning.
3. Calculate weighted totals and give a clear recommendation.
4. State what new information would change the recommendation.

RULES:
Use only the facts I gave. Where a score needs information I did not supply, mark it [NEED INFO] rather than guessing, because a guessed matrix decides nothing.

OUTPUT:
The matrix table, then a 3-sentence recommendation.
tips: If two topics tie, pick the one with the more reliable primary outcome measurement.
prompts.try: A: CPAP adherence in OSA (cohort, 8/month). B: Lung ultrasound vs X-ray for pneumonia (diagnostic, 25/month).

prompts.t: Thesis title that passes the committee
prompts.use: When your topic is fixed and you need the formal thesis title.
prompts.p:
You are a university thesis committee member who has seen hundreds of titles rejected for being vague, too long or overclaiming.

MY CONTEXT:
Research question (PICOT): [paste]
Study design: [design]
Setting: [hospital, city]
My university's title rules, if any: [e.g. word limit, must mention design]

TASK:
1. Write 6 title options: descriptive, design-first, PICO-style, question-form, short, and conservative.
2. Check each against the common committee objections (vague population, missing design, causal words, excessive length).
3. Recommend one and explain why.

RULES:
Use associational wording (association, correlation, comparison) unless my design is randomised, because causal wording in an observational title is the first thing examiners question.

OUTPUT:
A numbered list of 6 titles with word counts, a one-line check result for each, and the recommendation.
tips: Most universities like the design and setting in the title: "A prospective observational study at a tertiary care centre in north India".
prompts.try: Association of serum albumin with 28-day mortality in adult sepsis, prospective cohort, AIIMS Rishikesh.

prompts.t: What could kill this topic? A risk register
prompts.use: Right after your topic is approved, before protocol writing.
prompts.p:
You are a research operations manager who has seen theses fail for practical reasons: recruitment, equipment breakdowns, lost records and ethics delays.

MY CONTEXT:
Approved topic and design: [paste]
Recruitment source and expected numbers: [brief]
Key equipment or tests: [list]
People I depend on (lab, radiology, statistician): [list]

TASK:
1. List the 10 most likely risks to completing this thesis on time.
2. For each, rate likelihood and impact (low / medium / high).
3. Give one prevention step and one fallback plan for each.
4. Highlight the 3 risks to discuss with my guide now.

RULES:
Be specific to my topic, not generic. Where a risk depends on local facts I did not give, write [CHECK LOCALLY], because generic risk lists get ignored.

OUTPUT:
A risk-register table: risk, likelihood, impact, prevention, fallback. Then the top 3.
tips: Review this register every 3 months. Add risks as they appear.
prompts.try: Prospective cohort of 150 stroke patients needing MRI within 72 hours.

prompts.t: Choose a measurable primary outcome
prompts.use: When your topic is agreed but the primary outcome is still vague ("better outcome", "improvement").
prompts.p:
You are a trial methodologist who insists every primary outcome is defined precisely enough for two observers to agree.

MY CONTEXT:
Research question: [PICOT]
Candidate outcomes I am considering: [list]
Follow-up I can actually do: [e.g. in-hospital only, 30-day phone call, 3-month OPD visit]

TASK:
1. Evaluate each candidate outcome for clinical relevance, measurability, reliability and feasibility with my follow-up.
2. Recommend one primary outcome and up to 3 secondary outcomes.
3. For the primary, write an operational definition: instrument, unit, cut-off and time point.

RULES:
Prefer validated scales and objective measures. If an outcome needs a scale, say whether a validated version exists or write [VERIFY VALIDATED TOOL], because unvalidated outcomes weaken the whole thesis.

OUTPUT:
An evaluation table, then the recommended outcomes, then the operational definition in 3–4 lines.
tips: Your sample size depends on the primary outcome. Fix this before you calculate anything.
prompts.try: Candidates for ARDS: mortality, ventilator-free days, P/F ratio at day 3, length of ICU stay.

prompts.t: The questions my guide will ask about my topic
prompts.use: Before your first topic discussion with your guide, or before a departmental topic presentation.
prompts.p:
You are an experienced thesis guide in [SPECIALTY] who probes every new resident's topic for weaknesses.

MY CONTEXT:
My topic and design: [paste]
What I know about the background: [brief notes]
My expected patient numbers and time: [brief]

TASK:
1. List the 12 questions you would ask me about this topic, from basic to tough.
2. For each, show what a weak answer and a strong answer look like.
3. Mark the 3 questions I am least prepared for, based on my notes.

RULES:
Ground the model answers in my notes. Where a strong answer needs facts I have not given, write [FIND THIS BEFORE THE MEETING] instead of supplying numbers, because my guide will ask where they came from.

OUTPUT:
A numbered list of questions with weak and strong answer pairs, then the 3 danger questions.
tips: Answer the 3 danger questions in writing before the meeting.
prompts.try: Topic: point-of-care lung ultrasound vs chest X-ray for pneumonia in children under 5.

prompts.t: Topics from the gaps in a clinical guideline
prompts.use: When a recent guideline in your field lists recommendations based on weak evidence or states "further research needed".
prompts.p:
You are a guideline methodologist familiar with GRADE and with how evidence gaps turn into research agendas.

MY CONTEXT:
Guideline document or recommendations section: [PASTE OR UPLOAD THE GUIDELINE / SECTION]
My specialty and setting: [brief]

TASK:
1. Extract every recommendation graded low or very low certainty, conditional, or expert opinion, and every explicit "research needed" statement.
2. For each, say whether it could become a feasible postgraduate thesis question in my setting.
3. Turn the best 5 into PICOT questions with a suggested design.

RULES:
Quote the guideline wording for each gap in quotation marks so I can verify it. Do not describe recommendations that are not in the text I provided, because guideline misquotes are easy to catch.

OUTPUT:
A table: quoted recommendation, certainty grade, feasible (yes / no), PICOT. Then the top 5.
tips: Topics built on guideline gaps are easy to justify in the introduction. The gap is already published.
prompts.try: Upload the research-gaps section of a recent national TB or sepsis guideline.

prompts.t: Four-week feasibility check before you commit
prompts.use: After topic approval, before the full protocol, if recruitment numbers are uncertain.
prompts.p:
You are a research methodologist who believes in testing recruitment before promising it.

MY CONTEXT:
Topic and design: [paste]
Assumed eligible patients per month: [N]
Key procedures per patient: [list]

TASK:
1. Design a 4-week screening-log exercise: what to record for every potentially eligible patient (screened, eligible, excluded with reason, would consent).
2. Give a simple log template with columns.
3. Define go / amend / stop criteria based on the numbers the log produces.
4. Explain how to present the log to my guide and the IEC.

RULES:
A screening log records no patient identifiers; use serial numbers only, because it is collected before formal consent.

OUTPUT:
A step list, the log template as a table, and the decision criteria.
tips: A 4-week log is the strongest evidence you can give that your sample size is realistic.
prompts.try: Diabetic foot ulcer patients undergoing offloading, assumed 12 per month.

prompts.t: Five original angles on a crowded topic
prompts.use: When the topic you love turns out to be heavily studied.
prompts.p:
You are a researcher skilled at finding original angles within well-studied areas without resorting to trivial changes.

MY CONTEXT:
Crowded topic: [describe]
What is already well established (from my reading): [brief]
My setting's special features: [e.g. rural referral hospital, high TB co-infection, altitude, tribal population]

TASK:
Give 5 original angles, one each from: a different population, a different setting, a different outcome, a different measurement method, and longer follow-up. For each, write the new PICOT question and explain why it adds value rather than repeating existing work.

RULES:
Ground each angle in my setting's special features. Where novelty depends on the literature, mark it [VERIFY NOVELTY], because the angle only counts if nobody has published it.

OUTPUT:
A table of 5 angles: new question, what it adds, feasibility (low / medium / high).
tips: The strongest angles usually come from what is unusual about your hospital's patients.
prompts.try: Crowded topic: HbA1c and outcomes in diabetic foot. Setting: tribal district hospital in Jharkhand.

prompts.t: Two-month project for an MBBS student (ICMR-STS style)
prompts.use: When you are an undergraduate applying for a short-term studentship or doing your first research project.
prompts.p:
You are a medical college research mentor who has guided many MBBS students through short, two-month research projects, including ICMR Short-Term Studentship applications.

MY CONTEXT:
My year of MBBS: [e.g. 2nd year]
Departments where I have access or a willing mentor: [list]
Time available: about 2 months, alongside classes
Interests: [list]

TASK:
1. Suggest 6 projects completable in 2 months by a student, e.g. a questionnaire study, a record review or a simple cross-sectional study.
2. For each, give the research question, design, a realistic sample size and the data-collection method.
3. Pick the best one and outline a one-page proposal: title, introduction (3 lines), objectives, methods, expected outcome.

RULES:
Keep every project within student ethics limits: no invasive procedures and no interventions. Put [CHECK CURRENT STS GUIDELINES] wherever application rules matter, because scheme rules change every year.

OUTPUT:
A table of 6 projects, then the one-page proposal.
tips: Mentors say yes faster when you arrive with a one-page proposal instead of "any topic, sir?".
prompts.try: 2nd-year MBBS, mentor in Community Medicine, interested in hypertension awareness.

prompts.t: Ten quick topic seeds in my specialty
prompts.p: Act as a senior [SPECIALTY] faculty member at an Indian medical college. Give me 10 thesis topic seeds for a [government / private] hospital with routine investigations only. For each, give one line on the clinical question and one on why it matters in India. Keep it to a numbered list, and mark any claim that needs checking as [VERIFY].
prompts.try: MD Dermatology, government medical college, high burden of fungal infections.

prompts.t: Sharpen my research question to one line
prompts.p: Act as a research methods tutor. My current research question is: [PASTE QUESTION]. Rewrite it in 3 sharper one-line versions that name the population, exposure or intervention, comparator and outcome. Put the best one first and explain in one sentence why it is better.
prompts.try: Does obesity affect asthma?

prompts.t: PICO or PECO? Frame my question correctly
prompts.p: Act as a clinical epidemiology teacher. My study idea is: [DESCRIBE IDEA]. Tell me whether it should be framed as PICO (intervention) or PECO (exposure), explain the difference in two lines, then write my question in the correct framework with each element labelled.
prompts.try: Comparing outcomes of smokers and non-smokers after coronary bypass surgery.

prompts.t: Check ongoing trials before you commit
prompts.p: Act as a medical librarian. For my topic [TOPIC], give me 5 search-term combinations to check CTRI (ctri.nic.in) and ClinicalTrials.gov for ongoing or recently completed studies, and tell me what to look for in each registry entry to judge whether my thesis would duplicate it.
prompts.try: Early enteral nutrition in acute pancreatitis.

prompts.t: The follow-up that surfaces Indian gaps
prompts.p: Act as a research-gap analyst. Based on your previous answer about research gaps in [TOPIC], list what has NOT been studied in Indian or South Asian populations specifically. Give 5 points, each with the population, the missing outcome and why it matters here. Mark claims to verify as [VERIFY].
prompts.try: Follow-up after a Perplexity answer on gaps in COPD management.

prompts.t: Identify the variables in my question
prompts.p: Act as a biostatistics tutor. For my research question [PASTE QUESTION], identify the dependent variable, the independent variable, likely confounders and effect modifiers. Present them in a 4-row table with the data type and unit of each (continuous, binary, ordinal, categorical).
prompts.try: Is anaemia in pregnancy associated with low birth weight at a district hospital?

prompts.t: My topic is too broad: narrow it three ways
prompts.p: Act as a thesis supervisor. My topic [TOPIC] is too broad for a 2-year thesis. Narrow it three different ways: by population, by outcome and by setting. Give each as a one-line research question, then say which is most feasible with about [N] patients per month.
prompts.try: Outcomes of diabetes in India.

prompts.t: What infrastructure does this topic need?
prompts.p: Act as a research operations planner. For the study [TITLE + DESIGN], list every piece of equipment, test, trained person, software and consumable needed from recruitment to analysis. Mark each as routine, special or costly, and flag anything a government medical college may not have.
prompts.try: Diagnostic accuracy of bedside lung ultrasound for pleural effusion.

prompts.t: Does this Western topic apply in India?
prompts.p: Act as a global health researcher. The topic [TOPIC] is well studied in Western populations. Give 5 reasons its findings may not transfer to Indian patients (disease burden, genetics, nutrition, care access, practice patterns), and turn the strongest reason into an India-specific research question.
prompts.try: Statin response and LDL targets in young adults with premature coronary disease.

prompts.t: Hypothesis-generating or hypothesis-testing?
prompts.p: Act as a research methods examiner. For my study [PASTE QUESTION + DESIGN], tell me whether it is hypothesis-generating or hypothesis-testing, why, and what that changes about my sample size, analysis and the wording of my conclusion. Keep it under 150 words.
prompts.try: A cross-sectional survey of sleep quality among ICU nurses on night shifts.

prompts.t: Summarise my topic on one slide
prompts.p: Act as an academic presentation coach. Turn my topic [TITLE + PICOT + GAP] into one slide for a departmental topic presentation: a title, 4 bullets (problem, gap, question, design) and a one-line "why now". Keep each bullet under 15 words.
prompts.try: Frailty index and post-operative complications in elderly emergency laparotomy.

prompts.t: Build a reproducible, multi-database search
prompts.use: After your topic is provisionally approved, before you read a single paper in depth.
prompts.why: "I searched PubMed" is not a method. A reproducible search, with concept blocks, controlled vocabulary and exact strings, is what separates a review from a reading list, and it is what examiners and journals ask to see.
prompts.p:
You are a medical librarian and systematic-review methodologist who has co-authored Cochrane reviews and trained postgraduates in reproducible searching. You are precise about search syntax and sceptical of shortcuts.

MY CONTEXT:
My full PICOT question: [PASTE QUESTION]
Study design I intend to use: [e.g. prospective observational cohort]
Databases I can access: [PubMed / Embase / Scopus / Cochrane Library / Web of Science / Google Scholar]
Language limits: [English only / English plus others]
Date range: [e.g. 2010 to present, and tell me if I should widen it]
Reference manager: [Zotero / Mendeley / EndNote / none]

TASK:
1. Break my question into concept blocks. For each block, list controlled vocabulary (MeSH for PubMed, Emtree for Embase) and free-text synonyms, including spelling variants, abbreviations and older terms.
2. Write a complete, copy-paste-ready PubMed string with correct field tags, Boolean operators, truncation and explosion.
3. Translate it into Embase and Cochrane Library syntax.
4. Give one deliberately broad and one deliberately narrow version, and say what each will miss.
5. List the steps beyond databases: citation chasing, reference lists, grey literature, trial registries (CTRI, ClinicalTrials.gov) and preprint servers relevant to my field.
6. Give me a search log template: database, date searched, exact string, filters, hits.

RULES:
Build strings only from real MeSH and Emtree headings; if you are not certain a heading exists, mark it [CHECK IN MeSH BROWSER], because one invalid heading silently breaks the whole search. Do not report any studies or hit counts from memory.

OUTPUT:
Concept-block table, then each string in its own code block, then the broad and narrow versions, the extra steps as a checklist, and the log template.

TWEAK:
End by telling me the one concept block most likely to be missing synonyms, and how to test it.
tips: Run the PubMed string and check the hit count. Under 50 is usually too narrow; over 3,000 is usually too broad.
Save the exact string and the date you ran it. Examiners and journals ask for both.
Test the string: pick 3 papers you already know are relevant. If any is missing from the results, add its keywords.

prompts.t: Search documentation that survives the viva
prompts.use: After you have run your searches, while every string, date and count is still in front of you.
prompts.why: Examiners and journal reviewers increasingly ask "how exactly did you search?". A documented search (strings, dates, hits, deduplication) turns your ROL from a narrative into a method, and saves you from redoing it months later.
prompts.p:
You are a systematic-review methodologist who reviews search reporting for journals and applies the PRISMA 2020 and PRISMA-S reporting standards.

MY CONTEXT:
Databases searched, with date of each search: [list]
Exact strings used: [PASTE STRINGS HERE]
Hits per database: [numbers]
Duplicates removed (and how): [number, tool]
Records screened, full texts assessed, studies included: [numbers]
Reasons for full-text exclusion with counts: [list]
Other sources (registries, citation chasing, experts): [list with counts]

TASK:
1. Write the search-methods paragraph for my thesis methodology chapter.
2. Produce a PRISMA 2020 flow diagram description with my numbers slotted in, box by box.
3. Check my numbers for internal consistency (screened minus excluded must equal full texts assessed, and so on) and flag any mismatch.
4. List the PRISMA-S items my documentation covers and the ones it is missing.
5. Draft a one-page search appendix table: database, platform, date, string, limits, hits.

RULES:
Use only the numbers I gave. Where a number is missing, write [MISSING — FILL IN] rather than estimating, because an inconsistent flow diagram is the first thing a reviewer checks. Keep my exact strings unchanged.

OUTPUT:
The methods paragraph (about 150 words), the flow-diagram box list, a consistency check table, the PRISMA-S gap list, and the appendix table.

TWEAK:
Finish with the two questions an examiner is most likely to ask about my search, and model answers based only on my documentation. Then tell me which single piece of documentation I should create today because it cannot be reconstructed later (for example, the original hit counts or the date of the first search).
tips: Draw the final flow diagram in PowerPoint or draw.io from the box list. Don't ask the AI to draw it.
Keep screenshots of each database's results page with the date visible.
Re-run the search just before submission and report the update date.

prompts.t: Search rescue: iterate until the results are right
prompts.use: When your search returns far too many, far too few, or irrelevant results, and you have already tried tweaking it.
prompts.why: Searching is iterative. Most residents give up after one bad result, or keep reading 4,000 irrelevant titles. This prompt makes the AI diagnose what went wrong and fix it one change at a time.
prompts.p:
You are an expert search consultant at a medical library who debugs failed searches daily. You change one thing at a time and explain the effect of each change.

MY CONTEXT:
My research question: [PICOT]
Database and current search string: [PASTE STRING HERE]
Hit count: [N]
What is wrong: [too many / too few / irrelevant results]
Five titles from the results that are irrelevant (if any): [PASTE TITLES]
Two or three papers I know should appear but do not: [titles or PMIDs]

TASK:
1. Diagnose the problem: which concept block, operator, field tag or truncation is causing it.
2. Propose a revised string with one change, and explain what the change should do to the hit count.
3. Ask me to run it and report back the new count and 5 sample titles.
4. Repeat for up to 4 rounds until the known papers appear and the irrelevant titles drop out.
5. Then give the final string with a one-line rationale for each block.

RULES:
Change one thing per round, because changing several at once makes it impossible to tell what worked. Do not invent MeSH terms; mark uncertain ones [CHECK IN MeSH BROWSER]. Wait for my results before the next round.

OUTPUT:
One round per turn: a short diagnosis, the revised string in a code block, the expected effect on the hit count and the known papers, and exactly what I should report back to you. Keep each round under 200 words so I can act on it quickly.

TWEAK:
At the end, summarise the search in 3 sentences suitable for my methods chapter.
tips: Known papers are the best test of a search. Keep 3 "must-find" papers handy.
Irrelevant titles tell you which synonym is too loose. Paste them rather than describing them.
If the tweaks never converge, your question is probably too broad. Go back to section 1.1.

prompts.t: MeSH terms and synonyms for one concept
prompts.use: When you are building a search and stuck on one concept.
prompts.p:
You are a medical librarian who knows the MeSH hierarchy well and teaches residents to search systematically.

MY CONTEXT:
The concept I need to search: [e.g. acute kidney injury]
My wider question for context: [one line]

TASK:
1. Give the most relevant MeSH heading(s), where each sits in the hierarchy, and whether to explode it.
2. List entry terms and free-text synonyms, including abbreviations, spelling variants (British / American) and outdated terms used in older papers.
3. Combine them into one PubMed block using [MeSH] and [tiab] tags with OR.

RULES:
Only give MeSH headings you are confident exist; mark others [CHECK IN MeSH BROWSER], because an invalid heading returns nothing without warning.

OUTPUT:
A short table (term, type, tag), then the combined block in a code block.
tips: Check the MeSH introduction year. Papers older than that are indexed under a different term.
prompts.try: Concept: ventilator-associated pneumonia.

prompts.t: PICO → concept blocks table
prompts.use: The first step of any search, straight after your question is fixed.
prompts.p:
You are a search-methods tutor who teaches residents to turn clinical questions into structured searches.

MY CONTEXT:
My PICOT question: [PASTE QUESTION]
Database I will start with: [PubMed / Embase / Google Scholar]

TASK:
1. Split the question into concept blocks and say which PICO elements to search and which to leave out (usually comparator and outcome), with the reason.
2. For each block, give controlled vocabulary and free-text terms.
3. Show how the blocks combine: OR within blocks, AND between blocks.
4. Suggest a validated study-design filter if one fits my question.

RULES:
Explain every exclusion decision in one line, because searching every PICO element is the most common reason searches miss relevant papers.

OUTPUT:
A concept-block table, then the combined string, then a one-paragraph explanation.
tips: Most good searches use 2 or 3 blocks, not 5.
prompts.try: In adults with community-acquired pneumonia, does procalcitonin-guided therapy reduce antibiotic duration compared with standard care?

prompts.t: Fix the syntax of my search string
prompts.use: When PubMed gives an error, a strange translation, or zero results.
prompts.p:
You are a meticulous search-syntax checker who spots misplaced brackets and wrong field tags at a glance.

MY CONTEXT:
My search string: [PASTE STRING HERE]
Database: [PubMed / Embase / Scopus / Google Scholar]
What PubMed shows under "Details" or "Search translation": [PASTE IF AVAILABLE]

TASK:
1. Check brackets, Boolean operators (upper case), field tags, quotation marks, truncation and proximity operators.
2. List every error with its correction.
3. Give the corrected string.
4. Explain how PubMed's automatic term mapping will treat any untagged terms.

RULES:
Keep my intended logic unless it is clearly wrong; if you change the logic, say so explicitly, because a silent change alters which papers I find.

OUTPUT:
An error table (error, why it matters, fix), then the corrected string in a code block.
tips: Always read PubMed's search translation. It shows what PubMed actually searched, not what you typed.
prompts.try: (asthma OR wheez*) AND inhaler adherence AND (child* OR paediatric

prompts.t: Too many or too few hits: fix my search
prompts.use: When your search returns thousands of results, or almost none.
prompts.p:
You are a search consultant who balances sensitivity and precision for postgraduate literature reviews.

MY CONTEXT:
Research question: [PICOT]
Current string: [PASTE STRING HERE]
Database and hit count: [PubMed, N]
Is this for a narrative ROL or a systematic review?: [narrative / systematic]

TASK:
1. Diagnose why the count is too high or too low.
2. Suggest 3 targeted changes (e.g. major-topic MeSH, title-only terms, removing a block, adding synonyms, a design filter), ranked by likely effect.
3. Give the revised string for the best option.
4. Say what relevant papers each change risks losing.

RULES:
For a systematic review, prefer sensitivity and never restrict by abstract availability or free full text, because those filters introduce bias.

OUTPUT:
Diagnosis in 2–3 lines, a ranked table of changes, then the revised string.
tips: For a thesis ROL, 150 to 800 well-targeted hits is a workable range.
prompts.try: "sepsis AND lactate" returning 9,000 PubMed results.

prompts.t: Translate my PubMed string for other databases
prompts.use: When your PubMed search is final and you need Embase, Scopus, Cochrane or Web of Science versions.
prompts.p:
You are a medical librarian fluent in the syntax of PubMed, Embase (Ovid and Elsevier), Scopus, Cochrane Library and Web of Science.

MY CONTEXT:
Final PubMed string: [PASTE STRING HERE]
Target databases and platforms: [e.g. Embase.com, Scopus, Cochrane Library]

TASK:
1. Translate the string for each target database, mapping MeSH to Emtree where relevant and converting field tags, truncation and proximity operators.
2. Note any concept that has no equivalent heading, and how you handled it.
3. List any syntax difference that could change the results.

RULES:
Mark any Emtree term you are unsure of as [CHECK IN EMTREE], because MeSH and Emtree headings often differ in name and scope.

OUTPUT:
One code block per database, with a short notes list under each.
tips: Scopus has no controlled vocabulary. Strengthen the free-text terms there.
prompts.try: PubMed string for "high-flow nasal oxygen in acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure".

prompts.t: Use PubMed filters without biasing the review
prompts.use: Before applying filters such as date, language, age group, species or article type.
prompts.p:
You are a systematic-review methodologist who warns residents about filters that silently exclude relevant evidence.

MY CONTEXT:
My question: [PICOT]
Filters I plan to use: [e.g. last 10 years, English, humans, adults, RCT only]
Purpose of my search: [thesis ROL / systematic review / quick clinical question]

TASK:
1. For each filter, explain what it actually does in PubMed, including how it treats recently added, not-yet-indexed records.
2. Say whether each is appropriate for my purpose, and the bias it could introduce.
3. Suggest safer alternatives (e.g. search-term blocks instead of the "Humans" filter).
4. Give my final string with the recommended filters applied.

RULES:
Be explicit about which filters depend on MeSH indexing, because the newest papers are not yet indexed and would be excluded.

OUTPUT:
A filter table (filter, what it does, keep or drop, reason), then the final string.
tips: Justify every filter in your methods section. Unexplained filters look like cherry-picking.
prompts.try: Filters: humans, English, last 5 years, free full text.

prompts.t: Find studies from Indian centres
prompts.use: When you need the Indian evidence for your introduction and ROL, beyond global studies.
prompts.p:
You are a research librarian at an Indian medical college who specialises in finding Indian and South Asian clinical studies.

MY CONTEXT:
Topic: [TOPIC]
Main PubMed string so far: [PASTE STRING HERE]

TASK:
1. Show how to add an India block using the [Affiliation] and [tiab] fields (India, Indian, state and major city names, major institutions).
2. Suggest regional and Indian sources to search beyond PubMed, including Indian journals and thesis repositories, and say what each is useful for.
3. Explain how to handle Indian journals that are not indexed in PubMed.
4. Give Google Scholar search tips for Indian studies.

RULES:
Name only sources you are confident exist and are currently accessible; mark uncertain ones [VERIFY ACCESS], because Indian indexing services change often.

OUTPUT:
The India block in a code block, then a source table (source, what it covers, access), then 4 tips.
tips: Affiliation searches miss studies whose authors list only the city. Add major city names as free text.
prompts.try: Topic: scrub typhus in children.

prompts.t: Grey literature and trial-registry search plan
prompts.use: For any systematic review, and for a thesis ROL where unpublished or ongoing work may matter.
prompts.p:
You are an evidence-synthesis specialist who knows that missing grey literature leads to publication bias.

MY CONTEXT:
Topic and question: [PICOT]
Type of review: [thesis ROL / systematic review / scoping review]

TASK:
1. List the grey-literature sources to search: trial registries (CTRI, ClinicalTrials.gov, WHO ICTRP), preprint servers, conference abstracts, theses repositories (including Indian ones), and government or WHO reports.
2. For each, give a simple search approach and what to record.
3. Explain how to handle registry entries with no published results.
4. Give a documentation table template.

RULES:
Keep the list relevant to my topic and field, not generic. Mark any source whose current search interface you are unsure of as [CHECK SITE], because registries change their search tools.

OUTPUT:
A source table, then the handling notes, then the documentation template.
tips: A trial registered in CTRI years ago with no publication is itself a finding. Note it in your discussion.
prompts.try: Systematic review of yoga interventions for hypertension in Indian adults.

prompts.t: Backward and forward citation chasing plan
prompts.use: After screening, when you have 3–10 key included papers.
prompts.p:
You are a systematic reviewer who uses citation chasing to find the studies that keyword searches miss.

MY CONTEXT:
My key papers (title, year, DOI or PMID): [PASTE LIST HERE]
Tools I can use: [Google Scholar / Scopus / Web of Science / PubMed "cited by" / Semantic Scholar]

TASK:
1. Explain backward chasing (the reference lists) and forward chasing (papers that cite these), and when each adds most.
2. Give step-by-step instructions for each tool I can use.
3. Suggest screening rules to keep chasing manageable.
4. Give a log template to record what each round found.

RULES:
Do not list papers that cite mine from memory; tell me how to retrieve them, because any list you produce without live search may be fabricated.

OUTPUT:
A numbered method, tool-specific steps, and a log table.
tips: Forward chasing from a landmark paper is the fastest way to find the newest work on your topic.
prompts.try: Key paper: a well-known RCT on corticosteroids in severe community-acquired pneumonia.

prompts.t: Map the research landscape in Perplexity
prompts.use: At the very start of a new topic, in Perplexity with Academic mode switched on.
prompts.p:
You are a research-landscape analyst who summarises a field in minutes using cited, current sources.

MY CONTEXT:
Topic: [TOPIC]
Population and setting of interest: [e.g. Indian adults in tertiary care]
Time window: [e.g. last 5 years]

TASK:
1. Summarise what is well established, with citations.
2. Summarise what is contested or uncertain, and why.
3. Summarise what is unstudied or under-studied in my population and setting.
4. List the 5 most important recent studies or reviews, with year and journal, and a clickable source.
5. Suggest 5 search terms I should use in PubMed next.

RULES:
Cite a source for every claim. If you cannot find a source for a statement, leave the statement out, because I will verify every citation before using it.

OUTPUT:
Headed sections with short bullets and numbered citations.
tips: Follow up with: "What has NOT been studied in Indian patients specifically?" It surfaces the most useful gaps.
prompts.try: Topic: long-term outcomes after dengue shock syndrome.

prompts.t: Find the systematic reviews before anything else
prompts.use: At the start of any ROL or research question, to avoid reinventing existing syntheses.
prompts.p:
You are an evidence-based medicine tutor who always starts with the highest level of existing evidence.

MY CONTEXT:
My question: [PICOT]
My main search string: [PASTE STRING HERE]

TASK:
1. Show how to find systematic reviews and meta-analyses: the PubMed systematic-review filter, the Cochrane Library, and PROSPERO for registered reviews in progress.
2. Give the modified strings for each.
3. Explain how to judge whether an existing review already answers my question (scope, date, quality, population).
4. Tell me what to do if a recent high-quality review exists: update it, narrow the angle, or change the question.

RULES:
Do not name specific reviews from memory; show me how to retrieve them, because an invented review would mislead my whole plan.

OUTPUT:
Numbered steps, the strings in code blocks, and a short decision guide.
tips: A registered PROSPERO review on your exact question means someone is already doing it. Check before you start.
prompts.try: Question: effect of early tracheostomy on mortality in mechanically ventilated adults.

prompts.t: Identify the landmark papers in my field
prompts.use: When you need the must-cite trials and studies for your introduction, ROL or seminar.
prompts.p:
You are a senior academic who knows how to identify landmark literature systematically rather than by memory.

MY CONTEXT:
Topic: [TOPIC]
Current guidelines I can access: [name them or "none yet"]

TASK:
1. Explain 4 reliable ways to identify landmark papers: guideline reference lists, highly cited papers in Scopus or Google Scholar, reviews' "key studies" sections, and editorials.
2. Give the search steps for each.
3. Suggest a table for recording each landmark paper: design, population, intervention, key finding, why it changed practice.
4. List candidate landmark studies you believe are relevant, each marked [VERIFY PMID].

RULES:
Every paper you name must carry the [VERIFY PMID] tag, because trial names and years are frequently misremembered by AI. Name fewer papers rather than guessing.

OUTPUT:
The 4 methods as a numbered list, the recording table, then the candidate list.
tips: If a paper appears in the reference list of every major guideline, it is a landmark.
prompts.try: Topic: fluid resuscitation in septic shock.

prompts.t: Set up alerts so new papers find you
prompts.use: Once your search is final, so you do not miss papers published during your thesis.
prompts.p:
You are a research productivity coach who sets up literature alerts for busy clinicians.

MY CONTEXT:
Final search string: [PASTE STRING HERE]
Tools I use: [PubMed with My NCBI / Google Scholar / journal alerts / RSS]
How often I want updates: [weekly / monthly]

TASK:
1. Give step-by-step instructions to save the search and create an email alert in each tool I use.
2. Suggest a tighter version of the string so alerts are not flooded.
3. Suggest 5 key journals in my field for table-of-contents alerts.
4. Describe a 15-minute monthly routine to process alerts into my reference manager.

RULES:
Keep instructions tool-specific. Where an interface may have changed, say [CHECK CURRENT MENU], because step-by-step menus go out of date.

OUTPUT:
Numbered steps per tool, the alert string, the journal list, and the monthly routine.
tips: Re-run your full search before submission anyway. Alerts can miss papers indexed late.
prompts.try: Search on "prone positioning in non-intubated COVID-19" with weekly PubMed alerts.

prompts.t: Reference manager set-up and deduplication
prompts.use: Before you import your first search results.
prompts.p:
You are a research-skills trainer who has set up Zotero and Mendeley for hundreds of thesis students.

MY CONTEXT:
Reference manager: [Zotero / Mendeley / EndNote]
Word processor: [MS Word / Google Docs]
Citation style required by my university: [e.g. Vancouver]
Expected number of records: [N]

TASK:
1. Give set-up steps: install, browser connector, word-processor plug-in, and the citation style.
2. Explain how to import results from PubMed and other databases.
3. Give a deduplication workflow, including records the tool will miss.
4. Suggest a folder or tag structure for screening (to screen, included, excluded with reason).
5. List the 5 mistakes that corrupt thesis references, and how to avoid each.

RULES:
Keep steps specific to my tool. Where menus may have changed, write [CHECK CURRENT VERSION], because outdated steps waste hours.

OUTPUT:
Numbered sections, each with short steps.
tips: Never type a reference by hand into your thesis. Insert every citation through the plug-in.
prompts.try: Zotero with MS Word, Vancouver style, about 600 records.

prompts.t: Write the search-methods paragraph
prompts.use: When writing the methodology or ROL chapter, after your search is complete.
prompts.p:
You are an academic editor who writes concise, reproducible search-methods sections for theses and journals.

MY CONTEXT:
Databases and platforms: [list]
Dates of search: [dates]
Search terms and full strings: [PASTE HERE]
Limits applied and why: [list]
Additional sources: [registries, reference lists, experts]
Screening process: [who screened, how disagreements were resolved]

TASK:
1. Write a 120–180 word search-methods paragraph in past tense.
2. Write a one-line pointer to the appendix containing the full strings.
3. List anything a reviewer would say is missing.

RULES:
Use only the details I gave. Where something standard is missing (e.g. the date of the last search), insert [ADD DETAIL] instead of inventing it, because search methods must be exactly reproducible.

OUTPUT:
The paragraph, the pointer line, and a short missing-items list.
tips: Name the platform as well as the database, e.g. "Embase via Ovid". The results differ.
prompts.try: PubMed and Cochrane searched 10 March 2026, English only, two reviewers screening independently.

prompts.t: Legal ways to get the full text of a paper
prompts.use: When a key paper is behind a paywall.
prompts.p:
You are a medical college librarian who helps students and residents access literature legally.

MY CONTEXT:
Paper details: [title, journal, year, DOI]
My institution's access, if known: [e.g. institutional subscription, national consortium, none]

TASK:
1. List the legal routes in order of speed: institutional access and library, national or consortium access schemes in India, open-access versions (PubMed Central, Unpaywall, author repositories), interlibrary loan, and contacting the author.
2. For each, give the steps.
3. Draft a short, polite email to the corresponding author requesting the PDF for thesis use.

RULES:
Recommend only legal routes. Mark any national scheme whose current coverage you are unsure of as [CHECK WITH LIBRARY], because access programmes change.

OUTPUT:
A numbered list of routes with steps, then the email (under 100 words).
tips: Authors almost always reply. Most are happy to share their paper with a student.
prompts.try: A 2024 RCT in a paywalled critical-care journal.

prompts.t: Peer review my search strategy (PRESS checklist)
prompts.use: Before you run the final search for a systematic review or a thesis ROL your examiners will scrutinise.
prompts.p:
You are an information specialist who peer reviews search strategies using the PRESS (Peer Review of Electronic Search Strategies) checklist.

MY CONTEXT:
My research question: [PICOT]
My full search string and database: [PASTE STRING HERE]
Limits applied: [list]

TASK:
1. Review the strategy against the PRESS elements: translation of the question, Boolean and proximity operators, subject headings, text-word searching (spelling, synonyms, truncation), spelling and syntax, and limits and filters.
2. For each element, rate it as no revision, revision suggested, or revision required, with a reason.
3. Give the revised string with all required changes applied.

RULES:
Explain every required change in one line, because I must be able to justify the final strategy myself. Do not add concepts that are not in my question.

OUTPUT:
A PRESS review table, then the revised string in a code block.
tips: Ask a colleague or librarian to run the same review. Two reviews catch more errors than one.
prompts.try: A PubMed search on anticoagulation in cancer-associated venous thromboembolism.

prompts.t: Boolean operators explained with my topic
prompts.p: Act as a medical librarian teaching a first-time searcher. Explain AND, OR, NOT, brackets, quotation marks and truncation in under 150 words, using my topic [TOPIC] for every example. End with one complete example search string built from my topic.
prompts.try: Topic: iron-deficiency anaemia in adolescent girls.

prompts.t: Every synonym for my concept
prompts.p: Act as a medical terminology expert. For the concept [CONCEPT], list all synonyms, abbreviations, British and American spellings, older terms and common misspellings used in paper titles and abstracts. Group them in a table and mark the 5 most important for a search.
prompts.try: Concept: chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

prompts.t: Explode, major topic, subheadings: explained
prompts.p: Act as a PubMed trainer. Using the MeSH term [MeSH TERM], explain in plain language what "explode", "major topic" and subheadings do, and when each helps or hurts a search. Give one example string for each. Keep it under 150 words.
prompts.try: MeSH term: Diabetes Mellitus.

prompts.t: Adapt my search for Google Scholar
prompts.p: Act as a search specialist. Rewrite my PubMed string [PASTE STRING] for Google Scholar, which has no MeSH and limited Boolean support. Give the adapted query, explain the 3 main limitations of Google Scholar for a thesis search, and say how to use it as a supplementary source.
prompts.try: A PubMed string on tuberculosis preventive therapy in household contacts.

prompts.t: Which databases for my specialty?
prompts.p: Act as a medical librarian. For a thesis in [SPECIALTY] on [TOPIC], tell me which databases to search (core and supplementary), what each adds, and which I can reasonably skip. Present it as a table and mark anything with uncertain access as [CHECK ACCESS].
prompts.try: Specialty: Psychiatry. Topic: depression in caregivers of dialysis patients.

prompts.t: Email an author for their paper or data
prompts.p: Act as an academic communication coach. Write a short, polite email to [AUTHOR NAME], author of [PAPER TITLE], asking for [the full text / clarification of a method / supplementary data] for my MD thesis on [TOPIC]. Keep it under 100 words, with a clear subject line.
prompts.try: Asking for the supplementary table of a cohort study on sepsis biomarkers.

prompts.t: Has this paper been retracted or corrected?
prompts.p: Act as a research-integrity officer. Tell me step by step how to check whether a paper [TITLE / DOI] has been retracted, corrected or flagged, using the journal page, PubMed and the Retraction Watch database. Explain how to cite or handle it if it has.
prompts.try: A 2020 COVID-19 treatment paper you plan to cite.

prompts.t: Where does this study sit in the evidence hierarchy?
prompts.p: Act as an evidence-based medicine tutor. For the study I describe, [PASTE ABSTRACT], identify the design, its level in the evidence hierarchy, the 2 biggest threats to validity, and how much weight it should carry in my review. Answer in 5 bullet points.
prompts.try: A single-centre retrospective study of 60 patients on a new antifibrotic.

prompts.t: Turn my question into Perplexity and Consensus queries
prompts.p: Act as an AI research-tools trainer for doctors. Convert my PICOT question [PASTE QUESTION] into 3 Perplexity Academic queries (broad, focused, India-specific) and 3 Consensus yes/no questions. Explain in one line what I should look for in each tool's results, and how to verify its citations.
prompts.try: Does pulmonary rehabilitation reduce readmissions in COPD patients in India?

prompts.t: How far back should my search go?
prompts.p: Act as a systematic-review methodologist. For my topic [TOPIC], help me choose a search date range. Consider when key definitions, diagnostic criteria, guidelines or treatments changed. Give a recommended start year, the reason, and one sentence I can use to justify it in my methods.
prompts.try: Topic: sepsis outcomes (definitions changed in 2016).

prompts.t: The four-movement thesis introduction
prompts.use: After your topic and protocol are approved, when you begin writing the thesis itself.
prompts.why: Examiners read the introduction to see whether you understand why your question matters. A four-movement structure (global burden, Indian burden, what is known and unknown, the gap and objective) does that in about 500 words, without a single invented statistic.
prompts.p:
You are a senior academic and thesis examiner in [YOUR SPECIALTY] who has supervised and marked postgraduate dissertations for over 20 years. You are strict about two things: introductions that read like textbook chapters, and burden figures quoted without a source. You write in formal scientific register.

MY CONTEXT:
Specialty: [e.g. Respiratory Medicine]
Exact thesis title: [paste]
Study design: [cross-sectional / case-control / cohort / diagnostic accuracy / interventional]
Setting: [hospital, unit, catchment; tertiary / district / private]
Population: [who exactly]
Primary objective: [one line]
The gap in one sentence, in my own words: [what is not yet answered]
Sources I can cite for burden data: [ICMR / NFHS / NCDIR / WHO / Global Burden of Disease / national programme reports / none yet]

TASK:
Write a structured introduction of 450–550 words in four movements, each flowing into the next, without sub-headings:
1. Global burden: the scale and clinical importance of the condition.
2. Indian or regional burden: narrow to India or South Asia, point to where national data exists, and state plainly where good Indian data is missing.
3. What is known and what is not: summarise what the literature broadly shows, then state precisely what remains unanswered.
4. The gap and the objective: close on an explicit statement of the gap this study addresses and one clean sentence stating the objective.

RULES:
Leave every epidemiological figure as a slot: [CITE] for the source and [VERIFY — INSERT SOURCED FIGURE] for any number I have not supplied, because invented prevalence figures are the most common reason introductions are sent back. Describe the evidence generically unless I supply papers. Frame the question; do not write a literature review. Use associational language unless my design supports causation.

OUTPUT:
The 4-paragraph draft within the word limit, then a numbered checklist of every sentence containing a factual claim I must source before submission.

TWEAK:
Finish with the one paragraph an examiner is most likely to call "textbook", and a tighter rewrite of it.
tips: Write your own rough three-movement draft first, then use intro-refine-draft to polish the language only.
Take the sourcing checklist to PubMed and your national data portals before you start the ROL.
Rewrite the final draft in your own voice. A sudden jump to flawless academic English is a red flag to a guide who knows how you write.

prompts.t: Refine my own introduction draft (language only)
prompts.use: After you have written a rough introduction yourself. This is the golden rule: draft first, AI refines.
prompts.why: Your guide and examiners want your thinking, not the model's. Refining your own draft keeps the ideas, the sources and the voice yours, while fixing structure, flow and academic register, and it keeps you on the right side of your university's AI policy.
prompts.p:
You are an academic writing editor for medical theses. You improve clarity, structure and register while strictly preserving the author's content, claims and citations. You never add facts.

MY CONTEXT:
My thesis title: [paste]
Programme and university: [e.g. MD Pathology, state health university]
Target length: [e.g. 400–500 words]
Citation style: [Vancouver / other]
My rough draft, with citations as I have them: [PASTE DRAFT HERE]

TASK:
1. Check the structure against the four movements (background, Indian burden, what is known and unknown, the gap and objective), and tell me which movement is weak or missing.
2. Refine the language paragraph by paragraph: formal academic register, clear topic sentences, smooth transitions, consistent tense.
3. Keep every citation attached to the claim it supports.
4. Mark each place where a claim has no citation with [CITE].
5. Show a list of the substantive changes you made, so I can accept or reject each one individually.

RULES:
Do not add any new fact, statistic, study or reference; improve language and structure only, because anything new would be unsourced and not mine. Keep my meaning exactly, and always flag rather than fix any sentence whose meaning is unclear by writing [UNCLEAR — PLEASE CLARIFY]. Stay within the target length.

OUTPUT:
