Base the parametric versus non-parametric choice on the variable's distribution and sample size, not on a normality test alone, because normality tests are unreliable in small and very large samples.

OUTPUT:
A decision table (objective, outcome type, groups, test, alternative, effect measure, assumptions).
tips: Paste this table into your analysis plan and quote it in your viva when asked "why this test?".
prompts.try: Objectives comparing CRP (skewed) between 3 groups and mortality (yes/no) between 2 groups.

prompts.t: Is my data normally distributed? Decide sensibly
prompts.use: Before choosing between parametric and non-parametric methods.
prompts.p:
You are a biostatistician who teaches sensible distribution checks rather than blind reliance on normality tests.

MY CONTEXT:
Variable and what it measures: [brief]
Sample size per group: [n]
Summary statistics (mean, SD, median, IQR, min, max): [paste]
Histogram or Q-Q plot description, or the Shapiro-Wilk result: [paste]

TASK:
1. Assess the distribution from the summaries (e.g. SD large relative to the mean for a positive-only variable suggests skew) and the plot.
2. Explain what the normality test does and does not tell me at my sample size.
3. Recommend how to summarise the variable (mean ± SD or median with IQR) and which test family to use.
4. Mention transformation (e.g. log) as an option, with its trade-offs.

RULES:
Combine clinical knowledge of the variable with the data, because a normality test alone is underpowered in small samples and oversensitive in large ones.

OUTPUT:
The assessment, the explanation, the recommendation, then the transformation note.
tips: Hospital-stay length, CRP and most lab counts are usually skewed. Expect medians.
prompts.try: ICU length of stay: mean 6.2, SD 5.8, median 4, IQR 3–8, n = 90.

prompts.t: Choose and report the right non-parametric test
prompts.use: When your data is skewed or ordinal and parametric tests don't fit.
prompts.p:
You are a biostatistician who explains non-parametric methods in plain language.

MY CONTEXT:
Outcome and its type: [skewed continuous / ordinal]
Groups and whether independent or paired: [brief]
Sample sizes: [n per group]

TASK:
1. Name the right test (Mann-Whitney U, Wilcoxon signed-rank, Kruskal-Wallis, Friedman) and why.
2. Explain what it actually tests in plain language.
3. Tell me which summary and effect measure to report (median, IQR, Hodges-Lehmann estimate or rank-biserial correlation).
4. Give the post-hoc approach if there are more than 2 groups.
5. Show the reporting sentence template.

RULES:
Avoid saying the test compares medians unless the distributions have similar shapes, because that is a common reporting error.

OUTPUT:
The test choice, explanation, reporting guidance, then the template.
tips: Report the median and IQR per group alongside the p value. A p value alone tells readers nothing about the size of the difference.
prompts.try: Pain scores (0–10) compared among three anaesthesia techniques.

prompts.t: Chi-square, Fisher's exact or something else?
prompts.use: When comparing proportions or categorical variables between groups.
prompts.p:
You are a biostatistics tutor who explains categorical-data tests precisely.

MY CONTEXT:
Variables and categories: [brief]
Table layout and cell counts (paste the cross-table if you have it): [PASTE TABLE]
Are the groups independent or paired?: [brief]

TASK:
1. Decide between chi-square, chi-square with continuity correction, Fisher's exact, chi-square for trend and McNemar, based on my table and design.
2. Explain the expected-count rule and check it on my table.
3. Name the effect measure to report (risk difference, relative risk or odds ratio with 95% CI).
4. Show the reporting sentence template.

RULES:
Base the expected-count check on expected, not observed, counts, because that distinction is commonly confused.

OUTPUT:
The decision, the expected-count check, the effect measure, then the template.
tips: For ordered categories (mild, moderate, severe), a trend test uses the order and has more power.
prompts.try: A 2 × 2 table of smoking status by post-operative pneumonia with one cell containing 3.

prompts.t: Before-after or matched data: paired analysis
prompts.use: When the same patients are measured twice, or cases are matched to controls.
prompts.p:
You are a biostatistician who catches residents analysing paired data as independent groups.

MY CONTEXT:
What is measured and when: [brief]
Outcome type: [continuous / binary / ordinal]
Sample size: [n pairs]

TASK:
1. Confirm whether the data is truly paired, and why that matters.
2. Name the test: paired t-test, Wilcoxon signed-rank or McNemar.
3. Name the effect measure: mean difference with 95% CI, median difference, or discordant-pair odds ratio.
4. Explain the assumption checks (e.g. distribution of the differences).
5. Show the reporting sentence template.

RULES:
Check the distribution of the differences, not of each time point separately, because that is the assumption the paired t-test actually makes.

OUTPUT:
Numbered answers, then the template.
tips: Paired designs need fewer patients. Say so when justifying your sample size.
prompts.try: HbA1c before and after 3 months of a lifestyle intervention in 60 patients.

prompts.t: Outcomes measured three or more times
prompts.use: When the same patients have an outcome measured at several time points.
prompts.p:
You are a biostatistician who teaches repeated-measures analysis without unnecessary complexity.

MY CONTEXT:
Outcome and time points: [brief]
Groups (if comparing): [brief]
Sample size and missing follow-ups: [brief]
Software: [SPSS / R / Jamovi]

TASK:
1. Explain why running separate t-tests at each time point is wrong.
2. Compare repeated-measures ANOVA, a linear mixed model and the Friedman test for my data.
3. Recommend one, with its assumptions and how it handles missing time points.
4. Give the software steps or syntax.
5. Show how to present the results (a line graph with error bars, and a table).

RULES:
Recommend a mixed model if follow-ups are missing, and explain why, because repeated-measures ANOVA drops every patient with any missing time point.

OUTPUT:
The explanation, the comparison, the recommendation, the steps, then the presentation guide.
tips: A clear line graph of means over time with 95% CIs often explains your result better than any p value.
prompts.try: SOFA score at day 1, 3 and 7 in two sepsis treatment groups.

prompts.t: Correlation or agreement? Methods comparison done right
prompts.use: When comparing two methods of measuring the same thing, or relating two variables.
prompts.p:
You are a measurement statistician who explains why correlation is not agreement.

MY CONTEXT:
The two measurements and what they measure: [brief]
Purpose: [do they agree? / are they related?]
Sample size: [n]

TASK:
1. Tell me whether my question is about association (correlation) or agreement (interchangeability).
2. For association: choose Pearson or Spearman and explain why.
3. For agreement: explain the Bland-Altman analysis (bias, limits of agreement) and ICC, and when to use each.
4. Define in advance what limits of agreement would be clinically acceptable.
5. Show how to report the result.

RULES:
Do not use correlation to claim agreement, because two methods can correlate perfectly and still disagree systematically.

OUTPUT:
The diagnosis of my question, the method, then the reporting template.
tips: Decide the clinically acceptable limits of agreement before looking at your data.
prompts.try: Comparing a pulse oximeter with arterial blood gas SaO2 in ICU patients.

prompts.t: ROC curve, AUC and the best cut-off
prompts.use: When your study evaluates a continuous marker or score for diagnosis or prognosis.
prompts.p:
You are a diagnostic statistician who explains ROC analysis honestly, including its limits.

MY CONTEXT:
Marker or score: [brief]
Outcome (reference standard): [brief]
Sample size and number with the outcome: [brief]
Software: [SPSS / MedCalc / R / Jamovi]

TASK:
1. Explain what the ROC curve and AUC represent in plain language.
2. Give the steps to run the analysis in my software.
3. Explain how to choose a cut-off (Youden index versus clinically chosen sensitivity), and report sensitivity, specificity, predictive values and likelihood ratios at it.
4. Warn about optimism when the cut-off is derived and tested in the same data.
5. Show the reporting template.

RULES:
Report the AUC with its 95% CI, and call a data-derived cut-off exploratory unless it is validated, because optimistic cut-offs are a common reviewer criticism.

OUTPUT:
Explanation, steps, cut-off guidance, then the template.
tips: Compare your marker's AUC with an existing score's AUC in the same patients. It makes the result meaningful.
prompts.try: Serum lactate for predicting 28-day mortality in sepsis.

prompts.t: Time-to-event analysis: Kaplan-Meier and Cox
prompts.use: When your outcome is time until an event (death, relapse, readmission) and follow-up varies.
prompts.p:
You are a biostatistician who teaches survival analysis to clinicians clearly.

MY CONTEXT:
Event and time origin: [brief]
Follow-up duration and how censoring occurs: [brief]
Groups and covariates: [brief]
Number of events: [n]
Software: [SPSS / R / Stata]

TASK:
1. Define time zero, the event and censoring for my study.
2. Explain Kaplan-Meier curves and the log-rank test for group comparison.
3. Explain the Cox model, the hazard ratio, and the proportional-hazards check.
4. Say how many covariates my events can support.
5. Give software steps and a reporting template (median survival, HR with 95% CI, number at risk under the curve).

RULES:
Warn me if informative censoring is likely (e.g. sicker patients lost to follow-up), because it biases survival estimates.

OUTPUT:
Definitions, methods, the covariate limit, steps, then the template.
tips: Always show the number at risk beneath your Kaplan-Meier plot. Reviewers expect it.
prompts.try: Time to first exacerbation after discharge in COPD, comparing two inhaler regimens.

prompts.t: Handle missing data honestly
prompts.use: At the analysis-planning stage, and again when your dataset is complete.
prompts.p:
You are a biostatistician who treats missing data as a bias problem, not a nuisance.

MY CONTEXT:
Variables with missing values and the percentage missing: [PASTE TABLE]
Why values are missing, as far as I know: [brief]
Sample size: [N]

TASK:
1. Classify the likely mechanism for each variable (MCAR, MAR or MNAR) in plain language.
2. Recommend an approach for each: complete-case analysis, multiple imputation or sensitivity analysis.
3. Explain what to report in the thesis (amount missing, pattern, handling).
4. Warn against single mean imputation and last observation carried forward.
5. Give software steps if imputation is needed.

RULES:
Recommend reporting missingness transparently even when it is small, because silent exclusion is an examiner favourite.

OUTPUT:
A variable table (variable, % missing, likely mechanism, approach), then the reporting guidance and steps.
tips: Compare the characteristics of patients with and without missing outcomes. It is a simple, powerful sensitivity check.
prompts.try: 12% missing 30-day outcomes, 8% missing baseline albumin in a 200-patient cohort.

prompts.t: Data-cleaning checklist before analysis
prompts.use: After data entry is complete, before any analysis.
prompts.p:
You are a clinical data manager who has cleaned hundreds of thesis datasets.

MY CONTEXT:
Dataset description (variables, types, N): [brief or PASTE CODEBOOK]
Software: [Excel / SPSS / R]

TASK:
1. Give a step-by-step checklist: duplicates, IDs, ranges, impossible values, date logic (discharge after admission), unit consistency, coding consistency and missing-value codes.
2. For each step, give the formula or software method.
3. Describe how to log each correction with its source document.
4. Describe how to lock the final dataset.

RULES:
Tell me never to overwrite the raw data file, and to correct only against the source document, because undocumented corrections are indistinguishable from data manipulation.

OUTPUT:
A numbered checklist with methods, then a correction-log template.
tips: Frequency tables of every categorical variable catch half of all coding errors in five minutes.
prompts.try: 180-row Excel sheet of ICU patients with vitals, labs and outcomes.

prompts.t: Step-by-step SPSS instructions for my analysis
prompts.use: When you run the analysis yourself in SPSS.
prompts.p:
You are an SPSS trainer who gives exact menu paths and explains which output to read.

MY CONTEXT:
SPSS version: [e.g. 26 / 29]
Analysis needed: [e.g. independent t-test of BMI by group, chi-square of mortality by group]
Variable names in my file: [list]

TASK:
1. Give the exact menu path for each analysis (Analyze → …).
2. Say which boxes to tick and options to select (including effect sizes and CIs).
3. Explain which output tables to read and which rows or columns matter.
4. Give the equivalent syntax so I can save and re-run it.

RULES:
Mark any menu item that may differ by version as [MAY DIFFER BY VERSION], because SPSS menus change between releases.

OUTPUT:
Numbered steps per analysis, then the syntax block, then an output-reading guide.
tips: Always paste the syntax into a syntax file. It is your record of exactly what you ran.
prompts.try: Mann-Whitney U test of hospital stay by diabetes status, SPSS 27.

prompts.t: R code for my thesis analysis
prompts.use: When you want free, reproducible analysis in R or RStudio.
prompts.p:
You are an R programmer and biostatistician who writes clean, commented code for clinical researchers.

MY CONTEXT:
Data file and format: [e.g. thesis.csv]
Variable names and types: [list]
Analyses needed: [list]
My R experience: [none / basic / comfortable]

TASK:
1. Write a complete, commented script: load packages, import data, check structure, Table 1, primary analysis, secondary analyses, and figures.
2. Use widely used packages (e.g. tidyverse, gtsummary) and explain why.
3. Include assumption checks.
4. Explain how to run it step by step for my experience level.

RULES:
Use my exact variable names and don't recode anything without a comment explaining it, because hidden recoding changes results.

OUTPUT:
One code block with section comments, then running instructions.
tips: Run the script on a copy of the data first. Keep the raw file untouched.
prompts.try: CSV with age, sex, group, CRP, and a binary outcome "death28".

prompts.t: Free point-and-click analysis in Jamovi
prompts.use: When you don't have an SPSS licence and want a free, simple tool.
prompts.p:
You are a statistics trainer who teaches Jamovi to clinicians.

MY CONTEXT:
Analyses needed: [list]
Variable names and types: [list]

TASK:
1. Explain how to import my data and set the measure type (nominal, ordinal, continuous) for each variable.
2. Give the exact steps for each analysis, including effect sizes and assumption checks.
3. Explain how to export tables and plots for my thesis.
4. Tell me how to cite Jamovi and its R packages in my methods.

RULES:
Mark any menu wording that may have changed as [CHECK CURRENT VERSION], because the interface is updated regularly.

OUTPUT:
Numbered steps per analysis, then the export and citation notes.
tips: Setting the measure type correctly is the step most beginners skip. It decides which tests Jamovi offers.
prompts.try: Independent t-test, chi-square, and a Pearson correlation.

prompts.t: Effect sizes and confidence intervals for every result
prompts.use: When planning or writing results, so you report more than p values.
prompts.p:
You are a biostatistician who insists that every comparison is reported with an effect size and CI.

MY CONTEXT:
My comparisons, each with outcome type and design: [list]

TASK:
1. For each comparison, name the right effect measure (mean difference, risk difference, relative risk, odds ratio, hazard ratio, correlation, AUC).
2. Explain what each means clinically in one line.
3. Explain how to obtain its 95% CI in my software.
4. Show a reporting sentence for each.

RULES:
Choose relative risk over odds ratio where the design allows and the outcome is common, and explain why, because odds ratios exaggerate effects when outcomes are common.

OUTPUT:
A table (comparison, effect measure, clinical meaning, CI method), then the sentences.
tips: A CI crossing the line of no effect but including large effects means "inconclusive", not "no effect".
prompts.try: Comparisons of mortality (binary), ICU stay (skewed) and SOFA change (continuous) between two groups.

prompts.t: Multiple comparisons: correct or not?
prompts.use: When you test many outcomes, subgroups or time points.
prompts.p:
You are a biostatistician who explains multiplicity pragmatically.

MY CONTEXT:
Number and type of tests planned: [brief]
Primary versus secondary outcomes: [brief]
Sample size: [N]

TASK:
1. Explain the multiplicity problem using my number of tests.
2. Recommend whether to correct (Bonferroni, Holm, false discovery rate) or to pre-specify and label outcomes as secondary or exploratory.
3. Explain the trade-off (power versus false positives).
4. Write a methods sentence describing my approach.

RULES:
Keep the primary outcome uncorrected if there is only one, and say so, because over-correcting a single primary outcome is a common error.

OUTPUT:
The explanation, the recommendation, the trade-off, then the sentence.
tips: Pre-specifying one primary outcome is the simplest multiplicity strategy there is.
prompts.try: 12 lab parameters compared between 3 groups.

prompts.t: Subgroup and sensitivity analyses that hold up
prompts.use: When planning extra analyses beyond the primary one.
prompts.p:
You are a trial statistician who is sceptical of subgroup claims.

MY CONTEXT:
Primary analysis: [brief]
Subgroups I am interested in: [list]
Assumptions I am unsure about (missing data, outliers, definitions): [list]

TASK:
1. Recommend which subgroups to pre-specify, with a biological rationale.
2. Explain why subgroup analyses should use an interaction test rather than separate p values.
3. Design 2–3 sensitivity analyses that test my key assumptions.
4. Explain how to label and report them.

RULES:
Label all subgroup results exploratory unless the study was powered for them, because spurious subgroup findings are among the commonest misleading results in medicine.

OUTPUT:
A subgroup table (subgroup, rationale, method), a sensitivity-analysis list, then reporting guidance.
tips: A forest plot of subgroup estimates with CIs shows readers how consistent your result is.
prompts.try: Primary: effect of early antibiotics on mortality; subgroups: age, diabetes, source of infection.

prompts.t: Report p values and CIs the way journals want
prompts.use: When writing results, tables and abstracts.
prompts.p:
You are a statistical editor for a medical journal who corrects p-value reporting daily.

MY CONTEXT:
My results as I have written them: [PASTE RESULTS TEXT OR TABLE]
Target: [thesis / journal name]

TASK:
1. Check each reported result for: exact p values (not "NS" or "p < 0.05" when an exact value is available), the correct number of decimals, CIs alongside estimates, and correct presentation of very small p values (e.g. p < 0.001).
2. Check wording: "significant" qualified as statistical, no "trend towards significance", and no "p = 0.000".
3. Return the corrected text.

RULES:
Change formatting and wording only; never change a number, because the numbers must match the software output exactly.

OUTPUT:
An issue table (original, problem, corrected), then the corrected text.
tips: Report the effect estimate first and the p value last: "RR 0.72 (95% CI 0.55–0.94; p = 0.02)".
prompts.try: "Mortality was significantly lower (p = 0.000) and there was a trend towards shorter stay (p = 0.07)."

prompts.t: Quick analysis inside Google Sheets with AI add-ons
prompts.use: For quick descriptive statistics and simple tests while your data is still in Google Sheets or Excel.
prompts.p:
You are a practical data coach who uses Gemini in Sheets, ChatGPT for Sheets and similar add-ons, and who knows their limits.

MY CONTEXT:
Sheet structure (columns and types): [brief]
Analyses I need: [e.g. descriptives by group, a chi-square test, a correlation]
Tool: [Gemini in Sheets / ChatGPT for Sheets / Julius AI]

TASK:
1. Write the exact prompts to type into the tool's side panel for each analysis, e.g. "Compare mean systolic BP between the intervention and control columns. Check normality first, tell me which test is appropriate, then run it and report the exact p value."
2. Explain how to check each result by hand or with a spreadsheet formula.
3. List the analyses I should move to proper statistical software instead.

RULES:
Tell me to verify every key number in a second tool before it goes into my thesis, because AI add-ons can produce realistic but wrong statistics.

OUTPUT:
A prompt list per analysis, verification methods, then the "move to software" list.
tips: Use add-ons for exploration and data cleaning. Use proper software for the final thesis analysis.
prompts.try: A sheet of 120 diabetic patients with HbA1c, BMI, treatment group and complications.

prompts.t: Classify my variables correctly
prompts.p: Act as a biostatistics tutor. Classify each of my variables, [PASTE VARIABLE LIST], as continuous, discrete, binary, nominal or ordinal, name the right summary statistic for each (mean ± SD, median with IQR, n with %), and flag any variable I should not convert into categories.
prompts.try: Age, sex, BMI, NYHA class, smoking (yes/no), number of admissions, CRP.

prompts.t: Mean or median for this variable?
prompts.p: Act as a biostatistician reviewing a thesis Table 1. For my variable [VARIABLE] with these summaries, [MEAN, SD, MEDIAN, IQR, MIN, MAX, n], tell me whether to report the mean ± SD or the median with IQR, and explain your reasoning in 3 lines using the numbers.
prompts.try: Hospital stay: mean 7.1, SD 6.4, median 5, IQR 3–9, range 1–42, n = 110.

prompts.t: What does my p value actually mean?
prompts.p: Act as a biostatistics examiner. Explain what my result [e.g. p = 0.03 for the difference in X] does and does not mean, in plain language, in under 100 words. Include the 2 most common misinterpretations and why they are wrong.
prompts.try: p = 0.04 for a difference in mortality between two antibiotic regimens.

prompts.t: Interpret my confidence interval
prompts.p: Act as a clinical epidemiologist teaching residents. Interpret this confidence interval, [ESTIMATE AND 95% CI], for a clinician in under 100 words: what range of true effects is plausible, whether it excludes no effect, and whether it excludes a clinically important effect.
prompts.try: Mean difference in systolic BP −6 mmHg (95% CI −11 to −1).

prompts.t: Odds ratio or relative risk for my study?
prompts.p: Act as an epidemiology tutor. For my design [DESIGN] and outcome frequency [e.g. 25%], tell me whether to report an odds ratio or a relative risk, why, and how much an odds ratio would overstate the relative risk here. Answer in under 120 words.
prompts.try: Prospective cohort, outcome occurring in 30% of patients.

prompts.t: Explain statistical power with my study
prompts.p: Act as a biostatistics teacher. Explain statistical power, alpha and beta using my study, [BRIEF STUDY AND SAMPLE SIZE], as the example. Include what happens if my study is underpowered, and how to phrase a non-significant result honestly. Keep it under 150 words.
prompts.try: Two-arm trial of 60 patients comparing two antiemetics.

prompts.t: My result isn't significant: now what?
prompts.p: Act as a biostatistician and thesis guide. My primary result was [ESTIMATE, 95% CI, p]. Explain in plain words what this means, whether the study was likely underpowered, how to write it honestly in results and discussion, and which phrases to avoid (e.g. "trend towards").
prompts.try: RR 0.80 (95% CI 0.55–1.16), p = 0.24, in a 150-patient cohort.

prompts.t: Should I test baseline differences in my trial?
prompts.p: Act as a trial statistician. Explain whether I should report p values for baseline characteristics in Table 1 of my randomised trial [BRIEF DESCRIPTION], what CONSORT recommends, and what to do instead if the groups look imbalanced. Keep it under 120 words.
prompts.try: A 2-arm RCT of 80 patients where mean age differs by 4 years between groups.

prompts.t: Interpret my kappa value
prompts.p: Act as a measurement statistician. Interpret my inter-observer agreement result, [KAPPA OR WEIGHTED KAPPA WITH 95% CI], for my measurement [MEASUREMENT], explain what the value means in practice, mention the prevalence paradox, and give the sentence for my results section.
prompts.try: Kappa 0.62 (95% CI 0.48–0.76) for two readers grading chest X-ray consolidation.

prompts.t: Which assumptions does my test need?
prompts.p: Act as a biostatistics tutor. For the test [TEST] on my variables [VARIABLES], list each assumption, exactly how to check it in [SOFTWARE], what violation looks like, and the fallback test if it fails. Present it as a short table.
prompts.try: One-way ANOVA of FEV1 across three smoking categories in SPSS.

prompts.t: Sanity-check an AI-generated sample size
prompts.p: Act as a biostatistician. An AI tool gave me a sample size of [n] for [DESIGN AND OUTCOME] with these inputs, [INPUTS]. Recalculate it step by step, tell me whether the number is right, and give the exact OpenEpi or G*Power inputs to confirm it.
prompts.try: n = 96 for estimating a prevalence of 50% with ±10% precision.

prompts.t: Explain any statistics term for the viva
prompts.p: Act as a viva examiner who wants clear answers. Explain [STATISTICAL TERM] clearly in 3 levels for my thesis viva: one sentence, a 60-word explanation with an example from my thesis on [TOPIC], and the examiner's likely follow-up question with its answer.
prompts.try: Term: confounding. Thesis: vitamin D and TB treatment outcomes.

prompts.t: Build Table 1 from my variables
prompts.p: Act as a clinical biostatistician. From my variable list with types, [PASTE LIST], build a Table 1 template by group: rows, the summary format for each (n (%), mean ± SD, median [IQR]), units in the row labels, and footnotes. Leave the values as placeholders.
prompts.try: Age, sex, BMI, diabetes, hypertension, SOFA, lactate, in survivors versus non-survivors.

prompts.t: Write the Results chapter from my analysis output
prompts.use: After your analysis is complete and verified, before writing the discussion.
prompts.why: The results chapter is where transcription errors, interpretation creep and text that repeats the tables creep in. Writing it from your verified numbers in a fixed order (flow, baseline, primary, secondary) keeps it accurate, readable and defensible.
prompts.p:
You are a medical journal editor who writes and edits results sections. You report findings in past tense, in a logical order, with effect estimates and confidence intervals, and you never interpret in the results.

MY CONTEXT:
Design and reporting guideline: [e.g. prospective cohort, STROBE]
Participant flow numbers (screened, eligible, enrolled, lost, analysed): [numbers]
Table 1 baseline characteristics (paste the table): [PASTE TABLE]
Primary outcome result with effect estimate, 95% CI and p: [paste exactly]
Secondary outcome results: [paste exactly]
Tables and figures I have, with numbers and titles: [list]
Target length: [e.g. 800–1,200 words for a thesis; 500–700 for a journal]

TASK:
1. Open with participant flow, referring to the flow diagram.
2. Describe baseline characteristics briefly, highlighting only clinically important features and referring to Table 1.
3. Report the primary outcome with its effect estimate, 95% CI and exact p value.
4. Report secondary outcomes in the order of the objectives.
5. Report any pre-specified subgroup or sensitivity analyses, labelled as such.
6. Refer to each table and figure at the right point, and highlight rather than repeat their contents.
7. After the draft, list every number used with its source (table or output), for cross-checking.

RULES:
Use only the numbers I pasted, reproduced exactly, because a single mistyped number undermines the credibility of the whole chapter. No interpretation, no comparison with literature and no causal words. Report non-significant results with their estimates and CIs, never as "no effect". Qualify "significant" as statistically significant.

OUTPUT:
The results text with sub-headings by objective, then the number-source table.

TWEAK:
End with the 3 results an examiner will look at first, and whether my text presents each one clearly.
tips: Write results before the discussion. It stops you writing results to fit your story.
Check every number in the text against its table. Mismatches are the commonest results error.
If the text simply repeats a table, cut the text to the key finding and refer to the table.

prompts.t: Plan every table and figure in my results
prompts.use: After analysis and before writing, to decide how your results will be displayed.
prompts.why: Examiners and reviewers read tables and figures first. A planned set, where each item answers an objective and nothing is duplicated, makes results easy to follow. A random pile of SPSS outputs and pie charts makes them hard work.
prompts.p:
You are a scientific data-visualisation editor for a medical journal. You match each result to the display that shows it most honestly and clearly, and you follow journal conventions for tables and figures.

MY CONTEXT:
Objectives: [PASTE OBJECTIVES]
Results for each objective (brief, with the variable types): [PASTE SUMMARY]
Number of tables and figures allowed (thesis or journal): [e.g. no limit / 4 tables + 2 figures]
Software I'll use for figures: [Excel / GraphPad / R / SPSS]
My university's or journal's figure requirements, if any: [e.g. 300 dpi, greyscale, maximum width]

TASK:
1. Propose the complete set: which results go in tables, which in figures, and which only in text.
2. For each table: title, rows, columns, summary format, footnotes and abbreviations.
3. For each figure: chart type and why (bar with error bars, box plot, forest plot, Kaplan-Meier, ROC, scatter with fit line, flow diagram), axes, units, labels and legend.
4. Flag displays to avoid for my data (pie charts, 3D charts, dynamite plots for skewed data, dual axes).
5. Give step-by-step instructions to create each figure in my software.
6. Number everything in order of mention in the text.
7. Say which displays could go in an appendix instead of the main chapter.

RULES:
Choose displays that show the distribution or uncertainty (CIs, IQRs) rather than hiding it, because misleading displays are a frequent examiner criticism. Use placeholders instead of values.

OUTPUT:
A display plan table (number, type, objective served, content), then table templates, figure specifications, the "avoid" list and the software steps.

TWEAK:
End with the single figure that best tells the story of my thesis, and why.
tips: One figure that shows your primary result clearly is worth more than ten decorative charts.
Keep fonts, colours and decimal places consistent across all tables and figures.
Make every table understandable on its own, with a full title and footnotes.

prompts.t: Consistency audit: text, tables, figures and abstract
prompts.use: When the thesis or manuscript is drafted, before submission.
prompts.why: Inconsistent numbers between the abstract, text, tables and figures are among the most common reasons reviewers lose trust in a paper, and examiners spot them fast. A systematic audit catches them all at once.
prompts.p:
You are a meticulous statistical reviewer for a medical journal who cross-checks every number in a manuscript for consistency and plausibility.

MY CONTEXT:
Abstract: [PASTE ABSTRACT]
Results text: [PASTE RESULTS TEXT]
Tables (as text): [PASTE TABLES]
Figure legends and any numbers shown in figures: [PASTE LEGENDS]
Total N and group sizes: [numbers]
Missing data per key variable: [brief]
Version of the document and date: [e.g. draft 3, 12 May]

TASK:
1. Extract every number from each section and match it across sections.
2. Flag any number that differs between sections.
3. Check internal arithmetic: percentages match their numerators and denominators, subgroup counts sum to totals, means lie within their ranges, and CIs contain their point estimates.
4. Check that p values are consistent with the CIs (a 95% CI excluding the null should go with p < 0.05).
5. Check that the denominators change sensibly where there is missing data, and that the missing data is reported somewhere.
6. Check that every table and figure is cited in the text, in order.
7. Check that the abstract's conclusion matches the primary result as reported in the results text.

RULES:
Report discrepancies without deciding which value is right, because only the original source output can settle that. Do not alter any numbers yourself.

OUTPUT:
A discrepancy table (number, location A, location B, issue), then the arithmetic and consistency check results, then the citation-order check and the abstract check.

TWEAK:
Finish with the 3 discrepancies most likely to be noticed by an examiner or reviewer, to fix first.
tips: Fix discrepancies from the original output, never by adjusting the text to match a table.
Re-run this audit after every major revision. New inconsistencies appear with each edit.
Ask a colleague to check 10 random numbers against the raw output as an independent check.

prompts.t: Describe Table 1 in two short paragraphs
prompts.use: When writing the baseline characteristics paragraph of your results.
prompts.p:
You are a journal editor who keeps baseline descriptions short and informative.

MY CONTEXT:
Table 1 (paste as text): [PASTE TABLE]
Design (randomised or observational): [brief]
Groups: [brief]
Target: [thesis / journal]

TASK:
1. Write 2 short paragraphs describing the study population: key demographics, key clinical features, and notable differences between groups.
2. Highlight only clinically important features, not every row.
3. For an RCT, describe balance without p values; for observational studies, note the differences that may confound results.

RULES:
Reproduce numbers exactly and refer to Table 1 rather than repeating it, because text that repeats a table wastes the reader's time.

OUTPUT:
The two paragraphs.
tips: Readers use Table 1 to judge whether your results apply to their patients. Make the setting and severity clear.
prompts.try: Table 1 of a 200-patient sepsis cohort comparing survivors and non-survivors.

prompts.t: Report the primary outcome properly
prompts.use: For the most important paragraph of your results.
prompts.p:
You are a medical statistician who writes primary-outcome paragraphs that are accurate and complete.

MY CONTEXT:
Primary objective: [paste]
Result: event counts or group summaries, the effect estimate with 95% CI, and exact p value: [paste exactly]
Adjusted result, if any: [paste]

TASK:
1. Write the primary-outcome paragraph: summaries in each group, the effect estimate with 95% CI and p value, and the adjusted estimate if applicable.
2. Refer to the relevant table or figure.
3. Write a one-sentence version for the abstract.

RULES:
Report the estimate and CI before the p value, and use past tense without interpretation, because readers need the size and precision of the effect, not just significance.

OUTPUT:
The paragraph, then the abstract sentence.
tips: Give absolute numbers as well as relative measures, e.g. "18/100 vs 30/100 (RR 0.60, 95% CI …)".

prompts.t: Report secondary outcomes without clutter
prompts.use: When you have several secondary outcomes to report.
prompts.p:
You are an editor who reports multiple outcomes clearly and briefly.

MY CONTEXT:
Secondary objectives: [list]
Results for each (estimates, CIs, p values): [PASTE RESULTS]
Table where they are shown: [e.g. Table 3]
Which analyses were pre-specified and which were added later: [brief]

TASK:
1. Report each secondary outcome in the order of the objectives, in 1–2 sentences each.
2. Group related outcomes where sensible.
3. Refer to the table rather than repeating every number.
4. Label exploratory analyses clearly, and keep them after the pre-specified ones.

RULES:
Report non-significant secondary outcomes as fully as significant ones, because selective reporting is a form of bias that examiners recognise.

OUTPUT:
The paragraphs.
tips: If a secondary outcome surprised you, report it plainly here. The interpretation belongs in the discussion.
prompts.try: Secondary outcomes: ICU stay, ventilator days, AKI incidence, and 90-day mortality.

prompts.t: Participant flow diagram and paragraph
prompts.use: For the first figure and paragraph of your results.
prompts.p:
You are a reporting-guideline expert who builds CONSORT and STROBE flow diagrams.

MY CONTEXT:
Numbers: assessed for eligibility, excluded (with reasons and counts), enrolled, allocated (if applicable), lost to follow-up (with reasons), analysed: [numbers]
Design: [RCT / cohort / cross-sectional / diagnostic]

TASK:
1. Describe the flow diagram box by box with my numbers, following CONSORT or STROBE conventions.
2. Check that the numbers add up at every step.
3. Write the participant-flow paragraph for the results.

RULES:
Flag any step where the numbers don't add up instead of adjusting them, because flow-diagram arithmetic errors are easy to spot.

OUTPUT:
The box list with arrows, the arithmetic check, then the paragraph.
tips: Draw the diagram in PowerPoint or draw.io from the box list. It's quicker than fixing an AI-drawn one.
prompts.try: 312 screened, 94 excluded (not meeting criteria 61, declined 33), 218 enrolled, 12 lost, 206 analysed.

prompts.t: The best figure for this result
prompts.use: When you are unsure how to display a particular result.
prompts.p:
You are a data-visualisation specialist for medical research.

MY CONTEXT:
The result to display: [brief]
Variable types and groups: [brief]
Where it will appear: [thesis / journal / poster / slide]
Sample size per group: [n]

TASK:
1. Recommend the best chart type and explain why.
2. Name 2 alternatives and when they would be better.
3. Name the chart types to avoid for this result.
4. Specify the axes, labels, error bars or intervals, and legend.

RULES:
Prefer displays that show individual data or uncertainty for small samples, because bar charts of means hide the distribution.

OUTPUT:
The recommendation, alternatives, avoid list, then the specification.
tips: For skewed data in small groups, a box plot with the individual points overlaid is usually best.
prompts.try: CRP levels (skewed) in three groups of 25 patients each.

prompts.t: Build the chart step by step in my software
prompts.use: When you know which figure you want and need to make it.
prompts.p:
You are a practical graphics trainer who creates publication-quality charts in common software.

MY CONTEXT:
Chart type and data: [brief]
Software: [Excel / Google Sheets / GraphPad / R ggplot2 / SPSS]
Output target: [thesis print / journal / slide]

TASK:
1. Give step-by-step instructions (or code) to create the chart.
2. Specify formatting: font sizes, axis titles with units, removing chart junk, colour-blind-safe colours, and error bars or CIs.
3. Explain how to export at the right resolution (e.g. 300 dpi for print).
4. Write the figure title and legend.

RULES:
Keep the axes honest: start bar charts at zero, and use the same scale when figures are compared, because distorted axes mislead readers.

OUTPUT:
Numbered steps or a code block, formatting rules, export settings, then the legend.
tips: Make the chart in greyscale first. If it still works, colour will only improve it.
prompts.try: Kaplan-Meier curves for two groups with the number at risk, in R.

prompts.t: Format my table to journal standard
prompts.use: When your tables are copied from software output and look messy.
prompts.p:
You are a journal production editor who formats tables to house style.

MY CONTEXT:
My table (as text): [PASTE TABLE]
Target: [thesis / journal name]
What the table is meant to show: [one line]

TASK:
1. Restructure the table: a clear title, logical row order, grouped variables, units in the row labels, and consistent decimals.
2. Remove software clutter (test statistics columns readers don't need, redundant rows).
3. Add footnotes: abbreviations, the tests used, and symbols.
4. Return the formatted table.

RULES:
Keep every value exactly as given; only restructure and format, because tables must still match the software output.

OUTPUT:
The formatted table, then a list of the changes made.
tips: Use horizontal lines only (top, below the header, bottom). Journals rarely accept vertical lines.
prompts.try: An SPSS crosstab output pasted with all its default columns.

prompts.t: Titles, legends and footnotes for my tables and figures
prompts.use: When finalising tables and figures.
prompts.p:
You are a scientific editor who writes self-explanatory table titles and figure legends.

MY CONTEXT:
Table or figure content and purpose: [brief or PASTE]
Abbreviations used: [list]
Tests used: [list]
Target: [thesis / journal / poster]

TASK:
1. Write a title that states what, who, where and when.
2. Write a legend or footnotes: abbreviations, statistical tests, what the error bars represent, and sample sizes.
3. Check that the item can be understood without reading the text.

RULES:
State exactly what error bars or ranges represent (SD, SE or 95% CI), because unlabelled error bars are uninterpretable.

OUTPUT:
The title, then the legend or footnotes.
tips: A good title tells the reader the finding's context. A great one lets them skip the text.
prompts.try: A bar chart of mean ventilator days by group, with error bars.

prompts.t: Remove interpretation from my results
prompts.use: When your guide says your results read like a discussion.
prompts.p:
You are a strict methods editor who keeps results and discussion separate.

MY CONTEXT:
My results text: [PASTE TEXT]
My objectives, so you can check the order: [PASTE OBJECTIVES]
Target: [thesis / journal]

TASK:
1. Mark every sentence that interprets, explains, compares with literature or speculates.
2. Suggest moving each to the discussion or deleting it.
3. Return the cleaned results text in neutral past tense, ordered by objective.
4. Collect the removed interpretive sentences in a separate list for my discussion.

RULES:
Keep all numbers and factual findings unchanged, because the cleaning must remove only interpretation, not results.

OUTPUT:
A table of flagged sentences (sentence, problem, move or delete), then the cleaned text.
tips: Words such as "interestingly", "surprisingly", "suggesting", "due to" and "because" usually signal interpretation.
prompts.try: A results paragraph saying "mortality was lower, probably due to earlier antibiotics".

prompts.t: Stop repeating my tables in the text
prompts.use: When your results text restates every row of the tables.
prompts.p:
You are a journal editor who cuts results sections to their essential points.

MY CONTEXT:
Results text: [PASTE TEXT]
Tables it refers to: [PASTE TABLES]
Target length: [words]

TASK:
1. Identify the text that duplicates table contents.
2. Rewrite the text to highlight only the key findings (the primary result, important differences, surprises) with a pointer to the table.
3. Give the word count before and after.
4. List any table row that should be moved to an appendix.

RULES:
Keep the primary outcome's numbers in the text even if they are in a table, because readers expect the key result stated in full.

OUTPUT:
The rewritten text, then the word counts.
tips: A useful rule: the text tells the story, the tables hold the evidence.
prompts.try: 600 words describing every row of a 20-row Table 2.

prompts.t: Report a non-significant result honestly
prompts.use: When your primary or key result is not statistically significant.
prompts.p:
You are a research-integrity-minded statistician who reports null results clearly and without spin.

MY CONTEXT:
The result (estimate, 95% CI, p): [paste]
Sample size and whether the study was powered for this outcome: [brief]

TASK:
1. Write the result sentence neutrally with the estimate and CI.
2. Explain what the CI does and does not rule out.
3. List spin phrases to avoid (e.g. "trend towards", "marginally significant", "no effect").
4. Suggest how the discussion should handle it (and point to that section).

RULES:
Do not suggest any re-analysis to reach significance, because that is p-hacking.

OUTPUT:
The result sentence, the CI explanation, the avoid list, then the discussion pointer.
tips: A well-reported null result from a well-conducted study is publishable. Spin is what gets it rejected.
prompts.try: OR 1.35 (95% CI 0.88–2.07), p = 0.17 for diabetes and wound dehiscence.

prompts.t: Report diagnostic accuracy results (STARD)
prompts.use: When your thesis evaluates a test.
prompts.p:
You are a diagnostic-research editor who applies STARD reporting.

MY CONTEXT:
2 × 2 table (true positives, false positives, false negatives, true negatives): [numbers]
Indeterminate results and how they were handled: [brief]
Pre-specified threshold: [value]

TASK:
1. Calculate sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, LR+ and LR− with 95% CIs, showing the formulas.
2. Write the results paragraph in STARD style.
3. Present the 2 × 2 table cleanly.
4. Remind me which measures depend on prevalence.

RULES:
Show the formulas and arithmetic so I can check them, and recommend confirming the CIs in MedCalc or OpenEpi, because hand-calculated CIs are error-prone.

OUTPUT:
The calculations, the table, then the paragraph.
tips: Report the prevalence in your sample. PPV and NPV mean nothing without it.
prompts.try: TP 72, FP 14, FN 8, TN 106 for lung ultrasound versus CT.

prompts.t: Present regression results clearly
prompts.use: When reporting a multivariable model in your results.
prompts.p:
You are a biostatistical editor who formats regression tables for clinical journals.

MY CONTEXT:
Model type and outcome: [brief]
Output with crude and adjusted estimates and CIs for each variable: [PASTE OUTPUT]
Number of observations and events: [numbers]

TASK:
1. Build a table: variable, category or reference, crude estimate (95% CI), adjusted estimate (95% CI), p value.
2. Add footnotes: model type, variables adjusted for, n and events, and fit statistics if relevant.
3. Write a results paragraph describing the key adjusted associations.

RULES:
Mark reference categories clearly and report estimates exactly as in the output, because reversed or missing reference categories flip the meaning.

OUTPUT:
The table, the footnotes, then the paragraph.
tips: Put the exposure of interest in the first row. Readers look for it first.
prompts.try: Logistic regression for 30-day mortality with age, lactate, SOFA and diabetes.

prompts.t: Condense results for an abstract or poster
prompts.use: When you need the key results in 80–150 words.
prompts.p:
You are an abstract editor for a medical conference who picks the numbers that matter.

MY CONTEXT:
Full results text or key numbers: [PASTE HERE]
Word limit: [e.g. 100 words]
Format: [structured abstract results / poster panel / slide]

TASK:
1. Select the key results: sample, primary outcome with its estimate and CI, and one or two important secondary results.
2. Write them within the limit.
3. List what was left out.

RULES:
Keep numbers exactly as in the source, and include the primary outcome even if it is non-significant, because selective abstract reporting is a form of spin.

OUTPUT:
The condensed results with word count, then the left-out list.
tips: One primary result stated clearly beats five results crammed in.
prompts.try: A 900-word results chapter condensed to 120 words for a conference abstract.

prompts.t: One result, one sentence
prompts.p: Act as a medical journal editor. Turn this result, [PASTE RESULT WITH NUMBERS], into one correctly reported sentence in past tense for my thesis results: group values, effect estimate with 95% CI and exact p value, no interpretation and no causal words.
prompts.try: Mean LOS 6.2 vs 8.1 days, difference −1.9 (95% CI −3.4 to −0.4), p = 0.01.

prompts.t: Check my percentages and denominators
prompts.p: Act as a numbers checker for a thesis. Check these counts and percentages, [PASTE TABLE OR TEXT], for arithmetic errors, wrong denominators (especially with missing data) and inconsistent rounding. List each error with its correct value and the denominator used.
prompts.try: "Diabetes 42 (35%), hypertension 51 (41%)" with a total of 120 patients.

prompts.t: How many decimal places?
prompts.p: Act as a statistical editor. Tell me how many decimal places to use for means, SDs, percentages, odds ratios, CIs and p values in my [thesis / journal] results, with the reasoning, and correct each of these examples: [PASTE EXAMPLES].

prompts.t: Table or figure for this result?
prompts.p: Act as a data-presentation editor. For this result, [DESCRIBE RESULT], tell me whether a table, a figure or a single sentence of text shows it best, why, and exactly what the recommended display should contain. Answer in under 100 words.
prompts.try: Prevalence of 6 comorbidities in 150 patients.

prompts.t: Check my chart for common errors
prompts.p: Act as a figure reviewer for a medical journal. From this description of my chart, [DESCRIBE CHART OR PASTE SETTINGS], check axis labels and units, the axis starting point, error-bar definition, legend, colour use and chart junk. List each problem with its fix.
prompts.try: A 3D pie chart of the distribution of blood groups.

prompts.t: Describe a figure in the text
prompts.p: Act as a results editor. Write 1–2 sentences for my results text that point the reader to [FIGURE NUMBER] and state the main pattern it shows, using these numbers: [KEY NUMBERS]. No interpretation, past tense, under 50 words, and refer to the figure by number.
prompts.try: Figure 2 shows Kaplan-Meier curves; median time to event 14 vs 22 days.

prompts.t: Label an exploratory analysis correctly
prompts.p: Act as a trial statistician. Write the sentence that introduces my exploratory or post-hoc analysis, [DESCRIBE ANALYSIS], in the results, making clear that it was not pre-specified and is only hypothesis-generating, and give the matching caution sentence for the discussion.
prompts.try: A subgroup analysis by diabetes status that was added after seeing the data.

prompts.t: Fix the tense in my results
prompts.p: Act as a copy-editor for medical theses. Correct the tense in this results text, [PASTE TEXT], using past tense for findings and present tense only when referring to tables and figures ("Table 2 shows"). Return the corrected text and list the changes.
prompts.try: "The mortality is lower in group A and Figure 3 showed the trend."

prompts.t: Write the discussion: ten paragraphs, no overclaiming
prompts.use: After results are final. This is the section examiners and reviewers read most closely.
prompts.why: The discussion is where good data gets ruined by overclaiming, and it is the only section where your scientific judgement is visible. A fixed structure (answer, compare, explain, implications, strengths, limitations, future, conclusion) keeps it honest and complete.
prompts.p:
You are a journal editor and senior academic who has written and revised hundreds of discussion sections and rejected many more. You are ruthless about over-interpretation, unsupported causal language, and limitation sections that hide the real weaknesses.

MY CONTEXT:
Design: [state] · Sample size: [state]
Primary objective: [state]
Primary result with effect estimate and CI: [paste exactly as computed]
Secondary results: [paste, with numbers]
Findings that surprised me or contradicted my hypothesis: [state]
Findings that were not significant: [state]
Known limitations: [list]
Setting: [Indian tertiary / rural / private, etc.] · Target: [thesis / journal name]
I have uploaded the [N] most relevant published papers. Use only these, plus anything you retrieve through live search with a verifiable PMID or DOI.

TASK:
Draft a discussion of about [800–1,200] words:
1. Paragraph 1: answer the research question in 1–3 sentences with the principal finding and its numbers. No literature.
2. Paragraphs 2–4: for each key comparison, state what the prior study found, whether mine agrees or differs, and the likely reason (population, setting, definitions, measurement, sample size, follow-up). End every comparison with an interpretive sentence.
3. Paragraph 5: the most plausible mechanism, marked clearly where speculative.
4. Paragraph 6: clinical implications: who could act on this and how; say plainly if it is not yet practice-changing.
5. Paragraph 7: strengths, without inflation.
6. Paragraph 8: limitations in order of threat to the conclusion, each with the likely direction of bias.
7. Paragraph 9: specific, doable future research, not "further studies are needed".
8. Paragraph 10: a 2–3 sentence conclusion that does not exceed the data.

RULES:
Use associational language unless my design is randomised; "caused", "led to", "resulted in" and "prevented" are banned otherwise, because causal overreach is the most common reviewer criticism. Qualify every "significant" as statistical or clinical. Never call a non-significant result a "trend". Where a comparison needs a source I have not supplied, write [CITATION NEEDED — FIND SOURCE]. Introduce no result that is not in my results section.

OUTPUT:
The discussion in paragraphs with no sub-headings unless my target requires them, within the word range.

TWEAK:
Then list separately the three sentences a hostile reviewer would attack first, and how to rewrite each one defensively.
tips: Give the model your actual numbers. A discussion written around vague findings reads exactly as vague as it was written.
The hostile-reviewer list is worth more than the draft. Act on it before submission.
If the draft sounds more confident than you feel about your own data, the draft is wrong, not your instinct.

prompts.t: Limitations that are honest, ranked and specific
prompts.use: When writing the limitations paragraph, and before your viva.
prompts.why: Examiners judge your scientific maturity by your limitations. A generic list ("small sample, single centre") signals you didn't think. Limitations ranked by threat, each with the direction of bias and what you did to reduce it, signal that you did.
prompts.p:
You are a clinical epidemiologist and journal reviewer who evaluates limitation sections for honesty and insight. You expect each limitation to state how it could have changed the result.

MY CONTEXT:
Design and setting: [paste]
How participants were selected and how many declined or were lost: [brief with numbers]
How the exposure and outcome were measured, and by whom: [brief]
Confounders measured and not measured: [lists]
Sample size, and whether the study was powered for each reported outcome: [brief]
Primary result: [estimate with CI]
Limitations I have thought of: [list]

TASK:
1. Identify all important limitations under selection, information (measurement), confounding, sample size or precision, and generalisability.
2. Rank them by how much they threaten my main conclusion.
3. For each, state the likely direction of bias (towards or away from the null, or unpredictable) and whether it could explain my result entirely.
4. For each, state what I did in the design or analysis to reduce it, if anything.
5. Write the limitations paragraph (180–250 words) in ranked order, honest but not self-defeating.
6. Separately, list 2 limitations I should acknowledge in the viva even if they are not in the thesis text.

RULES:
Be specific to my study, because generic limitations suggest you haven't understood your own design. Don't invent limitations my design doesn't have, and don't hide real ones behind softer wording. Keep numbers exactly as I gave them.

OUTPUT:
A ranked limitation table (limitation, type, direction of bias, mitigation, impact), then the paragraph, then the viva list.

TWEAK:
End with a one-line statement of how confident a reader should be in my primary conclusion, given these limitations.
tips: Start with the limitation that matters most, not the most comfortable one.
"Single-centre" is only a limitation if you explain why your centre might differ from others.
Pair each limitation with what the next study should do differently. It leads naturally into future research.

prompts.t: Hostile-reviewer attack on my discussion
prompts.use: When your discussion is drafted, before your guide or a journal sees it.
prompts.why: The kindest thing you can do for your discussion is let someone attack it first. A structured hostile review finds overclaims, missing comparisons and weak logic, and it hands you defensive rewrites you can use on paper and at the viva.
prompts.p:
You are Reviewer 2: a senior, sceptical peer reviewer for a high-impact clinical journal. You are fair but relentless, and you target over-interpretation, selective comparisons and conclusions that outrun the data.

MY CONTEXT:
Design, sample size and primary result: [brief with numbers]
Target: [thesis / journal name and its readership]
My results section: [PASTE RESULTS]
My discussion: [PASTE DISCUSSION]

TASK:
1. Write a reviewer report on the discussion with major comments (threats to validity or interpretation) and minor comments (wording, clarity, missing references), each quoting the text it refers to.
2. Identify every sentence that claims more than the results show, and every causal claim unsupported by the design.
3. Identify comparisons with literature that seem selective, where only agreeing studies are cited, and say what kind of study is missing.
4. Identify results reported in the discussion that do not appear in the results.
5. Identify important limitations the discussion leaves out or understates.
6. For each major comment, write a defensive rewrite of the relevant text and a one-line response I could use in a reply to reviewers or at the viva.

RULES:
Quote the exact text for every criticism, because unquoted criticism cannot be acted on. Rewrites must not add new data or references; use [CITE] slots where a reference is needed. Keep my numbers unchanged.

OUTPUT:
The reviewer report (major, then minor), then a table (quoted sentence, problem, rewrite, one-line response).

TWEAK:
End with an overall verdict (accept, minor revision, major revision) with the single change that would most improve the discussion.
tips: Run this before your guide reads the draft. Their time is better spent on judgement than on catching overclaims.
Keep the responses. They are ready-made answers for viva questions about your interpretation.
Run it again after revising. The major comments should turn into minor ones.

prompts.t: Conclusion, recommendations and summary chapter
prompts.use: For the final chapters of your thesis: summary, conclusion and recommendations.
prompts.why: Many Indian theses end with separate summary, conclusion and recommendations chapters, and examiners read them first when time is short. They must match the objectives exactly and claim no more than the data shows.
prompts.p:
You are a senior examiner for MD/MS theses who reads the summary and conclusion first to judge whether the student understood their study. You insist that every conclusion maps to an objective and every recommendation is proportionate to the evidence.

MY CONTEXT:
Thesis title: [paste]
Objectives (numbered): [PASTE OBJECTIVES]
Key results for each objective (with numbers): [PASTE RESULTS]
Main limitations: [list]
My university's required end chapters and word limits: [e.g. Summary 500 words, Conclusion, Recommendations]
Design and setting: [brief]

TASK:
1. Write the summary chapter: background (2 lines), aims, methods (design, setting, sample, key measurements), key results by objective with numbers, and the conclusion, within the word limit.
2. Write the conclusion: one numbered statement per objective, each answering it directly and in associational terms where appropriate.
3. Write recommendations in 3 groups: for clinical practice (only if justified), for the department or health system, and for future research, each specific and feasible.
4. Build a check table showing each objective, its conclusion statement and the result that supports it.
5. Flag any result that is important but not captured by any conclusion.

RULES:
Every conclusion must answer an objective using a result I gave, because conclusions without matching results are a classic examiner criticism. Recommendations for practice must be proportionate: a single-centre observational study can suggest or support, not establish. Keep numbers exactly as supplied.

OUTPUT:
The summary, the numbered conclusions, the grouped recommendations, then the check table.

TWEAK:
End with the one conclusion statement most likely to be challenged at the viva, and a safer wording for it.
tips: Read your conclusion and your objectives side by side. They should mirror each other.
Future-research recommendations should name the design, population and outcome.
Keep the summary free of any number that doesn't appear in your results chapter.

prompts.t: The first paragraph of the discussion
prompts.use: To open your discussion.
prompts.p:
You are a journal editor who wants the discussion to open with the answer, not with background.

MY CONTEXT:
Primary objective: [paste]
Primary result with numbers: [paste]
Most important secondary result: [paste]
Design: [brief]

TASK:
1. Write the opening paragraph (60–100 words) stating the answer to the research question with the key numbers.
2. Add one sentence on the most important secondary finding.
3. Give an alternative version for a journal article of 50 words or fewer.

RULES:
No literature, no background and no interpretation in this paragraph, and use associational language for observational designs, because the first sentence is read as your main claim.

OUTPUT:
The two versions.
tips: If you can't state your main finding in one sentence, your results section needs work first.
prompts.try: Primary: in-hospital mortality 18% vs 27% between early and late mobilisation groups (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.45–0.99).

prompts.t: Compare one finding with the literature
prompts.use: For each key comparison paragraph in your discussion.
prompts.p:
You are a clinical academic who writes comparison paragraphs that interpret rather than list.

MY CONTEXT:
My finding with numbers: [paste]
Comparable studies I have read, with design, setting, population and result: [PASTE DETAILS OR UPLOAD PAPERS]

TASK:
1. Compare my finding with each study: agree, partly agree or differ.
2. For differences, give the most likely explanations (population, setting, definitions, measurement, timing, sample size).
3. Write a paragraph of 120–180 words that compares and interprets, ending with what the comparison means.

RULES:
Use only the studies I supplied, citing each with its reference number, because comparisons with unseen or invented studies are academic misconduct. Present disagreeing studies too, not only supporting ones.

OUTPUT:
A comparison table, then the paragraph.
tips: One paragraph per key finding is a good discipline. Don't mix three findings in one paragraph.
prompts.try: My finding: prevalence of sarcopenia 38% in COPD; three studies reported 15%, 25% and 40%.

prompts.t: Why my result differs from previous studies
prompts.use: When your result disagrees with published findings and you must explain it.
prompts.p:
You are an epidemiologist skilled at explaining discrepancies between studies without special pleading.

MY CONTEXT:
My study: design, population, setting, definitions, sample size and result: [brief]
The study or studies I differ from, with the same details: [brief]

TASK:
1. Compare the studies systematically on each methodological dimension.
2. Rank the plausible explanations for the difference.
3. Consider chance (sample size, CI overlap) explicitly.
4. Write a discussion paragraph presenting the difference and the most likely explanations, without dismissing either result.

RULES:
Don't claim my study is "better" without a specific methodological reason, and consider that my own study might be the outlier, because examiners respect balanced reasoning.

OUTPUT:
The comparison table, the ranked explanations, then the paragraph.
tips: Overlapping confidence intervals often mean the "difference" isn't really a difference. Check that first.
prompts.try: My study found no association between vitamin D and TB outcome; two earlier studies found one.

prompts.t: The mechanism paragraph, clearly labelled as speculation
prompts.use: When your discussion needs a biological or clinical explanation for your finding.
prompts.p:
You are a clinician-scientist who explains mechanisms carefully and labels speculation clearly.

MY CONTEXT:
My finding: [paste]
Relevant physiology or mechanisms I know of, with sources: [PASTE NOTES WITH CITATIONS]

TASK:
1. Suggest the 2–3 most plausible mechanisms for my finding.
2. For each, say how strong the supporting evidence is (established, plausible, speculative).
3. Write a paragraph of 100–150 words presenting them with hedged language.
4. Suggest what study could test the leading mechanism.

RULES:
Mark every mechanistic claim needing support as [CITE], and phrase speculation as speculation ("may", "could", "one possible explanation"), because mechanisms presented as fact are a common overreach.

OUTPUT:
The mechanism list with evidence strength, then the paragraph, then the testing suggestion.
tips: Keep this paragraph short. Examiners value an honest "the mechanism is unclear" over a confident guess.
prompts.try: Finding: low serum magnesium associated with higher ICU mortality.

prompts.t: Clinical implications without overreach
prompts.use: For the implications paragraph of your discussion.
prompts.p:
You are a guideline-panel member who judges how far a single study can change practice.

MY CONTEXT:
Main findings: [paste]
Design, sample size and setting: [brief]
Who could use the findings (clinicians, administrators, programmes): [list]

TASK:
1. State what the findings could mean for practice, and for whom.
2. Distinguish what can be acted on now, what needs confirmation, and what is hypothesis-generating.
3. Write the implications paragraph (100–150 words).
4. Flag any implication that overreaches the design.

RULES:
Use proportionate verbs (suggests, supports, may inform) for single-centre observational results, because "should be adopted" claims are rarely justified by one study.

OUTPUT:
The three-level classification, the paragraph, then the overreach flags.
tips: Name the specific clinical decision your findings touch, e.g. "whether to repeat lactate at 6 hours".
prompts.try: Finding: a bedside frailty score predicted post-operative delirium in elderly surgical patients.

prompts.t: Strengths without inflation
prompts.use: For the strengths paragraph of your discussion.
prompts.p:
You are a sceptical reviewer who dislikes inflated strength statements.

MY CONTEXT:
Design features: [e.g. prospective, consecutive recruitment, blinded outcome assessment, validated tools, low loss to follow-up]
Anything unique about my setting or population: [brief]

TASK:
1. Identify genuine methodological strengths and explain why each matters for validity.
2. Remove claims that are not real strengths (e.g. "first study in India" unless verified, or "large sample" when it isn't).
3. Write the strengths paragraph (80–120 words).

RULES:
Tie each strength to a bias it reduces, because a strength without a reason is just a claim. Do not claim novelty unless I confirm it has been checked; write [VERIFY NOVELTY] instead.

OUTPUT:
A strengths table (feature, bias reduced), the removed claims, then the paragraph.
tips: "Prospective, consecutive recruitment with complete follow-up" is a real strength. Say it plainly.
prompts.try: A prospective cohort of 180 patients with 97% follow-up and blinded outcome assessment.

prompts.t: Future research that someone could actually do
prompts.use: Instead of writing "further studies are needed".
prompts.p:
You are a research funder who only backs specific, feasible next studies.

MY CONTEXT:
My findings and limitations: [brief]
Open questions my study raised: [list]
My setting and the resources a follow-up study could realistically use: [brief]

TASK:
1. Propose 3–4 specific future studies, each with design, population, setting, outcome and why it follows from my findings.
2. Rank them by importance and feasibility, and say which one could be a thesis for a junior resident in my department.
3. Write the future-research paragraph (80–120 words).

RULES:
Make each proposal specific enough to become someone's thesis topic, because vague calls for research add nothing.

OUTPUT:
A proposal table, then the paragraph.
tips: Link each future study to one of your limitations. It shows you understand what your study couldn't answer.
prompts.try: My cross-sectional study found an association between sleep apnoea and poor asthma control.

prompts.t: A conclusion that doesn't exceed the data
prompts.use: For the final paragraph of your discussion or abstract.
prompts.p:
You are a journal editor who rewrites overreaching conclusions every day.

MY CONTEXT:
Primary objective: [paste]
Primary result: [paste]
Design and setting: [brief]
My current conclusion: [paste]
Target: [thesis / journal abstract / poster]

TASK:
1. Check my conclusion against the result and design, and list every overreach.
2. Rewrite it in 2–3 sentences: what was found, in whom, and what it suggests.
3. Write a one-sentence version for the abstract.

RULES:
Match the strength of language to the design and precision of the result, because the conclusion is the most-quoted sentence of any study.

OUTPUT:
The overreach list, the rewritten conclusion, then the abstract sentence.
tips: Your conclusion should answer your primary objective in the same words the objective used.
prompts.try: Current: "Early antibiotics save lives in sepsis." Design: retrospective cohort.

prompts.t: Scan my discussion for overclaiming
prompts.use: As a final check on any discussion or conclusion.
prompts.p:
You are a research-integrity editor who scans manuscripts for spin.

MY CONTEXT:
My design: [design]
My primary result: [estimate, CI, p]
My discussion text: [PASTE DISCUSSION]

TASK:
1. Flag causal language used with an observational design.
2. Flag spin: "trend towards", "marginally significant", emphasis on secondary results over a null primary result, and extrapolation beyond the population.
3. Flag unqualified "significant".
4. Give a corrected version of each flagged sentence.

RULES:
Keep the meaning where it is justified and change only the overreaching wording, because the goal is accuracy, not timidity.

OUTPUT:
A table (sentence, type of spin, corrected sentence), then a count by type.
tips: Search your text for "caus", "effect", "impact", "prevent", "led to", "due to". Most overclaims hide there.
prompts.try: A discussion claiming a supplement "improved outcomes" based on a before-after study.

prompts.t: Who do my results apply to?
prompts.use: For the generalisability part of your limitations or implications.
prompts.p:
You are an epidemiologist who thinks carefully about external validity.

MY CONTEXT:
Setting and how patients reached my hospital: [brief]
Population characteristics (severity, age, comorbidity, socio-economic profile): [brief]
Exclusions: [list]
Proportion of screened patients who were enrolled: [numbers]

TASK:
1. Describe the population my results apply to most directly.
2. Identify populations to whom they may not apply, and why.
3. Discuss referral bias for a tertiary centre, if relevant, and the likely direction of its effect on my estimates.
4. Write a generalisability paragraph (80–120 words).

RULES:
Base the assessment on my actual setting and exclusions, because generic statements about "single-centre studies" add nothing.

OUTPUT:
Headed notes, then the paragraph.
tips: Tertiary-centre patients are usually sicker. Say whether that makes your estimates higher or lower than in district practice.
prompts.try: ICU cohort at a referral hospital receiving transfers from 6 districts.

prompts.t: Discuss a surprising result
prompts.use: When a result contradicts your hypothesis or expectations.
prompts.p:
You are a thoughtful senior researcher who treats surprising results as information, not embarrassment.

MY CONTEXT:
What I expected, and why: [brief]
What I found, with numbers: [paste]
Possible issues with my data or methods: [brief]

TASK:
1. List the explanations in order: chance, bias, confounding, measurement error, and a genuine effect.
2. Evaluate each against my study details.
3. Suggest a check I can still run (e.g. a sensitivity analysis) if appropriate.
4. Write a paragraph (100–150 words) presenting the finding honestly.

RULES:
Don't explain away the finding, and don't overstate it, because examiners respect a balanced treatment of surprises.

OUTPUT:
The explanations table, the check, then the paragraph.
tips: Surprising findings often make the best future-research questions. Say so.
prompts.try: Expected obesity to worsen ARDS outcomes; found lower mortality in obese patients.

prompts.t: Discuss a non-significant primary result
prompts.use: When your primary outcome was not statistically significant.
prompts.p:
You are a statistician-editor who helps authors write honest, publishable null-result discussions.

MY CONTEXT:
Primary result (estimate, 95% CI, p): [paste]
Sample size and whether it met the calculated target: [brief]
Expected effect used for the sample size: [brief]

TASK:
1. Interpret the CI: what effect sizes are ruled out, and what remain plausible.
2. Discuss power: whether the study could have detected a clinically important effect.
3. Compare with the literature honestly.
4. Write the opening paragraph of the discussion for this result.

RULES:
Don't call the result a trend or imply a hidden effect, and don't call it proof of no effect, because both misrepresent a null result.

OUTPUT:
The CI interpretation, the power note, then the paragraph.
tips: "Our study was unable to demonstrate…" is better than "there was no difference".
prompts.try: RR 0.85 (95% CI 0.62–1.17), p = 0.32, sample of 180 against a target of 200.

prompts.t: Check the structure of my discussion
prompts.use: When your discussion is drafted and feels disorganised.
prompts.p:
You are a thesis-writing coach who maps discussions against a standard structure.

MY CONTEXT:
My discussion: [PASTE DISCUSSION]
My primary result: [paste]
Target structure, if my guide or journal prescribes one: [brief]

TASK:
1. Map each paragraph to a structural element: principal findings, comparison, explanation, mechanism, implications, strengths, limitations, future research or conclusion.
2. Identify missing, repeated or misplaced elements.
3. Suggest a reordering.
4. Check that the first paragraph states the principal finding and the last states a proportionate conclusion.

RULES:
Suggest structural changes only, keeping my text as it is, because the content and voice must remain mine.

OUTPUT:
A paragraph map table, the problems, then the suggested order.
tips: If your discussion opens with background, move it. The first paragraph must answer the question.
prompts.try: A discussion that opens with 2 paragraphs of epidemiology before mentioning the results.

prompts.t: The "Summary" chapter of an Indian thesis
prompts.use: When your university requires a separate summary chapter.
prompts.p:
You are an MD/MS thesis examiner who reads the summary first.

MY CONTEXT:
Title and objectives: [paste]
Methods in brief: [paste]
Key results by objective, with numbers: [paste]
Conclusion: [paste]
Word or page limit: [e.g. 500 words]

TASK:
1. Write the summary within the limit, with short paragraphs for background, aims, methods, results and conclusion.
2. Keep results in the order of the objectives, with the key numbers.
3. Check that every number appears in my results chapter.

RULES:
Add no information that isn't elsewhere in the thesis, because the summary must be a faithful miniature of it.

OUTPUT:
The summary with its word count, then the number check.
tips: Write the summary last and read it aloud. If it doesn't flow, your thesis argument doesn't either.
prompts.try: Summary for a thesis on thyroid dysfunction in chronic kidney disease, 500 words.

prompts.t: What my findings mean for Indian practice
prompts.use: For a paragraph relating your results to Indian clinical practice, programmes or policy.
prompts.p:
You are a public-health physician familiar with Indian health programmes and resource settings.

MY CONTEXT:
My findings: [brief]
Relevant national programmes, guidelines or practices I know of: [list with sources]
Resource context of typical Indian hospitals for this condition: [brief]

TASK:
1. Relate the findings to current Indian practice and resource realities.
2. Identify which national programme or guideline, if any, the findings are relevant to.
3. Discuss feasibility of acting on the findings in district and primary settings.
4. Write the paragraph (100–150 words).

RULES:
Mention a programme or guideline only if I listed it or you mark it [VERIFY PROGRAMME / GUIDELINE], because misnamed programmes undermine credibility.

OUTPUT:
Headed notes, then the paragraph.
tips: Examiners in India value this paragraph. It shows you thought beyond your own hospital.
prompts.try: Finding: low-cost bedside ultrasound detected pneumonia as accurately as X-ray in children.

prompts.t: Cut my discussion to the word limit
prompts.use: When your discussion is over the limit for your thesis or target journal.
prompts.p:
You are a journal editor who cuts discussions without losing substance.

MY CONTEXT:
My discussion: [PASTE DISCUSSION]
Current and target word count: [e.g. 1,900 → 1,200]
Parts I must keep: [list]

TASK:
1. Identify repetition of results, background that belongs in the introduction, over-long literature summaries and redundant limitations.
2. Produce the trimmed discussion at or under the target.
3. List what was cut, so I can restore anything essential.

RULES:
Keep all citations with their claims and all numbers unchanged, because trimming must not alter the evidence. Keep the standard structure intact.

OUTPUT:
The trimmed discussion with its word count, then the cut list.
tips: Repeated results are the easiest cut. The discussion should interpret results, not restate them.
prompts.try: A 2,000-word thesis discussion needing to become a 1,100-word journal discussion.

prompts.t: Practical recommendations from my thesis
prompts.use: When your thesis format requires a recommendations section.
prompts.p:
You are a health-policy adviser who writes recommendations that are proportionate to the evidence.

MY CONTEXT:
Key findings: [brief]
Design strength and limitations: [brief]
Stakeholders: [clinicians, hospital, programme, researchers]
My university's format for this section, if any: [brief]

TASK:
1. Write 4–6 recommendations grouped by stakeholder.
2. Grade each by the strength of support from my study (strong, moderate or preliminary).
3. Make each specific and feasible, with who should act, how, and what it would cost in effort.

RULES:
Base practice recommendations only on results my design can support, and phrase the rest as research recommendations, because examiners question recommendations that outrun the data.

OUTPUT:
The grouped, graded recommendations.
tips: One specific, feasible recommendation is worth more than five generic ones.
