3. Suggest 3–5 keywords, preferring MeSH terms.

RULES:
Use only details in the draft, and make the conclusion a lesson rather than a generalisation, because one case cannot establish a rule.

OUTPUT:
The abstract with its word count, then the keywords.
tips: Put the unusual feature in the first sentence. That is what makes an editor keep reading.
prompts.try: Case of Kikuchi disease presenting as fever of unknown origin in a young man.

prompts.t: Case report titles that follow the CARE convention
prompts.use: When choosing your case report's title.
prompts.p:
You are a journal editor who knows what titles attract readers and meet CARE conventions.

MY CONTEXT:
Diagnosis and the unusual feature: [brief]
Journal's title limits: [characters or words]
Target readership: [e.g. general physicians / specialists]

TASK:
1. Write 5 titles that include "case report" (or "a case report").
2. Put the key diagnosis or phenomenon first.
3. Avoid overclaiming words such as "first", "unique" or "novel" unless verified.
4. Recommend one, with the reason.

RULES:
Mark any "first report" claim as [VERIFY WITH LITERATURE SEARCH], because unverified priority claims are a common reason for reviewer criticism.

OUTPUT:
Five titles with character counts, then the recommendation.
tips: Titles that describe the lesson ("…mimicking…", "…presenting as…") are read more often.
prompts.try: Tuberculous pericarditis presenting as cardiac tamponade in a patient on dialysis.

prompts.t: Write the case presentation from my notes
prompts.use: For the main narrative of a case report.
prompts.p:
You are a clinical writer who produces concise, chronological case presentations.

MY CONTEXT:
De-identified notes: history, examination, investigations with results, management, and course: [PASTE NOTES]
Word limit for this section: [e.g. 400 words]

TASK:
1. Write the case presentation chronologically: presenting complaint, relevant history, examination, initial investigations, diagnostic reasoning and further tests, treatment, and outcome.
2. Include only details relevant to the diagnosis or lesson.
3. Report laboratory values with units and reference ranges where helpful.
4. Point to the timeline table and images at the right places.

RULES:
Use only facts in my notes; where a relevant detail is missing, write [ASK ME: …], because invented clinical details in a case report are fabrication.

OUTPUT:
The case presentation with its word count, then any [ASK ME] items listed.
tips: Negative findings that ruled out important differentials are relevant. Include them.
prompts.try: Notes on a 30-year-old with stroke found to have antiphospholipid syndrome.

prompts.t: Show how differentials were excluded
prompts.use: For the diagnostic-assessment part of a case report.
prompts.p:
You are a diagnostician who documents diagnostic reasoning transparently.

MY CONTEXT:
Final diagnosis: [diagnosis]
Differentials considered and the tests or findings used to exclude each: [PASTE NOTES]
The investigation that finally confirmed the diagnosis: [brief]

TASK:
1. Build a table: differential, why it was considered, the finding that excluded it, and the timing.
2. Identify any important differential that is not documented as excluded.
3. Write the diagnostic-assessment paragraph for the case report.

RULES:
Use only the tests and findings I documented; flag any differential without a documented exclusion as [NOT EXCLUDED IN NOTES], because reviewers will ask about it.

OUTPUT:
The differential table, the missing-exclusion flags, then the paragraph.
tips: Reviewers almost always ask "was X excluded?". This table answers it before they do.
prompts.try: Final diagnosis: adult-onset Still's disease; differentials: sepsis, lymphoma, SLE, TB.

prompts.t: Learning points that readers remember
prompts.use: For the "learning points" or "key messages" box of a case report.
prompts.p:
You are a medical educator who writes practical, memorable learning points.

MY CONTEXT:
Case summary and the lesson I think it teaches: [brief]
Journal's format (number of points, word limit): [paste]
Intended readers: [e.g. residents, general practitioners]

TASK:
1. Write 3–5 learning points, each one sentence.
2. Make each specific and actionable (e.g. "Consider X in patients with Y who do not respond to Z").
3. Avoid generic points ("a high index of suspicion is needed").
4. Check that each point follows from the case.

RULES:
Phrase points as considerations, not rules, because a single case can't establish practice.

OUTPUT:
The learning points, then a one-line check of each.
tips: If a point could apply to any case report, it's too generic. Rewrite it.
prompts.try: Case of methaemoglobinaemia after dapsone use, initially misdiagnosed as cyanotic heart disease.

prompts.t: "Images in clinical medicine" submission
prompts.use: When a case has one striking image but may not justify a full case report.
prompts.p:
You are an editor of a clinical-images section who selects images that teach at a glance.

MY CONTEXT:
The image(s) and what they show: [describe]
Brief clinical context: [2–3 lines]
Journal's clinical-image format (word limit, number of images, references): [paste]

TASK:
1. Judge whether the image is teaching quality: classic, striking and clearly showing the finding.
2. Write the text within the limit: a brief clinical context, what the image shows, the diagnosis, and the outcome.
3. Write the image legend with annotations described.
4. Suggest a title.

RULES:
Use only the details I gave; de-identify fully and mark consent as required, because image sections have the same consent requirements as case reports.

OUTPUT:
The judgement, the title, the text, then the legend.
tips: Image sections are a quick first publication for residents. The image must be excellent.
prompts.try: Chest X-ray showing a classic "air crescent" sign in invasive aspergillosis.

prompts.t: Journals for case reports: find and verify them
prompts.use: When deciding where to submit a case report.
prompts.p:
You are a publication adviser who knows the case-report publishing landscape and its predatory corners.

MY CONTEXT:
Specialty and the type of case: [brief]
Budget for publication charges: [amount or none]
Indexing needed: [PubMed / Scopus / none required]

TASK:
1. Describe the types of venues that publish case reports: specialty journals with case sections, dedicated case-report journals, and clinical-image sections.
2. Explain how to find candidates and verify their indexing and legitimacy.
3. List predatory red flags specific to case-report publishing.
4. Build a shortlist table from the journals I find.

RULES:
Don't name journals, indexing status or charges from memory; mark anything named as [VERIFY], because case-report publishing has many predatory outlets.

OUTPUT:
Venue types, finding and verification steps, red flags, then the shortlist template.
tips: Check your own specialty society's journal first. Many accept case reports.
prompts.try: Unusual paediatric neurology case, no publication budget, PubMed indexing preferred.

prompts.t: Patient-level table for a case series
prompts.use: For the central table of your case series.
prompts.p:
You are a clinical data editor who designs clear patient-level tables.

MY CONTEXT:
Variables available for all patients: [list]
Data for each patient (de-identified): [PASTE]

TASK:
1. Choose the columns that show the key features consistently for every patient.
2. Build the table with one row per patient (Case 1, Case 2…).
3. Add a summary row or column (counts, ranges or medians).
4. Write the table title and footnotes.

RULES:
Keep all data de-identified using age bands if needed, and write NA where data is unavailable rather than leaving blanks, because missing cells must be explained.

OUTPUT:
The table, then the title and footnotes.
tips: If the table is too wide, split it into clinical features and management/outcome tables.
prompts.try: Seven patients with scrub typhus meningoencephalitis.

prompts.t: Find previously reported similar cases
prompts.use: Before writing the discussion of a case report or series.
prompts.p:
You are a medical librarian who searches for case reports efficiently.

MY CONTEXT:
The key features of my case (diagnosis, unusual presentation, association): [brief]

TASK:
1. Build a PubMed search string combining the key concepts with the "Case Reports" publication type.
2. Suggest Google Scholar queries for non-indexed reports.
3. Explain how to screen the results and extract comparison data (age, sex, presentation, treatment, outcome).
4. Give a comparison-table template.

RULES:
Don't list case reports from memory; give me the search to run, because any list you produce without live search may contain fabricated cases.

OUTPUT:
The search strings, the screening steps, then the table template.
tips: Check the reference lists of the most recent similar case reports. They are often mini-reviews.
prompts.try: Case: Castleman disease presenting as a posterior mediastinal mass.

prompts.t: Patient-perspective section
prompts.use: For the CARE "patient perspective" item, when the patient agrees to contribute.
prompts.p:
You are a patient-centred clinician who helps patients describe their experience in their own words.

MY CONTEXT:
Brief case summary: [brief]
Notes from my conversation with the patient (their own words where possible): [PASTE NOTES]
Language the patient spoke in: [language]

TASK:
1. Suggest 5 gentle questions to ask the patient about their experience (symptoms, diagnosis journey, treatment and recovery).
2. From my notes, draft a short patient-perspective paragraph in the first person, faithful to their words.
3. Suggest how to have the patient review and approve the text.

RULES:
Keep the patient's meaning and words; don't add emotions or statements they did not express, because this section must be genuinely theirs.

OUTPUT:
The questions, the draft paragraph, then the approval steps.
tips: Translate carefully and read the translation back to the patient before you use it.
prompts.try: A patient who went undiagnosed for 2 years with a rare autoimmune condition.

prompts.t: Case report → conference poster
prompts.use: When presenting your case at a conference as a poster or e-poster.
prompts.p:
You are a conference poster designer who turns case reports into posters people stop to read.

MY CONTEXT:
Case report text or summary: [PASTE]
Key images: [list]
Poster size and format: [e.g. A0 portrait / e-poster 16:9]
Conference word limit, if any: [limit]

TASK:
1. Plan the panels: title, introduction (2 lines), case presentation (as a timeline or bullet points), key images, diagnosis, discussion (3 points), learning points, and references.
2. Write the text for each panel within about 400–600 words in total.
3. Suggest the layout and reading flow, with images central.
4. Suggest a one-line "hook" for the top of the poster.

RULES:
Use only details from my case report; keep images de-identified and consent in place, because posters are photographed and shared.

OUTPUT:
A panel-by-panel plan with text, then layout notes.
tips: People read posters from 2 metres away. If a panel needs a paragraph, it needs cutting.
prompts.try: Case report of a rare paediatric pulmonary condition with CT images.

prompts.t: Critique my case report draft
prompts.use: When your case report is drafted, before submission.
prompts.p:
You are a reviewer for a case-reports journal who applies CARE and the journal's standards.

MY CONTEXT:
My draft: [PASTE DRAFT]
Target journal and word limit: [brief]

TASK:
1. Score the draft on novelty, clarity of the timeline, completeness of the diagnostic reasoning, quality of the literature comparison, strength of the learning points, and CARE compliance.
2. Quote the passage behind each score.
3. List the top 5 fixes.
4. Flag privacy risks and missing consent statements.

RULES:
Base comments only on my text; quote rather than paraphrase, because vague feedback can't be acted on.

OUTPUT:
A scoring table, the top fixes, then the privacy flags.
tips: Run this again after revising. The timeline and diagnostic-reasoning scores usually rise the most.
prompts.try: A 1,400-word draft case report of paraquat poisoning with delayed lung fibrosis.

prompts.t: Adverse drug reaction case report with causality assessment
prompts.use: When a case involves a suspected adverse drug reaction.
prompts.p:
You are a clinical pharmacologist experienced in pharmacovigilance and ADR case reporting.

MY CONTEXT:
Suspected drug(s), doses, start and stop dates (relative), reaction, timeline, dechallenge and rechallenge, and other possible causes: [PASTE DE-IDENTIFIED DETAILS]

TASK:
1. Apply a causality assessment (e.g. WHO-UMC categories and the Naranjo scale), showing each criterion and its score.
2. Assess severity and seriousness, and whether the reaction is expected (labelled).
3. Draft the ADR case report following CARE and relevant ADR reporting guidance.
4. Remind me to report to the national pharmacovigilance programme, marked [VERIFY CURRENT REPORTING PROCESS].

RULES:
Show the reasoning for each causality criterion from my details only, and mark unknown elements as [NOT DOCUMENTED], because causality scores are often challenged.

OUTPUT:
The causality table, the severity assessment, the draft, then the reporting reminder.
tips: Report to the pharmacovigilance programme even if you don't publish. Every report counts.
prompts.try: Suspected linezolid-induced lactic acidosis in a patient on TB treatment.

prompts.t: Clinicopathological conference (CPC) write-up
prompts.use: When presenting or publishing a clinicopathological conference case, where the diagnosis is revealed at the end.
prompts.p:
You are a senior physician and pathologist who has run CPCs for years, and knows how to build diagnostic suspense while staying fair to the reader.

MY CONTEXT:
De-identified case details in chronological order (history, examination, investigations, course): [PASTE]
Final diagnosis and how it was established (histopathology, autopsy or test): [brief]
Audience: [residents / faculty / mixed]

TASK:
1. Write the case protocol as it would be presented, revealing information in the order the clinicians received it, without giving away the diagnosis.
2. Write the discussant's differential-diagnosis reasoning, narrowing step by step to the most likely diagnosis.
3. Write the pathology or final-diagnosis section with key findings.
4. Add 3 teaching points and 2 questions for the audience.

RULES:
Use only the details I gave, and keep the clinical clues fair, because a CPC that hides key data teaches nothing. Keep everything de-identified.

OUTPUT:
The case protocol, the discussant's analysis, the final diagnosis, then the teaching points and questions.
tips: Pick a case where the diagnosis could have been reached from the clinical data. Those make the best CPCs.
prompts.try: Fever, pancytopenia and splenomegaly in a young man, finally diagnosed as visceral leishmaniasis on marrow.

prompts.t: One line on why my case is worth reading
prompts.p: Act as a case-reports editor. From my case summary, [PASTE SUMMARY], write one clear sentence of under 30 words that states exactly what the case adds (a rare presentation, association, diagnostic lesson or management lesson), without unverified "first report" claims.
prompts.try: A young non-smoker with pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis diagnosed on cryobiopsy.

prompts.t: Keywords to search for similar cases
prompts.p: Act as a medical librarian. For my case, [KEY FEATURES], give me 8 useful search terms and synonyms (including older names and MeSH terms) and one ready-to-run PubMed search string limited to case reports, to find previously published similar cases.
prompts.try: Hypokalaemic periodic paralysis as the presenting feature of thyrotoxicosis.

prompts.t: Is my case report properly anonymised?
prompts.p: Act as a privacy reviewer for a medical journal. Check this case text and image list, [PASTE TEXT AND IMAGE LIST], for anything that could identify the patient: dates, places, occupation, rare details, faces, tattoos and image metadata. List each risk with a fix.
prompts.try: A case mentioning the village name, the exact admission date and a distinctive tattoo.

prompts.t: Cut my case report to the word limit
prompts.p: Act as a case-reports editor. Cut this case report, [PASTE TEXT], from [CURRENT] to [TARGET] words, keeping the timeline, key investigations, the excluded differentials and the learning points, and moving detail into the timeline table. Show the new word count.
prompts.try: A 1,600-word case report for a journal with a 1,000-word limit.

prompts.t: Legend for a clinical image
prompts.p: Act as a journal image editor. Write a legend for this image, [DESCRIBE IMAGE AND FINDINGS], that states the modality or type, the view, what the arrows or labels point to, and the key finding, in under 50 words, with abbreviations defined.
prompts.try: Contrast CT showing a ring-enhancing lesion with a target sign in the right frontal lobe.

prompts.t: Turn my case into a teaching caption
prompts.p: Act as a medical educator. Turn my case, [BRIEF CASE], into a 60-word teaching caption for a department WhatsApp group or case-of-the-week slide, written for junior residents: the presentation, the key finding, the diagnosis and one learning point, fully de-identified.
prompts.try: Elderly man with hiccups for 2 weeks found to have lateral medullary infarct.

prompts.t: Explain publication consent to my patient
prompts.p: Act as a compassionate clinician. Write a short, simple explanation (under 100 words) that I can say to my patient, [BRIEF CONTEXT], explaining why I want to publish their case, what will be shared, how their identity will be protected, and that they can refuse.
prompts.try: A patient who recovered from a rare poisoning, speaking Hindi.

prompts.t: Case report or case series?
prompts.p: Act as a journal editor. I have [N] patients with [SHARED FEATURE]. Tell me whether to write a single case report, a case series or a clinical image, what each would need, and which journals typically prefer which, in under 120 words.
prompts.try: Three patients with the same rare drug reaction in 6 months.

prompts.t: The key sentence of my case-report cover letter
prompts.p: Act as a senior author. Write the 2 key sentences of a cover letter to the editor for my case report, [TITLE AND ONE-LINE SUMMARY], explaining why the case matters to this journal's readers, [JOURNAL], without exaggerating novelty or making unverified priority claims.
prompts.try: Case of tuberculous mastitis mimicking breast carcinoma in a young woman.

prompts.t: Conference abstract to the exact word limit
prompts.use: Before a conference abstract deadline, once your results (or interim results) are verified.
prompts.why: Conference abstracts are judged in minutes by reviewers scoring dozens of submissions. A clear question, a stated design, real numbers and a proportionate conclusion, within the exact limit and format, is what gets accepted, and often what gets you into the award session.
prompts.p:
You are a scientific committee member for national and international medical conferences who scores hundreds of abstracts each year. You know what reviewers reward and what gets rejected.

MY CONTEXT:
Conference name and its abstract rules (word or character limit, headings, whether the title and authors count, category options): [PASTE RULES]
Study design, setting and period: [brief]
Sample size and participant flow: [numbers]
Primary result with estimate, CI and p: [paste exactly]
Key secondary results: [paste]
Whether the data is final or interim: [final / interim with n so far]

TASK:
1. Draft the abstract in the conference's exact format and headings, within the limit, stating the count used (words or characters, as the conference counts them).
2. Background: the problem and the gap in 2 sentences. Methods: design, setting, participants, key measurements and analysis. Results: the numbers that answer the objective. Conclusion: proportionate, and linked to practice or research.
3. Write 3 title options within any title limit.
4. Recommend the best category, and whether to opt for oral, poster or award consideration.
5. Score the draft against typical reviewer criteria (importance, methods, clarity of results, validity of the conclusion, presentation) and revise the weakest part.

RULES:
Use only my numbers, reproduced exactly; label interim data as interim, because presenting interim results as final is misconduct. No references unless the conference allows them. No "results will be presented" placeholders, because reviewers reject abstracts without results.

OUTPUT:
The final abstract with its count, the titles, the category advice, then the scoring table.

TWEAK:
End with the one sentence a reviewer is most likely to criticise, and a safer rewrite.
tips: Check how the conference counts: words or characters, and whether spaces, title and authors are included.
Submit a day early. Portals slow down or crash near deadlines.
Keep the abstract text. The journal version later must not contradict it.

prompts.t: Research poster from my manuscript or thesis
prompts.use: After abstract acceptance as a poster, 2–3 weeks before the conference.
prompts.why: Most posters are shrunken papers that nobody reads. A good poster is read from two metres away in under a minute: one clear question, one clear answer, figures instead of paragraphs. This prompt turns your paper into that.
prompts.p:
You are a scientific poster designer and conference judge who has evaluated hundreds of posters. You design for visual hierarchy, brevity and a clear take-home message.

MY CONTEXT:
Accepted abstract: [PASTE ABSTRACT]
Key results, tables and figures available: [list]
Poster specifications (size, orientation, print or e-poster, template requirements): [paste]
Design tool: [PowerPoint / Canva / other]
Institution logo and branding requirements: [brief]
Whether I will stand by the poster or it will be viewed alone: [brief]

TASK:
1. Write a one-line take-home message to feature prominently.
2. Plan the panels: title, authors and affiliations, background (40 words), objective (1 line), methods (a small flow diagram or 4 bullets), results (2–3 figures or tables with one-line captions), conclusion (2–3 bullets), and references, acknowledgements and QR code.
3. Write the text for every panel, 500–800 words in total.
4. Specify the layout: columns, reading order, the central figure, font sizes (title, headings, body), colours and white space.
5. Convert any results table into a figure where that would be clearer.
6. Give step-by-step build instructions in my tool.
7. Write a 90-second walk-through script for when judges stop by.

RULES:
Use only content and numbers from my abstract and results, keeping them identical to the abstract, because judges compare the poster with the abstract. Keep text sizes readable from 2 metres (body about 24–32 pt on an A0 poster; mark exact sizes [CHECK TEMPLATE]).

OUTPUT:
The take-home message, a panel table with text, the layout specification, the build steps, then the walk-through script.

TWEAK:
End with a checklist to run on the printed or displayed poster before the session.
tips: If your poster has more than 800 words, it has too many.
Put your main result graph in the centre, at eye level.
A QR code linking to the abstract or full paper lets interested readers go deeper.

prompts.t: Thesis → 8-minute oral paper, with slides and Q&A
prompts.use: When your abstract is accepted for oral or award-paper presentation.
prompts.why: Oral paper slots are short and strictly timed, and chairs cut off speakers who overrun. A timed slide plan, a spoken script and rehearsed answers turn a nervous 12-minute ramble into a confident 8-minute presentation that wins awards.
prompts.p:
You are a conference presentation coach and award-session judge who has trained many residents for oral paper presentations.

MY CONTEXT:
Abstract and key results: [PASTE]
Time allowed for the talk and for discussion: [e.g. 8 + 2 minutes]
Figures and tables available: [list]
Award session?: [yes / no]
My speaking pace and confidence: [brief]
What the audience will mostly be: [specialists / mixed / students]
Conference's slide requirements (template, aspect ratio, file format): [paste]

TASK:
1. Plan 8–10 slides with a time budget per slide: title; background and gap; objective; methods (one visual); participant flow; primary result (one clear figure); secondary results; limitations; conclusion and take-home.
2. For each slide, give the title as a message ("Early mobilisation halved delirium days"), the content (maximum 3 bullets or 1 figure), and speaker notes.
3. Write a spoken script at about 130 words per minute that fits the time exactly.
4. Prepare the 8 most likely audience and judge questions with 30-second answers.
5. Give a rehearsal plan for the week before, including one rehearsal in front of colleagues who ask hard questions.
6. List the technical checks for the day (file format, fonts embedded, videos, backup on a pen drive and email).

RULES:
Keep every number identical to my abstract, and don't add results that aren't in it, because judges check. Keep slides visual: no paragraphs, and at least 24 pt text.

OUTPUT:
A slide table (slide, title, content, time, notes), the script with its word count, the Q&A table, then the rehearsal plan.

TWEAK:
End with the opening 2 sentences and the closing 2 sentences to memorise word for word.
tips: Rehearse with a timer at least 5 times. Most residents overrun by 30–50%.
Write slide titles as messages, not topics. The audience should get the story from the titles alone.
Have 2–3 backup slides for predictable questions.

prompts.t: Choose the right conference for my work
prompts.use: When deciding where to submit your abstract.
prompts.p:
You are an academic mentor who guides residents on conference strategy.

MY CONTEXT:
Specialty and the topic of my work: [brief]
Stage of the work: [final results / interim / case report]
Budget and travel constraints: [brief]
Goals: [award, networking, first presentation, international exposure]

TASK:
1. Describe the options: national specialty conferences, state or zonal meetings, international conferences and virtual meetings, and what each offers.
2. Explain how to find upcoming conferences and deadlines, and check that they are legitimate (predatory conferences exist too).
3. Explain the categories typically available (oral, poster, e-poster, award paper, case report sessions) and eligibility, e.g. age or membership requirements for awards.
4. Build a comparison table from the conferences I find.

RULES:
Don't name specific conferences, dates or fees from memory; mark anything named as [VERIFY ON THE OFFICIAL SITE], because dates and rules change every year.

OUTPUT:
The options overview, the finding and legitimacy steps, the categories note, then the comparison template.
tips: Student and resident award sessions at national specialty conferences are among the best first stages for your work.
prompts.try: MD Pulmonary Medicine resident with final thesis results, limited travel budget.

prompts.t: Score my abstract like a conference reviewer
prompts.use: Before you submit a conference abstract.
prompts.p:
You are a conference abstract reviewer who scores submissions on a standard rubric.

MY CONTEXT:
My abstract: [PASTE ABSTRACT]
Conference and category: [brief]
Limit: [words or characters]

TASK:
1. Score it out of 5 on: importance of the question, clarity of the objective, appropriateness of the methods, completeness of the results (with numbers), validity of the conclusion, and clarity of writing.
2. Quote the text behind each score.
3. Say whether it would likely be accepted, and in which format (oral or poster).
4. Give the 3 most important revisions.

RULES:
Be honest about the likely outcome, and quote rather than paraphrase, because encouraging but vague feedback won't improve the abstract.

OUTPUT:
A scoring table, the verdict, then the revisions.
tips: Abstracts without numbers in the results are usually rejected. Check yours has them.
prompts.try: A 250-word abstract on ultrasound-guided versus landmark-guided central line insertion.

prompts.t: Adapt my poster into an e-poster
prompts.use: When the conference uses screen-displayed e-posters.
prompts.p:
You are a digital poster designer who adapts print posters for screens.

MY CONTEXT:
My poster content or file description: [PASTE OR DESCRIBE]
E-poster specification (aspect ratio, single or multiple slides, resolution, file type, interactivity allowed): [paste]

TASK:
1. Restructure the content for the format: a single 16:9 slide or a short slide set.
2. Reduce the text further for on-screen reading distance.
3. Suggest a reading flow and the use of any allowed interactivity (e.g. clickable panels).
4. Specify export settings.

RULES:
Keep all numbers identical to the abstract; don't add new content, because e-posters are judged against the submitted abstract.

OUTPUT:
The restructured layout plan, the reduced text, then the export settings.
tips: Check your e-poster on a laptop from 1.5 metres before submitting. If you can't read it, neither can judges.
prompts.try: An A0 portrait poster converted to one 16:9 e-poster slide.

prompts.t: Layout brief for Canva or PowerPoint
prompts.use: When building the poster yourself.
prompts.p:
You are a graphic designer who specialises in clean scientific posters.

MY CONTEXT:
Poster size and orientation: [e.g. A0 portrait, 841 × 1189 mm]
Panels and approximate text length for each: [list]
Figures: [list]
Tool: [Canva / PowerPoint]

TASK:
1. Give the page set-up for my tool (custom size, margins, grid).
2. Suggest a 3-column grid and the placement of each panel.
3. Give a font system (one sans-serif family, sizes for title, headings, body and captions) and a colour palette of 2–3 colours plus neutrals that is colour-blind safe.
4. Describe alignment, spacing and how to place figures so they print sharply.
5. Give print-export settings.

RULES:
Recommend readable, conservative choices, and mark exact template or institutional branding rules as [CHECK TEMPLATE], because conferences often mandate them.

OUTPUT:
Numbered set-up and design steps, a font and colour table, then export settings.
tips: Leave about 25% of the poster as white space. Crowded posters are skipped.
prompts.try: A0 landscape poster in PowerPoint with 3 figures and 1 table.

prompts.t: 90-second poster walk-through for judges
prompts.use: The week before your poster session.
prompts.p:
You are a poster-session judge who knows what makes a presenter memorable.

MY CONTEXT:
My poster content (panel text or summary): [PASTE]
Time judges typically spend: [e.g. 2–3 minutes]

TASK:
1. Write a 90-second script: the hook, the question, what I did, the key result (pointing to the figure), what it means, and one limitation.
2. Write a 30-second version for passers-by.
3. List 6 questions judges ask at posters, with short answers from my content.
4. Give body-language and positioning tips.

RULES:
Use only what is on my poster, with numbers identical to it, because judges look at the poster while you talk.

OUTPUT:
The two scripts with timing, the Q&A table, then the tips.
tips: Start with the question, not the background. "We asked whether…" gets attention.
prompts.try: Poster on the prevalence of vitamin B12 deficiency in metformin-treated diabetics.

prompts.t: Slide plan for a short oral presentation
prompts.use: When you need slides quickly for a 5–10 minute talk.
prompts.p:
You are a presentation designer for medical conferences.

MY CONTEXT:
Abstract and results: [PASTE]
Time limit: [minutes]
Slide template requirements: [brief]
Audience: [specialists / mixed]

TASK:
1. Recommend the number of slides (about one per minute).
2. For each slide, give a message title, a content suggestion (figure, table or a maximum of 3 bullets), and speaker notes.
3. Suggest the design: font sizes, contrast and one accent colour.
4. List slides to put in the backup section.

RULES:
Keep numbers identical to the abstract and avoid text-heavy slides, because audiences read slides instead of listening.

OUTPUT:
A slide table, the design notes, then the backup list.
tips: One figure per results slide, with the key number called out in large text.
prompts.try: 7-minute oral paper on anaemia prevalence among adolescent girls in a rural block.

prompts.t: Prepare for questions after my talk
prompts.use: In the days before your oral or poster presentation.
prompts.p:
You are a session chair who has asked and heard thousands of conference questions.

MY CONTEXT:
My abstract and key slides: [PASTE]
Known limitations: [list]
Audience: [specialists / mixed / award judges]

TASK:
1. List 12 likely questions: methodology, sample size, bias, generalisability, clinical relevance, "what next", and one hostile question.
2. Write a 30-second answer for each, grounded in my study.
3. Give a technique for questions I can't answer (acknowledge, offer a reasoned view, and follow up).
4. Suggest 2 backup slides that answer the most likely questions.

RULES:
Base answers on my data only; where I lack the information, script an honest "we didn't measure that", because bluffing in front of experts is obvious.

OUTPUT:
A Q&A table, the technique, then the backup-slide suggestions.
tips: Repeat the question before answering. It buys you thinking time and helps the audience hear it.
prompts.try: Oral paper on a retrospective cohort of snakebite outcomes.

prompts.t: Prepare for an award-paper session
prompts.use: When your paper is selected for a best-paper or young-investigator award session.
prompts.p:
You are an award-session judge at national medical conferences.

MY CONTEXT:
Abstract and presentation plan: [PASTE]
Award rules and judging criteria, if published: [paste]
Time limits: [brief]

TASK:
1. Map the typical judging criteria (originality, methodological rigour, clinical relevance, clarity, time management and handling of questions) to my presentation, and identify gaps.
2. Suggest changes to strengthen my weakest criterion.
3. Prepare answers to the judges' likely tough questions.
4. Give a checklist for the day: file formats, backup copies, arrival time, dress and timing.

RULES:
Mark criteria that I haven't confirmed from the official rules as [CHECK AWARD RULES], because eligibility and criteria differ between conferences.

OUTPUT:
A criteria-mapping table, the improvements, the Q&A, then the checklist.
tips: Judges remember speakers who finish on time and answer questions honestly.
prompts.try: Award session for a prospective cohort on high-flow nasal oxygen in COPD.

prompts.t: Application for a travel grant or bursary
prompts.use: When applying for conference funding from your institution, a society or a foundation.
prompts.p:
You are a grants officer who reviews travel-grant applications.

MY CONTEXT:
Conference, dates and the type of presentation accepted: [brief]
Estimated costs (registration, travel, stay): [amounts]
Funding body and its criteria: [paste]
My academic profile (programme, year, publications, presentations): [brief]

TASK:
1. Write a concise application letter or statement: what I'm presenting, why it matters, what I'll gain, and how I'll share the learning.
2. Build a cost table with justification.
3. List the documents usually required (acceptance letter, abstract, guide's recommendation, CV).

RULES:
Use only facts I provided and mark criteria I haven't confirmed as [CHECK FUNDER CRITERIA], because inaccurate applications are rejected.

OUTPUT:
The statement, the cost table, then the document list.
tips: Apply as soon as your abstract is accepted. Travel-grant deadlines are often earlier than you expect.
prompts.try: Oral presentation at an international respiratory conference, first-time applicant.

prompts.t: From conference presentation to published paper
prompts.use: After the conference, while feedback is fresh.
prompts.p:
You are a publication mentor who helps residents turn presentations into papers.

MY CONTEXT:
My abstract and presentation: [PASTE]
Questions and feedback received at the conference: [brief]
Whether the abstract was published in a journal supplement: [yes / no]

TASK:
1. List the feedback that should shape the paper.
2. Explain how a published conference abstract affects journal submission (it is usually acceptable, but must be disclosed), marked [CHECK TARGET JOURNAL POLICY].
3. Make a plan for writing the full paper within 6 weeks.
4. Draft the disclosure sentence about the prior presentation.

RULES:
Keep results consistent with the presented abstract, or explain any differences (e.g. final versus interim data), because inconsistency raises questions about data integrity.

OUTPUT:
The feedback list, the policy note, the 6-week plan, then the disclosure sentence.
tips: Conference momentum fades in weeks. Start the paper the week you return.
prompts.try: Poster on inhaler technique errors that received strong interest at a national meeting.

prompts.t: Record a presentation for a virtual or hybrid conference
prompts.use: When the conference asks for a pre-recorded talk or you present online.
prompts.p:
You are a medical educator who produces clear, professional recorded talks on a modest budget.

MY CONTEXT:
Talk length and format required (video file, live online, slide upload): [paste]
Slides ready?: [yes / no]
Equipment available: [laptop, phone, microphone, quiet room]

TASK:
1. Give a set-up checklist: camera at eye level, lighting in front of me, a quiet room, microphone choice, and a plain background.
2. Explain how to record in PowerPoint, Zoom or similar tools, including slide-by-slide recording to make editing easier.
3. Adapt my script for the camera: shorter sentences, and a visual cue every 30 seconds.
4. Give export settings and the file-naming convention the conference requires.
5. Plan for live Q&A online: internet backup, and mute and unmute etiquette.

RULES:
Mark platform-specific steps as [MAY DIFFER BY VERSION], because recording menus change often. Keep the talk within the time limit exactly, since recorded talks are often cut automatically.

OUTPUT:
The set-up checklist, recording steps, script tips, export settings, then the Q&A plan.
tips: Record one slide at a time. A mistake then costs 40 seconds, not the whole talk.
prompts.try: 10-minute pre-recorded oral paper for an international virtual respiratory conference.

prompts.t: An accurate, catchy abstract title
prompts.p: Act as a conference abstract reviewer. Write 4 titles for my abstract, [ONE-LINE SUMMARY WITH DESIGN], under [LIMIT] characters: two descriptive and two that state the finding. None should overclaim or use undefined abbreviations. Mark the one most likely to attract reviewers.
prompts.try: Prospective cohort showing frailty predicts delirium after hip fracture surgery.

prompts.t: 25-word summary for the conference programme
prompts.p: Act as a conference programme editor. Summarise my accepted presentation, [PASTE ABSTRACT], in 25 words or fewer for delegates for the printed conference programme or app: what I studied, in whom, where, and the main finding, accurately, clearly and without jargon.
prompts.try: Abstract on the diagnostic accuracy of lung ultrasound in paediatric pneumonia.

prompts.t: One-page handout or QR page for my poster
prompts.p: Act as a scientific communicator. Create the content for a one-page handout or QR-linked page for my poster, [PASTE POSTER TEXT]: title, key figure description, 3 key findings, the take-home message, contact email and the full abstract, in under 300 words.
prompts.try: Poster on vitamin B12 deficiency in patients on long-term metformin.

prompts.t: Will my talk fit the time?
prompts.p: Act as a presentation coach. Check my script, [PASTE SCRIPT], against a [N]-minute slot at about 130 spoken words per minute. Tell me how far over or under I am, and which sentences to cut or merge to fit, without losing the key result.
prompts.try: A 1,450-word script for an 8-minute oral paper.

prompts.t: The closing take-home slide
prompts.p: Act as a conference presentation coach. Write my closing slide for [ONE-LINE FINDING AND DESIGN]: a message title, 2–3 take-home bullets of under 12 words each, in plain language, and one line on what comes next, all proportionate to my design.
prompts.try: Retrospective cohort linking delayed antibiotics with higher sepsis mortality.

prompts.t: Follow-up email after the conference
prompts.p: Act as an academic networking coach. Write a short, professional follow-up email to [NAME, ROLE], whom I met at [CONFERENCE] after my presentation on [TOPIC], thanking them and proposing [collaboration / sharing data / advice on the next study]. Keep it under 120 words.
prompts.try: Following up with a senior researcher who asked about multicentre collaboration.

prompts.t: Mixed-audience seminar deck, clinically rigorous
prompts.use: When you have a departmental seminar on any topic and want a complete, evidence-based deck.
prompts.why: Departmental audiences are mixed: MBBS students, interns, residents and consultants in the same room. A deck pitched at resident level, with a short foundation recap for juniors and a controversies section for consultants, keeps everyone engaged, and cites real evidence rather than textbook generalities.
prompts.p:
You are a senior academic in [SPECIALTY] who has delivered and moderated hundreds of departmental seminars. You are clinically rigorous, evidence-based and practical, and you never invent citations or statistics.

MY CONTEXT:
Topic: [e.g. Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome: from pathophysiology to ventilator management]
Audience: mixed (MBBS students, interns, junior residents, senior residents, consultants)
Time available: [e.g. 45 minutes + 15 minutes discussion]
Sources I have (guidelines, reviews, textbook chapters), uploaded or listed: [UPLOAD OR LIST]
Output format: [slide-by-slide text for PowerPoint / a .pptx file if your tool can create one]

TASK:
1. Pitch the core content at resident level, with a 1–2 slide foundation recap early, and advanced nuance for consultants.
2. Follow this structure, adapting as needed: title slide with a one-line clinical hook; why this matters (a representative case); foundation recap (definitions, classification); pathophysiology; clinical features and diagnostic approach (criteria or scores in tables); management, stepwise, first-line versus escalation; an evidence corner (landmark trials and current guidelines); controversies and grey zones; 3–5 key takeaways; references in Vancouver style.
3. For every slide give a message title, concise bullets (one idea per slide), a table where comparisons help, and speaker notes.
4. Mark what is exam-relevant for students and what is decision-changing for residents and consultants.
5. Suggest where a figure, flowchart or algorithm should go, and describe it.

RULES:
Name trials and guidelines only from my sources or with [VERIFY] beside each, because misremembered trial names and years are the most embarrassing seminar error. Mark every drug dose as [VERIFY DOSE FROM CURRENT GUIDELINE]. Show me the slide-by-slide text for review before building any file.

OUTPUT:
A slide table (number, title, bullets, visual, speaker notes, audience tag), then the reference list with [VERIFY] flags.

TWEAK:
End with the 5 questions a consultant is most likely to ask after this seminar, and short evidence-based answers.
tips: Tuning levers: change the depth (resident ↔ consultant), the slide count (about 1 slide per minute) and the visual style.
Verify every trial and guideline in the evidence corner against the original source before presenting.
Rehearse the controversies section. It is where the discussion will go.

prompts.t: From topic to seminar blueprint in one sitting
prompts.use: The day your seminar topic is assigned, before you open any textbook.
prompts.why: Most residents start a seminar by reading everything and end with 80 slides and no structure. Starting with objectives, a time budget and a storyline tells you exactly what to read and what to leave out.
prompts.p:
You are a medical educator and senior faculty member who mentors residents on seminar preparation. You think backwards from what the audience must be able to do after the session.

MY CONTEXT:
Topic as assigned: [e.g. Approach to hyponatraemia]
Specialty and my year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience and its level: [brief]
Duration: [minutes]
Days until the seminar: [N]
Moderator's known expectations or style: [brief or "unknown"]

TASK:
1. Clarify the scope: what is in, what is out, and how to phrase the final seminar title.
2. Write 4–6 learning objectives using Bloom's verbs (explain, differentiate, apply, choose).
3. Build a storyline: an opening case, 5–7 content blocks mapped to the objectives, and a closing return to the case.
4. Create a time budget per block that fits the duration.
5. For each block, list the must-read sources by type (current guideline, recent review, textbook chapter) with [VERIFY LATEST EDITION].
6. Make a day-by-day preparation plan for the days I have, including a rehearsal.
7. Predict the moderator's 5 likely questions.

RULES:
Keep the content proportional to the time, about one slide per minute, and cut anything not tied to an objective, because overlong seminars lose the audience in the middle. Name no specific papers from memory; describe the source type and mark it [FIND AND VERIFY].

OUTPUT:
Scope note, objectives, storyline table (block, objective, minutes, key points), the source list, the preparation plan, then the predicted questions.

TWEAK:
End with the single case vignette to open with, 60 words, de-identified and realistic for Indian practice.
tips: Show the objectives and storyline to your moderator a week before. It avoids a last-minute restructure.
Read the guideline first, the review second and the textbook last.
Keep the opening case alive: return to it in every block.

prompts.t: Evidence pack: guidelines and trials, verified from my sources
prompts.use: When your seminar needs an evidence corner and you have gathered the guidelines and key papers.
prompts.why: The evidence section is where seminars go wrong: trials cited with the wrong year, outcomes overstated, or guidelines quoted from memory. Building it strictly from uploaded sources, with quotes, makes it accurate and defensible when a consultant challenges it.
prompts.p:
You are an evidence-based medicine specialist who prepares evidence summaries for clinical guideline panels. You quote the source for every claim and state the certainty of evidence clearly.

MY CONTEXT:
Seminar topic and the clinical questions it must answer: [list 3–5 questions]
Guidelines uploaded (name, organisation, year): [UPLOAD / LIST]
Key trials and meta-analyses uploaded: [UPLOAD / LIST]
Setting to apply the evidence to: [e.g. Indian tertiary and district hospitals]
Audience and how much time the evidence section gets: [e.g. residents and consultants, 8 minutes]
My specialty and year: [brief]

TASK:
1. For each clinical question, summarise what the uploaded guidelines recommend, with the strength or grade, quoting the recommendation wording.
2. Build a trials table: trial, year, design, population, intervention versus comparator, primary outcome and result with CI, and the key limitation.
3. Identify where guidelines disagree with each other, and why.
4. Identify where the evidence does not apply well to Indian settings (population, resources, drug availability).
5. Write 3 evidence-corner slides with speaker notes.
6. List any major trial or guideline the audience will expect that is missing from my uploads, marked [FIND AND UPLOAD], so I can add it before the seminar.

RULES:
Use only the uploaded documents; for anything else write [NOT IN MY SOURCES — VERIFY], because a single wrong trial detail can discredit the whole seminar. Reproduce effect sizes exactly. State certainty levels as the guideline states them.

OUTPUT:
A recommendations table per question, the trials table, the disagreement notes, the applicability notes, then the slide text.

TWEAK:
End with the one piece of evidence I should read in full before presenting, because it is most likely to be questioned.
tips: Upload the guideline PDFs themselves, not summaries of them.
Put the year on every trial and guideline on the slides. Consultants check it.
If two guidelines disagree, show both. That is where the best discussion happens.

prompts.t: Full speaker script for a 45-minute seminar
prompts.use: When your slides are ready and you want to rehearse to time.
prompts.why: Reading slides aloud is the commonest seminar failure. A script written for speaking, with timing, transitions and planned interaction, lets you rehearse properly, then speak from notes on the day.
prompts.p:
You are a speaking coach for medical educators who writes natural, spoken scripts and trims them to the second.

MY CONTEXT:
My slides (titles and bullets, or upload the file): [PASTE OR UPLOAD]
Duration of the talk (excluding discussion): [e.g. 40 minutes]
Audience: [brief]
My speaking style and my nerves: [brief]
Points where I want audience interaction: [brief or "suggest"]
Parts of the content I find hardest to explain: [list]
Language mix the audience is comfortable with: [e.g. English with occasional Hindi]

TASK:
1. Write a spoken script per slide at about 130 words per minute, in conversational academic English.
2. Mark timing checkpoints (e.g. "by slide 10: 12 minutes").
3. Add a transition sentence between sections, so the story flows.
4. Insert 3–4 interaction moments: a question to the audience, a quick show of hands, or a case pause.
5. Mark the lines to memorise word for word (opening, key message, closing).
6. Flag slides whose script runs long, and suggest cuts.
7. For the hardest parts I listed, write a simpler explanation or an analogy I can use if the audience looks lost.
8. Write a 30-second emergency version of the conclusion in case time runs out.

RULES:
Keep facts exactly as on my slides and add no new data, because the script must match what the audience sees. Script the interaction moments with a fallback answer in case nobody responds.

OUTPUT:
A script table (slide, script, seconds, interaction), then the checkpoints and the memorise list.

TWEAK:
End with a 5-step rehearsal plan for the next 3 days.
tips: Rehearse aloud with a timer. Silent reading always underestimates the time.
Don't read the script on the day. Speak from the checkpoints and the memorised lines.
Record one rehearsal on your phone. You'll hear your filler words immediately.

prompts.t: Case-based interactive seminar
prompts.use: When you want a seminar built around an unfolding case rather than a lecture.
prompts.why: Case-based seminars keep the audience thinking instead of copying. Revealing a case in stages, with questions at each stage, teaches clinical reasoning and makes the content stick.
prompts.p:
You are a clinician-educator who designs case-based learning sessions for residents, and who knows how to reveal information at the right pace.

MY CONTEXT:
Topic: [TOPIC]
Learning objectives: [PASTE OR "suggest"]
Audience and number: [brief]
Duration: [minutes]
A real case I can adapt (de-identified), or "create a realistic one": [PASTE OR REQUEST]
Setting where the case takes place: [emergency / ward / OPD / district hospital]
Common mistakes residents make with this condition: [list or "suggest"]

TASK:
1. Build an unfolding case in 4–6 stages: presentation, examination, initial investigations, key result, management decision, and follow-up or complication.
2. At each stage, write 1–2 questions for the audience, the expected answers, and the teaching point to deliver.
3. Map each stage to a learning objective.
4. Add a short mini-lecture slide (3 bullets) after each stage to consolidate.
5. Close with a summary of the reasoning path, and take-home points.
6. Suggest how to run it: small groups, polls or calling on people.
7. Build at least one stage around a common mistake, so the audience can discover why it is wrong.
8. Give the timing for each stage so the whole case fits the duration.

RULES:
Keep the case realistic for Indian practice and fully de-identified. Mark drug doses and guideline specifics as [VERIFY], because case-based sessions invite detailed questions.

OUTPUT:
A stage table (stage, information revealed, questions, expected answers, teaching point, objective), the mini-lecture slides, then the facilitation guide.

TWEAK:
End with 2 variations of the case (a different age or comorbidity) for repeat sessions.
tips: Reveal information on separate slides. Showing everything at once kills the reasoning.
Wait 10 seconds after asking a question. Silence is thinking time.
Keep a "parking lot" for tangent questions and answer them at the end.

prompts.t: Mock moderator: grill me before the real seminar
prompts.use: 2–3 days before your seminar, once the slides are final.
prompts.why: The dreaded part of a seminar is the moderator's questions. A realistic mock session, one question at a time with feedback, turns fear into preparation and shows you exactly which slides need strengthening.
prompts.p:
You are a senior professor and seminar moderator known for probing questions on basics, recent evidence and practical application. You are strict but fair, and you give frank feedback.

MY CONTEXT:
Seminar topic and my specialty and year: [brief]
My slide titles and key content: [PASTE]
Areas I feel weakest in: [list]
My moderator's known style or favourite themes: [brief or "unknown"]
Duration of the seminar and the discussion slot: [brief]

TASK:
1. Ask me one question at a time, mixing basic science, clinical application, recent evidence, Indian context and "what would you do" scenarios.
2. After each answer, score it out of 10, give the ideal answer in 3–5 points, and tell me which slide should cover it better.
3. Include 2 classic trap questions moderators use on this topic.
4. Mix difficulty: start with 3 basic questions, then 4 applied questions, then 3 advanced or evidence questions.
5. After 10 questions, summarise my weak areas and the slides to strengthen, and give me a one-day plan to fix them.

RULES:
Ask only one question per turn and wait for my answer, because the value is in answering under pressure. Base questions on my topic and slides. Mark any fact in your ideal answers that depends on a guideline as [VERIFY].

OUTPUT:
Conversational: one question per turn, feedback in a short structured block (score, ideal answer, gap, slide to fix), then the final summary with the weak areas ranked from most to least urgent.

TWEAK:
End with the 3 questions I should prepare backup slides for.
tips: Answer aloud before typing. The seminar is spoken.
Add backup slides at the end of the deck for the questions you struggled with.
Ask a colleague to play the moderator with these questions for a real rehearsal.

prompts.t: Turn a new guideline into a seminar
prompts.use: When a new or updated clinical guideline is released and your department wants a session on it.
prompts.why: "What's new in the guideline" seminars are common and often done badly: a slide per recommendation, read aloud. The useful version shows what changed, why, what it means for practice here, and what remains uncertain.
prompts.p:
You are a guideline methodologist and clinician who explains guideline updates to busy clinicians, focusing on what changes practice.

MY CONTEXT:
The guideline (upload the full text or the recommendations section): [UPLOAD]
The previous version, if available: [UPLOAD OR "not available"]
Audience and duration: [brief]
Local practice for this condition in my hospital: [brief]
Drugs, tests or devices the guideline recommends that my hospital lacks: [list or "unsure"]
My specialty and year: [brief]

TASK:
1. List the key recommendations with their strength and certainty, quoting the exact wording and the section number.
2. Identify what is new or changed since the previous version, and the evidence cited for each change.
3. Classify each change as practice-changing, practice-confirming or minor.
4. Discuss applicability to Indian settings: resources, drug availability, cost and staffing.
5. Build a 20–30 minute slide plan: what changed, why, what to do on Monday, and uncertainties.
6. Write a one-page summary handout.
7. Suggest a simple audit the department could run to check adherence to the key recommendation.
8. Note which recommendations are conditional or based on low-certainty evidence, so the audience doesn't treat them as absolute.

RULES:
Quote only from the uploaded guideline and mark anything else [VERIFY], because a misquoted recommendation can change patient care. Don't overstate the certainty of weak recommendations.

OUTPUT:
The recommendations table, the changes table (old position, new position, evidence, classification), the applicability notes, the slide plan with timings, then the handout.

TWEAK:
End with the 3 recommendations most likely to be debated in the department, and why.
tips: Lead with what changes practice. Nobody remembers the minor edits.
Bring the guideline's own algorithm figure if it has one, and credit it.
Invite a senior to comment on local applicability. It turns the seminar into a discussion.

prompts.t: Learning objectives with Bloom's verbs
prompts.use: At the very start of seminar preparation.
prompts.p:
You are a medical educator trained in curriculum design who writes precise, measurable learning objectives.

MY CONTEXT:
Topic: [TOPIC]
Audience level: [MBBS / interns / residents / mixed]
Duration: [minutes]

TASK:
1. Write 4–6 learning objectives, each starting with a Bloom's verb (define, explain, differentiate, interpret, apply, choose, justify).
2. Spread them across levels: recall, understanding and application.
3. Say which part of the seminar will deliver each objective.
4. Suggest one quick end-of-session check for each objective.

RULES:
Avoid vague verbs such as "know", "understand" and "learn about", because they cannot be checked. Keep the number realistic for the time available.

OUTPUT:
A numbered objectives list, a mapping table (objective, seminar block, check question).
tips: Put the objectives on slide 2 and return to them on the last slide. Moderators notice.
prompts.try: Topic: approach to a patient with haemoptysis, for MD Medicine residents, 40 minutes.

prompts.t: Minute-by-minute time plan
prompts.use: Once your outline is ready, to make sure it fits the time.
prompts.p:
You are a meticulous academic event planner who keeps speakers on time.

MY CONTEXT:
Outline or slide titles: [PASTE]
Total time and the split between talk and discussion: [e.g. 45 + 15 minutes]
Planned interactive moments: [list]

TASK:
1. Allocate minutes to each section and slide.
2. Show a running clock with checkpoints every 10 minutes.
3. Identify sections to cut if I am running late, in order of priority.
4. Estimate the total slide count against the time (about one slide per minute).

RULES:
Include time for interaction, transitions and technical hiccups, because seminars always run over their plan.

OUTPUT:
A timing table (section, slides, minutes, clock), then the cut list.
tips: Put the checkpoint times in small text in your speaker notes, not on the slides.
prompts.try: A 60-slide outline for a 40-minute seminar on diabetic ketoacidosis.

prompts.t: Narrow a huge seminar topic to something teachable
prompts.use: When your assigned topic is enormous ("tuberculosis", "heart failure").
prompts.p:
You are a seminar moderator who helps residents choose a sharp angle on broad topics.

MY CONTEXT:
Assigned topic: [TOPIC]
Duration and audience: [brief]
Recent seminars in the department on related topics: [list or "unknown"]

TASK:
1. Propose 5 focused angles (e.g. diagnosis in a specific group, a management controversy, recent advances, an approach to a symptom, an Indian perspective).
2. For each, write a working title and 3 learning objectives.
3. Recommend one angle for my audience and time, with the reason.
4. Suggest how to acknowledge the rest of the topic in 1 slide.

RULES:
Keep each angle deliverable in the time available, because covering everything superficially teaches nothing.

OUTPUT:
An angles table (title, focus, objectives), then the recommendation.
tips: Confirm the narrowed title with your moderator before you start preparing.
prompts.try: Assigned topic: "Tuberculosis", 45 minutes, MD Respiratory Medicine residents.

prompts.t: Pitch the same topic to different audiences
prompts.use: When you must present one topic to students, residents or consultants, or to a mix of them.
prompts.p:
You are a medical educator who adapts content depth skilfully for different audiences.

MY CONTEXT:
Topic and my current outline: [PASTE]
Audience: [MBBS students / interns / residents / consultants / nurses / mixed]

TASK:
1. Say what each audience already knows and what they need from this topic.
2. Adjust the outline: what to expand, what to compress, what to drop.
3. Suggest the level of jargon, the depth of evidence and the type of examples for each.
4. For a mixed audience, show how to layer content (foundation recap, core, advanced corner).

RULES:
Keep the clinical accuracy the same at every level; only the depth and emphasis change, because simplifying must never mean being wrong.

OUTPUT:
A comparison table by audience, then the adjusted outline.
tips: For a mixed audience, tell the room explicitly: "This slide is for students; this one is for the consultants."
prompts.try: Topic: interpretation of pulmonary function tests.

prompts.t: Pathophysiology as a visual story
prompts.use: When your seminar needs a pathophysiology section that doesn't bore the room.
prompts.p:
You are a physiology-minded clinician who explains mechanisms visually and links every step to a clinical feature.

MY CONTEXT:
Condition: [CONDITION]
Audience level: [brief]
Slides available for this section: [e.g. 3]
Sources I am using: [UPLOAD / LIST]

TASK:
1. Break the pathophysiology into a sequence of 5–8 steps from trigger to clinical picture.
2. Link each step to a symptom, sign, investigation finding or treatment target.
3. Describe a flowchart or diagram for each slide.
4. Write speaker notes explaining each arrow.

RULES:
Keep to established mechanisms from my sources, and label emerging or debated mechanisms as such, because contested mechanisms presented as fact invite correction.

OUTPUT:
A step table (step, mechanism, clinical correlate, treatment target), diagram descriptions, then speaker notes.
tips: If a pathophysiology step doesn't explain a clinical feature or a treatment, cut it from the seminar.
prompts.try: Condition: septic shock, 3 slides, for residents.

prompts.t: Turn a classification into a clear table
prompts.use: When your topic has a classification, staging or grading system.
prompts.p:
You are a medical educator who turns classification systems into clean, memorable tables.

MY CONTEXT:
Classification or staging system: [name, or "the one used in guideline X"]
My source for it: [UPLOAD / CITE]
Audience: [brief]

TASK:
1. Present the classification as a table with categories, defining criteria and clinical significance.
2. Note the year and version, and any older versions still used in papers.
3. Suggest a memory aid if it helps.
4. Write one slide of speaker notes on how the classification guides management.

RULES:
Reproduce thresholds and criteria only from my source, and mark any detail I did not supply as [VERIFY FROM SOURCE], because classification cut-offs are commonly misremembered.

OUTPUT:
The table, the version note, the memory aid, then the speaker notes.
tips: Always show which version you are using. Moderators love asking about the previous one.
prompts.try: GOLD grouping for COPD assessment, from the current GOLD report.

prompts.t: Diagnostic approach as an algorithm
prompts.use: When your seminar covers "approach to" a symptom, sign or abnormal result.
prompts.p:
You are a clinician-teacher who builds practical, stepwise diagnostic algorithms.

MY CONTEXT:
Presenting problem: [e.g. hyponatraemia, pancytopenia, pleural effusion]
Setting: [ward / emergency / OPD; resource level]
Sources: [UPLOAD / LIST]

TASK:
1. Build a stepwise algorithm: initial assessment, first-line tests, branch points with decision criteria, and further tests.
2. Mark "can't-miss" diagnoses and red flags at the right points.
3. Describe the algorithm as a flowchart (boxes and arrows) for a slide.
4. Add a resource-limited variant for district hospitals.
5. Write speaker notes walking through one example patient.

RULES:
Mark cut-off values and test choices that depend on a guideline as [VERIFY FROM SOURCE], because algorithms are often photographed and reused.

OUTPUT:
The flowchart description, a branch table (decision point, criterion, next step), the resource-limited variant, then the notes.
tips: Walk the audience through the algorithm with a real case. Algorithms alone are hard to follow.
prompts.try: Approach to a unilateral pleural effusion, tertiary and district versions.

prompts.t: Management section, stepwise and practical
prompts.use: For the management part of a seminar.
prompts.p:
You are a senior clinician who teaches management as clear steps, from first-line care to escalation.

MY CONTEXT:
Condition and severity range: [brief]
Setting and resources: [brief]
Guidelines or sources: [UPLOAD / LIST]

TASK:
1. Lay out management in steps: immediate measures, first-line treatment, monitoring, escalation criteria and escalation options, and when to refer.
2. Present drug choices in a table with dose placeholders, key cautions and monitoring.
3. Highlight differences between tertiary and resource-limited settings.
4. Add the common mistakes in managing this condition.

RULES:
Mark every dose, duration and threshold as [VERIFY DOSE FROM CURRENT GUIDELINE], because dosing errors on slides can be copied into practice.

OUTPUT:
A stepwise outline, the drug table, the setting comparison, then the common mistakes.
tips: A one-slide "management on a page" summary is often the most photographed slide of the seminar.
prompts.try: Management of acute severe asthma in adults, tertiary and district settings.

prompts.t: Drug comparison table for a seminar
prompts.use: When your topic involves several drugs or drug classes.
prompts.p:
You are a clinical pharmacologist who builds accurate, exam-useful drug tables.

MY CONTEXT:
Drugs or classes to compare: [list]
Aspects I want: [mechanism, indications, dose, adverse effects, interactions, monitoring, cost, availability in India]
Source: [UPLOAD / LIST]

TASK:
1. Build a comparison table with the aspects I listed.
2. Highlight the distinguishing features between similar drugs.
3. Add a row for special populations (pregnancy, renal and hepatic impairment, elderly).
4. Write speaker notes on how to choose between them.

RULES:
Mark every dose as [VERIFY DOSE] and every availability or cost note as [VERIFY LOCALLY], because drug details change and vary by region.

OUTPUT:
The drug table, then the choice guidance in notes.
tips: Split big tables across two slides. A 10-column table is unreadable from the back row.
prompts.try: Compare DOACs with warfarin for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation.

prompts.t: Landmark trials in one table
prompts.use: For the "evidence corner" of your seminar, once you have the trial papers or abstracts.
prompts.p:
You are an evidence-based medicine teacher who summarises trials accurately and critically.

MY CONTEXT:
Trials to include (upload the papers or paste the abstracts): [UPLOAD / PASTE]
The clinical question they address: [one line]

TASK:
1. Build a table: trial, year, design, population, intervention versus comparator, primary outcome and result, and key limitation.
2. Write a one-line "what it changed" for each trial.
3. Put the trials in a timeline showing how the evidence evolved.
4. Write speaker notes for a 3-minute evidence walk-through.

RULES:
Use only the uploaded or pasted trial details, with numbers reproduced exactly, and mark missing details [NOT IN SOURCE], because trial details are what experts in the audience check.

OUTPUT:
The trials table, the timeline, then the speaker notes.
tips: One slide with 4–6 trials is enough. Pick the ones that changed practice.
prompts.try: Trials of corticosteroids in septic shock.

prompts.t: Controversies and grey zones
prompts.use: For the section of your seminar that keeps consultants engaged.
prompts.p:
You are a senior clinician who presents controversies fairly, giving both sides their strongest evidence.

MY CONTEXT:
Topic: [TOPIC]
Controversial questions I am aware of: [list or "suggest"]
Sources for each side: [UPLOAD / LIST]

TASK:
1. Identify 3–4 genuine controversies in current practice.
2. For each, present the arguments and evidence on both sides.
3. State what current guidelines say, if anything.
4. Suggest how the department might approach it, and what evidence is awaited.
5. Write one slide per controversy with a debate question.

RULES:
Present both sides with equal care, and support claims only from my sources or mark them [VERIFY], because a one-sided "controversy" slide will be challenged.

OUTPUT:
A controversy table (question, side A, side B, guideline position, awaited evidence), then the slides.
tips: End each controversy slide with a question to the room. It starts the discussion you want.
prompts.try: Controversies in fluid resuscitation for sepsis.

prompts.t: Recent advances slide set
prompts.use: When your seminar needs a "what's new" section.
prompts.p:
You are an academic clinician who tracks new evidence and separates genuine advances from hype.

MY CONTEXT:
Topic: [TOPIC]
Time window: [e.g. last 3 years]
New papers, guidelines or approvals I have found: [UPLOAD / LIST]

TASK:
1. Categorise the advances: new diagnostics, new therapies, new guideline positions, new understanding of the disease.
2. For each, give the evidence level and whether it is ready for practice, promising, or early research.
3. Note whether each is available or relevant in India.
4. Write 2–3 slides with speaker notes.

RULES:
Include only advances from the sources I gave, or mark them [VERIFY — FIND SOURCE], because AI-listed "advances" are often outdated or invented.

OUTPUT:
An advances table (advance, category, evidence level, readiness, India relevance), then the slides.
tips: Use a search tool with live citations (Perplexity or Consensus) to find recent advances, then verify each paper yourself.
prompts.try: Recent advances in the management of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

prompts.t: The Indian perspective slide
prompts.use: For the section of your seminar on Indian epidemiology, guidelines and practice.
prompts.p:
You are a public-health physician who knows Indian data sources, national programmes and practice realities.

MY CONTEXT:
Topic: [TOPIC]
Indian data and guidelines I have found (with sources): [LIST]

TASK:
1. Summarise the Indian burden using my sourced figures.
2. Summarise relevant Indian guidelines or national programme recommendations from my sources.
3. Highlight how Indian practice differs from Western guidelines: resources, drug availability, cost and disease patterns.
4. Identify gaps in Indian data.
5. Write 1–2 slides with speaker notes.

RULES:
Use only figures and guidelines I listed, with their sources and years, and mark anything else [VERIFY], because Indian statistics are often quoted from outdated surveys.

OUTPUT:
The summary, the differences table, the data gaps, then the slides.
tips: Always give the survey name and year with a prevalence figure on the slide.
prompts.try: Topic: COPD in India, with burden data from national surveys and the Global Burden of Disease study.

prompts.t: Compare two or more guidelines
prompts.use: When different societies recommend different things on your topic.
prompts.p:
You are a guideline analyst who compares recommendations clearly and explains why they differ.

MY CONTEXT:
Guidelines to compare (upload or list with year): [UPLOAD / LIST]
Clinical questions to compare on: [list]

TASK:
1. Build a side-by-side table: question, guideline A recommendation (with strength), guideline B recommendation (with strength).
2. Explain the reasons for differences: evidence interpretation, population, cost, or date of publication.
3. Suggest which is more applicable to my setting, and why.
4. Write one comparison slide with speaker notes.

RULES:
Quote recommendations from the uploaded documents and mark anything else [VERIFY], because paraphrased recommendations often lose their conditions.

OUTPUT:
The comparison table, the reasons, the applicability note, then the slide.
tips: Put the publication year of each guideline in the table header. It often explains the differences.
prompts.try: Compare two international hypertension guidelines on blood-pressure targets in older adults.

prompts.t: References slide and citation check
prompts.use: When finalising your seminar deck.
prompts.p:
You are a reference editor who formats seminar references in Vancouver style.

MY CONTEXT:
Sources I used, as I have them: [PASTE LIST]
Number of reference slides allowed: [e.g. 1–2]

TASK:
1. Format each reference in Vancouver style.
2. Flag references missing essential details, without inventing them.
3. Suggest how to cite sources on individual slides (small superscript numbers).
4. Select the 10–15 most important if the list is too long.

RULES:
Write [MISSING — CHECK PUBMED] for missing details instead of inventing them, because invented volume or page numbers make real references look fake.

OUTPUT:
The formatted list, then the flagged items and citation tips.
tips: Cite figures and tables you adapt from papers on the slide itself: "Adapted from [ref]".
prompts.try: 18 sources, including 2 guidelines, 6 trials, 3 reviews and a textbook.

prompts.t: End-of-seminar quiz
prompts.use: To close your seminar with active recall and check the objectives.
prompts.p:
You are a medical educator who writes high-quality MCQs that test application, not trivia.

MY CONTEXT:
Seminar topic and learning objectives: [PASTE]
Audience level: [brief]
Format: [show of hands / online poll / paper]

TASK:
1. Write 5–8 MCQs mapped to the objectives, mostly clinical-vignette style.
2. For each, give the answer and a 2-line explanation.
3. Include one question on a common misconception.
4. Suggest how to run the quiz in 5 minutes.

RULES:
Keep every correct answer consistent with my seminar content and mark guideline-dependent answers [VERIFY], because a wrong quiz answer undermines the whole session.

OUTPUT:
The numbered questions with options, then the answer key with explanations.
tips: An online poll (Mentimeter, Google Forms or Slido) turns a quiz into the most engaging 5 minutes of the seminar.
prompts.try: Seminar on approach to acute kidney injury, for interns.

prompts.t: Take-home messages that stick
prompts.use: For the final slide of any seminar.
prompts.p:
You are a medical educator who writes memorable, accurate take-home messages.

MY CONTEXT:
Seminar content summary or slide titles: [PASTE]
Learning objectives: [PASTE]
Audience: [brief]

TASK:
1. Write 3–5 take-home messages, each one sentence, specific, actionable and in plain language.
2. Map each message to a learning objective.
3. Suggest a visual layout for the slide.
4. Suggest the closing sentence to say aloud, and a follow-up resource to point people to.

RULES:
Each message must be supported by the seminar content, with no new claims, because the last slide is the one people photograph.

OUTPUT:
The messages, the mapping, the layout, then the closing line.
tips: "Check magnesium in every hypokalaemic patient" is a take-home message. "Electrolytes are important" is not.
prompts.try: Seminar on management of diabetic foot infections.

prompts.t: One-page handout for the audience
prompts.use: When you want the audience to leave with a summary.
prompts.p:
You are a medical educator who designs concise, printable one-page summaries.

MY CONTEXT:
Seminar content: [PASTE SLIDES OR SUMMARY]
Audience: [brief]
Format: [printed A4 / PDF shared on WhatsApp]
My name and department for the footer: [brief]

TASK:
1. Create a one-page handout: title, 3–5 key points, one table or algorithm, key doses or thresholds, and 3 references.
2. Keep it under 350 words.
3. Suggest a layout with boxes or columns.

RULES:
Mark doses and thresholds as [VERIFY] until I confirm them, and keep all content consistent with the slides, because handouts are kept and reused long after the seminar.

OUTPUT:
The handout text with its layout plan.
tips: Put your name and the date on the handout. It becomes part of your teaching portfolio.
prompts.try: Handout for a seminar on oxygen therapy in the ward.

prompts.t: Opening clinical vignette
prompts.use: To open any seminar with a case that grabs attention.
prompts.p:
You are a clinician-storyteller who opens teaching sessions with vivid, realistic cases.

MY CONTEXT:
Topic and the key teaching points: [brief]
Audience: [brief]
A real case to adapt (de-identified), if any: [PASTE OR "create one"]

TASK:
1. Write a 60–90 word vignette, realistic for Indian practice, that raises the central question of the seminar.
2. End with one question to the audience.
3. Write 2 alternative vignettes with a different twist.
4. Say how to return to the vignette at the end.

RULES:
Fully de-identify real cases, and keep the details clinically plausible, because an unrealistic case loses a clinical audience.

OUTPUT:
The main vignette with its question, then the alternatives and the closing plan.
tips: Present the vignette in the present tense. It creates urgency.
prompts.try: Topic: pulmonary embolism in pregnancy.

prompts.t: Basic science seminar with clinical hooks
prompts.use: For anatomy, physiology, pharmacology, pathology or microbiology seminars.
prompts.p:
You are a basic-science teacher who makes every concept clinically relevant.

MY CONTEXT:
Topic: [e.g. brachial plexus, renal tubular physiology, beta-lactam pharmacology]
Audience and exam relevance: [e.g. MD residents; university exam]
Duration: [minutes]

TASK:
1. Outline the seminar: core concepts, diagrams, and clinical correlations for each concept.
2. Suggest diagrams to draw or show, described clearly.
3. Add "clinical hook" slides linking each concept to a patient scenario.
4. Add 5 viva-style questions examiners ask on this topic.

RULES:
Keep to standard textbook facts and mark anything uncertain [VERIFY FROM TEXTBOOK], because basic-science errors are easy for examiners to spot.

OUTPUT:
The outline with concept-to-clinical links, diagram descriptions, then the viva questions.
tips: Draw the key diagram live on a board if you can. It teaches better than any slide.
prompts.try: Topic: brachial plexus anatomy and lesions, for MS Orthopaedics residents.

prompts.t: Seminar on a procedure or surgery
prompts.use: When your seminar covers a procedure: indications, technique and complications.
prompts.p:
You are a senior surgeon and teacher who explains procedures step by step with safety in mind.

MY CONTEXT:
Procedure: [PROCEDURE]
Audience: [brief]
Sources and videos available: [LIST]

TASK:
1. Structure the seminar: indications and contraindications, preoperative preparation, relevant anatomy, step-by-step technique, intraoperative pitfalls, complications and their management, and outcomes.
2. Suggest images or video clips for each step.
3. Add a safety checklist slide.
4. Add 5 questions examiners ask about this procedure.

RULES:
