prompts.try: A cohort study of statin use and outcomes in sepsis.

prompts.t: Was this study adequately powered?
prompts.p: Act as a biostatistician. Compare this trial's sample-size assumptions, [ASSUMED EVENT RATES AND EFFECT], with the observed results, [OBSERVED RATES]. Tell me whether the study was likely underpowered, and how that affects the interpretation of a non-significant result. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: Assumed control mortality 30%, observed 18%, with a non-significant result.

prompts.t: Is this outcome a surrogate?
prompts.p: Act as an outcomes researcher. Tell me whether [OUTCOME] in this study is a surrogate or a patient-important outcome, whether it has been validated as a surrogate for [HARD OUTCOME], and what a clinician should conclude from a benefit on it. Keep it under 120 words.
prompts.try: HbA1c reduction as the primary outcome in a diabetes drug trial.

prompts.t: Would this change my practice?
prompts.p: Act as a pragmatic senior clinician. Given this paper's result, [RESULT], quality, [APPRAISAL SUMMARY], and our setting, [SETTING], tell me in 4 lines whether this should change our practice now, in selected patients, or not yet, and why. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: A single-centre RCT showing benefit of a new sedation protocol.

prompts.t: Explain a methods term from my paper
prompts.p: Act as an EBM tutor. Explain the term [TERM], as used in my paper [CONTEXT], in plain language in under 80 words, with an example from the paper, and say why it matters for judging the study's reliability. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: Term: "fragility index" in a trial of tranexamic acid.

prompts.t: Does the title overclaim?
prompts.p: Act as a research-integrity reviewer. Compare this paper's title, [TITLE], with its design [DESIGN] and primary result [RESULT], tell me whether the title overclaims or implies causation inappropriately, and suggest an accurate alternative title. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: A cross-sectional study titled "Vitamin D deficiency causes severe COVID-19".

prompts.t: Relative versus absolute risk for the audience
prompts.p: Act as a medical educator. Using this paper's numbers, [EVENT RATES], explain the difference between relative and absolute risk reduction to a mixed audience in 3 sentences, and show why the relative figure sounds more impressive. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: A drug that reduces stroke from 2% to 1% over 5 years.

prompts.t: Explain the key figure in three lines
prompts.p: Act as a data-presentation coach. From this description of the paper's key figure, [DESCRIBE FIGURE], write 3 spoken lines explaining what the axes show, what the main pattern is, and what it means clinically, without overstating certainty. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: A figure showing cumulative incidence of infection in two groups over 90 days.

prompts.t: A sharp question to ask the presenter
prompts.p: Act as an experienced journal-club participant. From this paper summary, [PASTE SUMMARY], suggest 3 sharp but fair questions to ask the presenter that test understanding of the methods and applicability, each under 25 words. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: Summary of a trial of early goal-directed therapy.

prompts.t: Summarise the paper for colleagues
prompts.p: Act as a medical science communicator. Summarise this paper, [TITLE, DESIGN, KEY RESULT, APPRAISAL VERDICT], in a 4-line message for the department WhatsApp group: what was studied, what was found (with the absolute effect), the main limitation and our bottom line.
prompts.try: A trial of balanced crystalloids versus saline in the ICU.

prompts.t: Redesign my existing deck, slide by slide
prompts.use: When your deck is text-heavy, cluttered or inconsistent, and the talk is in a few days.
prompts.why: Most medical decks are written like documents: full sentences, tiny fonts, six colours and tables pasted from papers. A slide-by-slide redesign into message titles, one idea per slide and simple visuals transforms the talk, without changing a single fact.
prompts.p:
You are a presentation designer who specialises in medical and scientific talks. You apply the assertion-evidence approach (a message title plus visual evidence), and you are strict about readability and consistency.

MY CONTEXT:
My deck (paste the slide text, or upload the .pptx or PDF): [PASTE OR UPLOAD]
Talk type, audience and duration: [e.g. departmental seminar, residents, 40 minutes]
Venue and screen: [e.g. seminar room projector / hall / online]
Template or branding rules: [institution template or "free"]
Tool I will edit in: [PowerPoint / Google Slides / Keynote / Canva]

TASK:
1. Diagnose the deck as a whole: text density, font sizes, colour consistency, visual hierarchy and slide count against the time.
2. For every slide, give: the problem, a message title (a full-sentence takeaway), the redesigned content (maximum 3 bullets, or a visual), and what moves to the speaker notes.
3. Identify slides to merge, split or delete.
4. Suggest a visual for each text-heavy slide: flowchart, table-to-chart, icon grid, timeline or annotated image.
5. Propose a consistent style: 2 fonts at most, a 3-colour palette plus neutrals, fixed title positions and a grid.
6. Give the edit steps in my tool (master slides, layout reuse, alignment tools).

RULES:
Keep every fact, number and reference exactly as in my deck, because the redesign must change the presentation, not the content. Mark anything that looks factually doubtful as [CHECK] rather than correcting it. Keep body text at 24 pt or more and titles at 32 pt or more for a projector.

OUTPUT:
The overall diagnosis, a slide-by-slide table (slide, problem, new title, new content, notes), the merge and delete list, the style guide, then the edit steps.

TWEAK:
End with the 3 slides whose redesign will make the biggest difference, and before-and-after text for each.
tips: Redesign the master slide first. Every slide improves at once.
Read only the slide titles in order. If they tell the story, the redesign has worked.
Keep the old deck. If time runs out, present the 10 most important redesigned slides.

prompts.t: A personal slide design system for all my talks
prompts.use: When you present often and want every deck to look consistent and professional without starting from scratch.
prompts.why: Doctors present dozens of times a year: seminars, journal clubs, case presentations, CMEs. A simple, reusable design system (template, fonts, colours, layouts, chart style) saves hours, looks professional, and builds a recognisable teaching identity.
prompts.p:
You are a brand and presentation designer who builds simple design systems for clinicians and academics, focusing on readability, accessibility and speed of use.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
Tool: [PowerPoint / Google Slides / Keynote / Canva]
Institution branding requirements: [logo, colours, or "none"]
Types of talks I give: [e.g. seminars, journal clubs, case presentations, CMEs]
Style I like, or examples I admire: [brief or "suggest"]
Screen types: [projector / large display / online]

TASK:
1. Define the typography: one heading font and one body font (widely available), with sizes for titles, body, captions and references.
2. Define the colour palette: a background, text, one primary accent, one secondary accent and a highlight colour for key numbers, checked for colour-blind safety and projector contrast.
3. Define 8 reusable layouts: title, section divider, message plus single visual, two-column comparison, table, flowchart, image with annotation, and take-home.
4. Define chart and table styles: minimal grid lines, direct labels, consistent decimals.
5. Define rules for icons, images and references on slides.
6. Give the step-by-step set-up of the master template in my tool.

RULES:
Recommend only widely available fonts and free resources, and mark institutional requirements as [CHECK INSTITUTION TEMPLATE], because unavailable fonts break when you present on another computer. Keep contrast high enough for poor projectors.

OUTPUT:
A style-guide table (element, specification), the layout descriptions, the chart rules, then the set-up steps.

TWEAK:
End with a one-page checklist to run on any deck before presenting.
tips: Embed fonts or use system fonts. Hospital computers rarely have your fancy fonts.
Save the template as a theme file so every new deck starts from it.
Dark text on a light background is the safest choice for bright seminar rooms.

prompts.t: Build a deck with AI tools, safely
prompts.use: When you want to use AI (Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot in PowerPoint, Gamma, Canva) to create a first draft of a deck quickly.
prompts.why: AI slide tools produce beautiful decks in minutes, with invented statistics, outdated guidelines and generic content. Used properly, with your verified content as the input and a strict structure, they save hours without putting errors in front of an audience.
prompts.p:
You are a medical educator and AI-tools trainer who builds presentation workflows that are fast and accurate.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
Topic, audience and duration: [brief]
AI tool I will use: [Claude / ChatGPT / Copilot in PowerPoint / Gamma / Canva Magic Design / other]
My verified content (outline, notes, key sources, numbers): [PASTE]
Design preferences or template: [brief]

TASK:
1. Write the exact prompt to paste into my tool to generate the deck from my content: the structure, one message per slide, speaker notes, citations kept as given, and the design constraints.
2. Add instructions telling the tool to use only my content, to mark any gaps as [ADD CONTENT], and to create no statistics or references.
3. Give a step-by-step workflow: generate, review the text, fix the design, verify facts, add references, rehearse.
4. Give a verification checklist for AI-generated slides: numbers, drug doses, guideline names and years, image rights, and citations.
5. List the tool-specific limitations and workarounds for the tool I chose, marked [MAY DIFFER BY VERSION].

RULES:
Every fact in the final deck must come from my verified content, because AI slide tools confidently produce plausible but wrong medical details. Show me the slide-by-slide text for approval before any file is built.

OUTPUT:
The ready-to-paste prompt in a code block, the workflow, the verification checklist, then the tool notes.

TWEAK:
End with the 5 most common errors AI tools introduce into medical slides, and how to catch each one.
tips: Give the AI your outline and sources, not just a topic. Topic-only prompts produce generic decks.
Always check drug doses and guideline years on AI-made slides. They are the most frequent errors.
Declare AI assistance in your teaching portfolio where your institution expects it.

prompts.t: Turn data and tables into clear slide visuals
prompts.use: When your talk includes results, statistics or comparisons that currently sit in dense tables.
prompts.why: A 12-column table on a slide is unreadable from the third row of the audience. Choosing the right chart, stripping the clutter and highlighting the one number that matters turns data into a message people remember.
prompts.p:
You are a data-visualisation specialist for medical talks who makes charts readable from the back of a lecture hall.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
The data or tables (paste): [PASTE DATA / TABLES]
The message each table should convey: [list, or "suggest"]
Tool: [PowerPoint / Excel / Google Sheets / Canva]
Audience and room size: [brief]

TASK:
1. For each table, identify the single message it supports.
2. Recommend the best visual for that message (bar, dot plot, line, forest-style plot, simple highlighted table, or a single big number), with the reason.
3. Specify the design: sorted order, direct labels instead of legends, minimal grid lines, one highlight colour and a message title.
4. Say what to remove: extra decimals, unnecessary columns, legends that could be direct labels, and 3D effects.
5. Give step-by-step build instructions in my tool.
6. Write the message title and a one-line speaker note for each visual.
7. Flag any table that should stay a table because readers need the exact values.
7. Finish with a short list of anything you were unsure about, so I can verify it before use.

RULES:
Keep every number exactly as in my data, and keep the axes honest (bars start at zero), because distorted charts mislead the audience and damage your credibility.

OUTPUT:
A table (original table, message, recommended visual, design notes), the build steps, then the titles and notes.

TWEAK:
End with the one chart that best tells the main story of the talk.
tips: If only one number matters, show only that number, in very large font, with context.
Sort bars by value, not alphabetically, unless the order has meaning.
Use colour to highlight, not to decorate. Grey everything except the key bar.

prompts.t: Rewrite slide titles as messages
prompts.use: When your slide titles are topic labels ("Pathophysiology", "Results").
prompts.p:
You are a scientific presentation coach who teaches the assertion-evidence method.

MY CONTEXT:
My slide titles and a one-line summary of each slide's content: [PASTE]
Talk type and audience: [brief]

TASK:
1. Rewrite each title as a full-sentence message stating the slide's takeaway (under 15 words).
2. Keep the titles consistent in tone and tense.
3. Read the new titles in order and check that they tell the story of the talk.
4. Flag slides with no clear message, which need rethinking.

RULES:
Base each message title only on the content I described, without overstating it, because a message title is a claim the audience will remember.

OUTPUT:
A before-and-after table, then the story check and the flags.
tips: "Early antibiotics were linked to lower mortality" teaches. "Results" does not.
prompts.try: Titles such as "Introduction", "Epidemiology", "Diagnosis", "Treatment", "Evidence", "Conclusion".

prompts.t: Turn a text-heavy slide into a visual
prompts.use: For any slide with more than about 40 words.
prompts.p:
You are an information designer for medical education.

MY CONTEXT:
The slide text: [PASTE SLIDE TEXT]
Purpose of the slide: [brief]
Tool: [PowerPoint / Google Slides / Canva]

TASK:
1. Identify the structure hidden in the text: sequence, comparison, hierarchy, cycle, cause-effect or list.
2. Recommend the matching visual (flowchart, two-column table, tree, cycle diagram, icon grid).
3. Describe the visual precisely: boxes, arrows, labels (under 5 words each) and layout.
4. Move the remaining detail to speaker notes.
5. Give the build steps in my tool (e.g. SmartArt or shapes).

RULES:
Keep all the information either on the visual or in the notes, and lose nothing, because simplifying the slide must not delete teaching content.

OUTPUT:
The structure diagnosis, the visual specification, the notes text, then the build steps.
tips: If you can't find a structure in the text, the slide probably tries to say two things. Split it.
prompts.try: A 90-word slide listing the causes, features and management of hyperkalaemia.

prompts.t: Simplify a table for a slide
prompts.use: When you want to show a table from a paper or guideline on a slide.
prompts.p:
You are a slide designer who makes tables readable from the back row.

MY CONTEXT:
The original table: [PASTE TABLE]
What the audience needs to take from it: [one line]

TASK:
1. Keep only the rows and columns needed for the message.
2. Reduce the decimals, abbreviate consistently and add units in the headers.
3. Highlight the key cell or row.
4. Split it into two slides if necessary.
5. Write the source line for the bottom of the slide.

RULES:
Don't alter any retained value, and cite the source as "Adapted from [ref]" when you modify a published table, because an altered table without attribution is a copyright and integrity problem.

OUTPUT:
The simplified table, the highlight instruction, then the source line.
tips: A table with more than 5 rows and 4 columns usually needs splitting or a chart.
prompts.try: A 10 × 8 table of antibiotic dosing across renal-function categories.

prompts.t: Build a flowchart slide
prompts.use: For processes, pathways and approaches.
prompts.p:
You are a clinical pathway designer who draws clean flowcharts.

MY CONTEXT:
The process or approach in text: [PASTE]
Tool: [PowerPoint / Google Slides / draw.io / Canva]

TASK:
1. Convert the process into steps and decision points.
2. Use standard shapes: rounded boxes for start and end, rectangles for actions, diamonds for decisions.
3. Keep the labels under 6 words, with yes and no on the decision branches.
4. Arrange it top-to-bottom or left-to-right, with no crossing arrows.
5. Give the build steps and the alignment tips.

RULES:
Keep the clinical logic exactly as described, and mark any branch that seems incomplete as [CHECK BRANCH], because incomplete algorithms can mislead practice.

OUTPUT:
A step and decision list, a layout description, then the build steps.
tips: If the flowchart needs more than 12 boxes, split it into two slides.
prompts.try: Approach to a patient with a low platelet count.

prompts.t: Adapt a guideline algorithm for a slide
prompts.use: When you want to show a published algorithm clearly.
prompts.p:
You are a medical illustrator who adapts complex guideline algorithms for teaching.

MY CONTEXT:
The algorithm (upload the figure or describe it): [UPLOAD / DESCRIBE]
Its source (guideline and year): [cite]
Audience: [brief]

TASK:
1. Identify the core pathway most relevant to my audience.
2. Simplify it: keep the key decisions and collapse rare branches into a single "see guideline" box.
3. Describe the redesigned algorithm with fewer, larger boxes.
4. Add a source credit line.
5. Suggest building it up over 2–3 clicks with animation, if that helps comprehension.

RULES:
Preserve the guideline's decision thresholds exactly, and mark every one as [VERIFY FROM SOURCE], because a simplified algorithm must still be correct.

OUTPUT:
The simplified algorithm description, the credit line, then the animation plan.
tips: Tell the audience you have simplified it, and where to find the full version.
prompts.try: A guideline algorithm for managing acute exacerbations of COPD.

prompts.t: Two conditions side by side
prompts.use: When teaching differences between two similar conditions, drugs or tests.
prompts.p:
You are a clinical teacher who builds memorable comparison slides.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience or purpose: [brief]
The two items to compare: [A and B]
Aspects to compare: [list, or "suggest"]
Source: [cite]

TASK:
1. Choose 5–7 comparison aspects that best discriminate between them.
2. Build a two-column table with short entries.
3. Highlight the 1–2 features that best distinguish them.
4. Write speaker notes with a clinical example.

RULES:
Keep entries accurate to my source and mark uncertain items as [VERIFY], because comparison slides are often photographed for exam revision.

OUTPUT:
The comparison table, the highlight, then the notes.
tips: Put the most discriminating feature first. That's the one students will remember.
prompts.try: Transudate versus exudate pleural effusion.

prompts.t: A timeline slide
prompts.use: For history, disease course, treatment phases or a patient journey.
prompts.p:
You are a visual storyteller for medical talks.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience or purpose: [brief]
Events with dates or time points: [PASTE]
Purpose: [history / clinical course / treatment plan]

TASK:
1. Select the 5–8 most important points.
2. Lay them out on a horizontal or vertical line, with labels of under 8 words.
3. Mark the key turning point visually.
4. Give the build steps.

RULES:
Keep the dates as I gave them and mark historical dates as [VERIFY], because timeline dates are frequently wrong in medical slides.

OUTPUT:
The selected points, the layout description, then the steps.
tips: For a patient's course, use relative time (Day 0, Day 3), which also protects privacy.
prompts.try: The clinical course of a dengue patient from fever onset to recovery.

prompts.t: Clinical image slide with annotation
prompts.use: When showing an X-ray, CT, ECG, clinical photo or histology slide.
prompts.p:
You are a radiology and pathology educator who annotates images for teaching.

MY CONTEXT:
The image and its key findings: [DESCRIBE]
Audience: [brief]
Source or ownership, and consent: [brief]

TASK:
1. Suggest the layout: a large image with a minimal title.
2. Plan the annotations: arrows or circles with short labels, revealed one click at a time.
3. Plan a "before" (unmarked) and an "after" (annotated) version.
4. Write the speaker notes, describing the findings systematically.
5. Write the credit or consent line.

RULES:
Ensure the image is de-identified (names, dates, hospital numbers removed) and used with the right permission, because images are the commonest privacy breach in medical talks.

OUTPUT:
The layout, the annotation plan, the notes, then the credit line.
tips: Let the audience look at the unmarked image for 10 seconds before showing the arrows.
prompts.try: A chest X-ray showing a left-sided tension pneumothorax.

prompts.t: Icons and simple graphics for concepts
prompts.use: When a slide explains abstract concepts that could be shown visually.
prompts.p:
You are a graphic designer for health education.

MY CONTEXT:
The concepts on the slide: [list]
Tool: [PowerPoint (built-in icons) / Canva / Noun Project / other]
Style of the deck: [brief]

TASK:
1. Suggest a simple icon for each concept, with search keywords for my tool.
2. Suggest a layout (icon grid, process row, or hub and spoke).
3. Keep the icons in one consistent style and colour.
4. Pair each icon with a label of under 4 words.

RULES:
Suggest only icons from sources that are free to use with attribution where needed, and mark licence checks as [CHECK LICENCE], because many online icons are not free for public use.

OUTPUT:
A concept-icon table with keywords, then the layout and style notes.
tips: Use icons from one family only. Mixed styles look amateur.
prompts.try: Concepts: risk factors for stroke (hypertension, diabetes, smoking, atrial fibrillation, dyslipidaemia).

prompts.t: Colours that work for everyone
prompts.use: When choosing a colour scheme, or checking an existing deck.
prompts.p:
You are an accessibility specialist for visual presentations.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
My current colours (names or hex codes): [list]
Background: [light / dark]
Venue: [projector / screen / online]

TASK:
1. Check the contrast between text and background, and flag failures.
2. Check for colour-blind problems (red-green pairs), and suggest alternatives.
3. Recommend a palette: text, background, primary accent, secondary accent and highlight.
4. Recommend redundant cues (labels, patterns) for charts.

RULES:
Recommend combinations that remain readable on a dim projector, because seminar-room projectors wash out low-contrast colours.

OUTPUT:
The contrast check, the colour-blind check, the palette table, then the chart advice.
tips: Never use red versus green alone to show good versus bad. Add labels or symbols.
prompts.try: A deck with light-blue text on a white background and red/green charts.

prompts.t: Fonts and sizes that are readable
prompts.use: When setting up a deck, or fixing one that's hard to read.
prompts.p:
You are a typography specialist for presentations.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Current fonts and sizes: [list]
Room size and screen: [brief]

TASK:
1. Recommend fonts: one sans-serif for headings and body, widely available.
2. Recommend sizes: titles, body, table text, captions and references.
3. Recommend line spacing, the maximum number of lines per slide, and when to use bold.
4. Flag the problems in my current setup.

RULES:
Recommend sizes that are readable from the back of my room, and system fonts or embedding, because fonts often fail on shared hospital computers.

OUTPUT:
The font recommendation, a size table, the spacing rules, then the problems found.
tips: Test your slide from the back of the room, or zoom out to 50% on your laptop.
prompts.try: A deck using a 14 pt script font for body text in a 100-seat hall.

prompts.t: When to use animation, and when not to
prompts.use: When deciding on builds and transitions for your deck.
prompts.p:
You are a presentation coach who uses animation only to support understanding.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Slides where I'm considering animation: [DESCRIBE]

TASK:
1. For each slide, say whether animation helps (e.g. building an algorithm step by step, or revealing a case) or distracts.
2. Recommend simple builds only (appear or fade), in a consistent style.
3. Recommend a transition style for the whole deck.
4. Warn about technical risks (PDF export, other computers).

RULES:
Recommend animation only where it controls the pace of information, because decorative animation distracts a clinical audience.

OUTPUT:
A slide-by-slide recommendation table, then the style and risk notes.
tips: Always keep a PDF backup. Animations disappear in PDF, so check the key slides still make sense.
prompts.try: An unfolding case presentation and a complex management algorithm.

prompts.t: Cut my deck to fit the time
prompts.use: When you have far more slides than minutes.
prompts.p:
You are a ruthless but fair presentation editor.

MY CONTEXT:
Slide titles with a one-line content summary for each: [PASTE]
Time available: [minutes]
The core message and objectives: [brief]

TASK:
1. Rank the slides by importance to the core message and objectives.
2. Identify slides to delete, merge or move to the backup section.
3. Produce the final slide list, fitting about one slide per minute.
4. Check that the story still flows after the cuts.

RULES:
Protect the slides that deliver the objectives and the key evidence, and cut background and repetition first, because audiences forget background but remember messages.

OUTPUT:
A ranking table, the cut list, then the final sequence.
tips: Move cut slides to a backup section after your conclusion. They're useful for questions.
prompts.try: 68 slides for a 30-minute seminar on anaemia.

prompts.t: Write speaker notes for my slides
prompts.use: When your slides are ready but you haven't planned what to say.
prompts.p:
You are a speaking coach who writes concise, speakable notes.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Slide text (all slides): [PASTE]
Talk duration: [minutes]
My knowledge sources for the details: [LIST]

TASK:
1. Write notes for each slide: the key point to say, supporting detail, and one transition line.
2. Keep each slide's notes under 80 words.
3. Mark the time checkpoints.
4. Add a "likely question" note on the key slides.

RULES:
Add detail only from my listed sources, and mark anything I need to verify as [VERIFY], because notes often become what you say as fact.

OUTPUT:
A slide-by-slide notes table.
tips: Notes are prompts, not a script. Bullet fragments are easier to glance at than sentences.
prompts.try: A 25-slide deck on the management of acute stroke.

prompts.t: Separate the slides from the handout
prompts.use: When you're tempted to put everything on the slides "so they have it".
prompts.p:
You are a medical educator who designs slides for listening and handouts for reading.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
My current deck (text-heavy): [PASTE]
Audience: [brief]

TASK:
1. Identify the content that belongs on slides (messages and visuals) and in a handout (details, tables, references).
2. Produce the trimmed slide content.
3. Produce the handout content (1–2 pages).
4. Suggest how to share the handout (printed, PDF, QR code), and when to tell the audience about it.

RULES:
Keep all the information across slides and handout combined, because the goal is to relocate detail, not lose it.

OUTPUT:
The trimmed slide list, then the handout text.
tips: Tell the audience at the start that a handout exists. They'll stop photographing every slide.
prompts.try: A 40-slide deck on antibiotic selection packed with dosing tables.

prompts.t: A design brief for building slides in Canva
prompts.use: When you'll build or polish the deck in Canva.
prompts.p:
You are a Canva power user who designs clean medical presentations.

MY CONTEXT:
Slide outline with content: [PASTE]
Style preference: [e.g. minimal, dark, light]
Branding: [institution colours / Parabox / none]

TASK:
1. Recommend search terms for suitable Canva presentation templates.
2. Specify the brand kit set-up (fonts, colours).
3. Map each slide in my outline to a Canva layout type.
4. Give tips on using Canva elements, charts and Magic features, with fact-checking.
5. Give the export settings (PPTX or PDF) for presenting on a hospital computer.

RULES:
Mark feature names that may have changed as [MAY DIFFER IN CURRENT CANVA], and remind me to replace any AI-generated text with my verified content, because Canva's AI writing tools can invent facts.

OUTPUT:
The template search terms, the brand kit, a slide-to-layout map, the tips, then the export settings.
tips: Export to PPTX and open it once on the presentation computer. Canva fonts sometimes don't carry over.
prompts.try: A 20-slide CME talk on thyroid disorders in pregnancy.

prompts.t: A prompt for AI slide generators
prompts.use: When using Gamma, Copilot in PowerPoint, Canva Magic Design or a similar tool.
prompts.p:
You are a prompt engineer for AI presentation tools.

MY CONTEXT:
Topic, audience and duration: [brief]
My verified content outline: [PASTE]
Tool: [name]

TASK:
1. Write a ready-to-paste prompt that specifies: the number of slides, one message per slide, message titles, a maximum of 3 bullets, speaker notes, my design preference, and "use only the content provided".
2. Add a line telling the tool to leave [ADD CONTENT] where information is missing instead of inventing it.
3. Suggest 3 follow-up prompts to refine the output.

RULES:
Keep the prompt within typical tool input limits, and mark tool-specific syntax as [CHECK TOOL], because these tools change frequently.

OUTPUT:
The main prompt in a code block, then the follow-up prompts.
tips: Paste your outline, not just the topic. The quality of the output follows the quality of the input.
prompts.try: 15-slide seminar on management of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.

prompts.t: Choose the right chart for a slide
prompts.use: When you have numbers to show and don't know which chart to use.
prompts.p:
You are a data-visualisation teacher for clinicians.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
The data and the comparison I want to show: [DESCRIBE]
Audience: [brief]

TASK:
1. Recommend the chart type and explain why.
2. Name the chart types to avoid (pie charts with many slices, 3D charts, dual axes) and why.
3. Specify the axes, labels, ordering and highlight colour.
4. Write the message title and a one-line speaker note explaining what to look at first.

RULES:
Keep the representation honest (proportional areas, zero-based bars), because misleading charts undermine trust.

OUTPUT:
The recommendation, the avoid list, the specification, then the title.
tips: A dot plot is often clearer than a bar chart for comparing a few values.
prompts.try: Prevalence of five risk factors in our cohort versus national data.

prompts.t: Citing sources on slides
prompts.use: When finalising slides that use published data, figures or guidelines.
prompts.p:
You are an academic presenter who cites cleanly without cluttering slides.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Sources used in my deck: [LIST]
Slides that use figures or tables from papers: [list]

TASK:
1. Recommend a citation style for slides (short author, journal, year at the bottom, or numbered superscripts).
2. Format the short citations for each source.
3. Write "Adapted from" credit lines for reused figures.
4. Format a references slide in Vancouver style.

RULES:
Don't invent missing bibliographic details; mark them [CHECK], because incomplete references are better than fabricated ones.

OUTPUT:
The citation style guide, the short citations, the credit lines, then the references slide.
tips: A small source line under each evidence slide lets the audience judge the evidence immediately.
prompts.try: 12 sources, including 3 figures reproduced from guidelines.

prompts.t: Title and opening slide design
prompts.use: When designing your first slide.
prompts.p:
You are a presentation designer who makes strong first impressions.

MY CONTEXT:
Talk title, my name, designation and institution: [brief]
Event and date: [brief]
Branding requirements: [brief]

TASK:
1. Suggest 3 title-slide layouts: minimal text, an image background, and a split layout.
2. Recommend what to include and what to leave out.
3. Suggest a strong visual or a one-line hook.
4. Recommend a second slide (objectives or opening case).

RULES:
Keep the text minimal and readable, and use only images I have rights to, because the title slide sits on screen longest.

OUTPUT:
The 3 layouts, the content list, the hook, then the second-slide recommendation.
tips: Put your name on the title slide once. Your institution's logo only needs to appear once, too.
prompts.try: Seminar on "Sepsis in 2026: what's changed?" by a second-year resident.

prompts.t: Section divider slides that guide the audience
prompts.use: For talks longer than 20 minutes with distinct sections.
prompts.p:
You are a presentation designer focused on audience navigation.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience or purpose: [brief]
My talk outline with its sections: [PASTE]

TASK:
1. Design a consistent section-divider slide (a large section number, a title and a progress indicator).
2. Write a divider title and a one-line "what's next" for each section.
3. Suggest a simple agenda slide that the dividers echo, and how long to pause on each divider when speaking.

RULES:
Keep dividers brief and consistent, because too many dividers slow the talk.

OUTPUT:
The divider design, the divider texts, then the agenda slide.
tips: A small progress bar or "Section 2 of 4" helps audiences stay with you in long talks.
prompts.try: A 50-minute seminar with 5 sections on chronic kidney disease.

prompts.t: Slides for online teaching and webinars
prompts.use: When presenting on Zoom, Teams, Google Meet or a recorded platform.
prompts.p:
You are an online medical educator.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
My deck: [PASTE OR DESCRIBE]
Platform and audience devices (many on phones?): [brief]

TASK:
1. Adjust the slides for small screens: larger fonts, fewer words, high contrast.
2. Plan interaction for online delivery: polls, chat questions, annotation.
3. Suggest pacing changes (more frequent visual changes).
4. Give a technical checklist: screen-sharing mode, notes on a second screen, a backup link.

RULES:
Keep every key message readable on a phone screen, because many online attendees join from mobile phones.

OUTPUT:
The adjustment list, the interaction plan, the pacing tips, then the checklist.
tips: Change something on screen at least every 60–90 seconds to keep online attention.
prompts.try: A 45-minute webinar on insulin titration for general practitioners.

prompts.t: Using images and figures legally
prompts.use: Before using images, figures or videos from the internet, papers or textbooks.
prompts.p:
You are an academic copyright adviser.

MY CONTEXT:
Images and figures I want to use and their sources: [LIST]
Where the talk will be shown or shared: [internal teaching / conference / recorded online / published slides]

TASK:
1. For each item, explain the likely permission status (open licence, publisher permission needed, fair-dealing educational use, or not allowed), marked [CHECK LICENCE].
2. Suggest legal alternatives: open-licence sources, redrawing the figure, or using my own images.
3. Write the credit lines.
4. Explain patient-image consent requirements.

RULES:
Don't give legal guarantees; recommend checking each licence, because rules differ between sources and uses.

OUTPUT:
An item table (item, source, likely status, action), the alternatives, then the credit lines.
tips: Redrawing a figure in your own style with "Adapted from" is usually the simplest safe option.
prompts.try: Figures from a textbook, a guideline PDF and images found through a search engine.

prompts.t: Turn a slide title into a message
prompts.p: Act as a presentation coach. Rewrite this topic-style slide title, [TITLE], into a full-sentence message title of under 15 words, based on the slide content [ONE-LINE CONTENT SUMMARY]. Give 3 options and mark the clearest one. Keep it accurate, without overclaiming.
prompts.try: Title: "Outcomes". Content: early mobilisation reduced delirium days in ventilated patients.

prompts.t: Check a slide for clutter
prompts.p: Act as a slide designer. Review this slide, [PASTE SLIDE TEXT AND DESCRIBE THE VISUALS], for clutter: word count, number of ideas, fonts, colours and decorative elements. Give a verdict and the 3 most useful fixes, keeping all the facts.
prompts.try: A slide with 8 bullets, 2 logos, a clip-art image and 3 font colours.

prompts.t: Paragraph to one clean slide
prompts.p: Act as an information designer. Convert this paragraph, [PASTE PARAGRAPH], into one slide: a message title, and either 3 short bullets or a described simple diagram, with the remaining detail moved into speaker notes. Keep every fact accurate. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: A paragraph on the stages of acute kidney injury and their criteria.

prompts.t: A three-colour palette for my deck
prompts.p: Act as a presentation designer. Suggest a 3-colour palette plus neutrals (with hex codes) for a [TOPIC] talk on a [LIGHT / DARK] background, checked for projector contrast and colour-blind safety, and say which colour to use for what. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: A paediatrics seminar on a light background.

prompts.t: Font sizes for my room
prompts.p: Act as a typography expert for presentations. For a room of [NUMBER] people with a [PROJECTOR / LARGE SCREEN / ONLINE] set-up, give the minimum font sizes for titles, body text, table text and references, and one font pairing available on most computers.
prompts.try: A 60-seat seminar hall with an old projector.

prompts.t: Icon ideas for my concepts
prompts.p: Act as a graphic designer for health education. Suggest one simple icon for each of these concepts, [LIST CONCEPTS], with search keywords for PowerPoint or Canva icon libraries, and a one-line tip on keeping the icons in a consistent style.
prompts.try: Concepts: fever, cough, weight loss, night sweats, haemoptysis.

prompts.t: Alt text for my slide images
prompts.p: Act as an accessibility specialist. Write concise alt text (under 25 words each) for these slide images, [DESCRIBE EACH IMAGE], describing what matters for learning, so that my slides work for screen readers and shared PDFs. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: A chest X-ray with consolidation, a flowchart and a bar chart of mortality.

prompts.t: A caption for a figure on a slide
prompts.p: Act as a scientific editor. Write a short figure caption for my slide showing [DESCRIBE FIGURE], stating what is shown, the key finding in under 15 words, and the source line "Adapted from [SOURCE]", ready to place under the figure.
prompts.try: A Kaplan-Meier curve from a published trial.

prompts.t: Should these bullets be a diagram?
prompts.p: Act as an information designer. Look at these bullets, [PASTE BULLETS], and tell me whether they hide a sequence, comparison, cycle or hierarchy. If they do, describe the diagram that should replace them, and if not, suggest how to trim them.
prompts.try: Bullets describing the steps of the coagulation cascade.

prompts.t: Design my final slide
prompts.p: Act as a presentation coach. Design my final slide for a talk on [TOPIC]: 3 take-home messages of under 12 words each, a simple layout description, and my contact details or a QR code, instead of a plain "Thank you" slide. Keep it memorable and accurate.
prompts.try: A seminar on stroke thrombolysis in district hospitals.

prompts.t: QR code slide content
prompts.p: Act as a medical educator. Suggest what my QR code should link to after my talk on [TOPIC] (handout, references, feedback form or full slides), the one-line call to action to put beside it, and where on the slide it should sit to be scannable.
prompts.try: A CME talk on hypertension management for general practitioners.

prompts.t: Should this table be a chart?
prompts.p: Act as a data-visualisation specialist. Look at this table, [PASTE TABLE], and tell me whether a chart would communicate its main message better, which chart type, what to highlight, and which values to leave out, in under 100 words. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: A table of mortality rates across 5 age groups in two treatment arms.

prompts.t: Does my slide pass the 6 × 6 rule?
prompts.p: Act as a presentation coach. Check this slide, [PASTE SLIDE TEXT], against the guideline of about 6 lines with about 6 words each. Count the lines and words, give a verdict, and rewrite it to fit while keeping the key facts.
prompts.try: A slide with 9 bullets of 15 words each on insulin types.

prompts.t: Invited CME talk or guest lecture, start to finish
prompts.use: When you are invited to speak at a CME, society meeting or another institution.
prompts.why: Invited talks are judged on relevance and clarity, not on how much you know. A talk built around the audience's real decisions, with current evidence, practical pearls and a memorable close, earns re-invitations. A textbook recital doesn't.
prompts.p:
You are a sought-after CME speaker and senior clinician who designs practical, evidence-based talks for practising doctors. You are known for clarity, good pacing and useful take-home points.

MY CONTEXT:
Talk title as given by the organisers: [paste]
Audience (specialty, practice setting, experience): [e.g. general practitioners and physicians in private practice]
Duration and format (talk plus Q&A, panel, workshop): [brief]
Organiser's brief or expectations: [paste or "none"]
My sources (guidelines, key trials, reviews): [UPLOAD / LIST]
Venue and technology: [hall, projector, online streaming]

TASK:
1. Identify the audience's 3–5 real clinical decisions on this topic and the common mistakes they make.
2. Define the one big idea of the talk and 3 supporting messages.
3. Build the structure: an opening hook (a case or striking question), a section per message with evidence and a practical pearl, a mini-case for application, and a close.
4. Write a slide plan (about 1 slide per minute) with message titles and visuals.
5. Include an evidence summary from my sources and a "what's new" slide.
6. Write the first 90 seconds and the last 60 seconds word for word.
7. Prepare 8 likely audience questions with short answers.
8. Suggest a one-page take-home handout.

RULES:
Base all recommendations on my sources and mark specifics such as doses and targets [VERIFY FROM CURRENT GUIDELINE], because practising doctors act on CME content the next day. Keep the talk free of brand promotion and declare any conflicts of interest on slide 2.

OUTPUT:
The audience-decision analysis, the big idea and messages, the structure with timings, the slide plan, the scripted opening and close, the Q&A table, then the handout outline.

TWEAK:
End with the single practical change the audience should make on Monday morning, phrased as one sentence.
tips: Ask the organiser who attended last year and what they asked. It tells you the audience's real needs.
A 60-second case in the middle of the talk re-captures attention.
Finish 2–3 minutes early. Organisers remember speakers who respect time.

prompts.t: Build any talk around a story
prompts.use: When your talk has good content but no shape.
prompts.why: Audiences remember stories, not lists. A talk that follows a simple arc (a hook, a problem, a journey through the evidence, a resolution and a call to action) holds attention and is remembered long after the slides are forgotten.
prompts.p:
You are a medical storyteller and speaking coach who helps clinicians turn information into memorable narratives, without sacrificing accuracy.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
Topic and audience: [brief]
Duration: [minutes]
My key content points (rough list): [PASTE]
A patient story or clinical moment that inspired this talk (de-identified): [PASTE OR "none"]
The one thing I want the audience to do or believe afterwards: [one line]

TASK:
1. Write the one big idea in a single sentence.
2. Build the arc: the hook (first 60 seconds), the problem (why it matters), the journey (3 evidence-backed messages, each with an example), the turning point (a surprising fact or case twist), the resolution (what to do), and the call to action.
3. Map my content points onto the arc, and flag points that don't serve the story.
4. Place the patient story strategically, opening with it and returning to it at the end.
5. Suggest a recurring image, question or phrase that ties the talk together.
6. Write the transitions between the sections.
7. Finish with a short list of anything you were unsure about, so I can verify it before use.

RULES:
Keep patient stories fully de-identified and respectful, and keep every fact accurate, because a story that distorts the evidence damages credibility. Cut content that doesn't serve the big idea, however interesting it is.

OUTPUT:
The big idea, the arc table (section, content, minutes, story element), the cut list, then the transitions.

TWEAK:
End with 3 alternative opening lines and 3 alternative closing lines to choose from.
tips: If you can't state your big idea in one sentence, the audience won't be able to either.
Return to the opening story in your final minute. It closes the loop.
Rehearse the transitions. They are where talks lose their thread.

prompts.t: Health talk for patients or the community
prompts.use: For health camps, patient-education sessions, school or community talks, radio or local TV.
prompts.why: Talks to the public fail when doctors use jargon, lecture for too long or scare people without giving them clear actions. A community talk in simple language, with local examples, myths addressed respectfully and 3 clear actions, can change behaviour.
prompts.p:
You are a public-health physician and experienced community educator who speaks to rural and urban Indian audiences in simple language, with warmth and respect.

MY CONTEXT:
Topic: [e.g. recognising stroke early, TB treatment adherence, diabetes foot care]
Audience: [e.g. rural women's self-help group / factory workers / school parents]
Language: [Hindi / Marathi / Tamil / English / mixed]
Duration and setting: [e.g. 20 minutes, open-air health camp, no projector]
Local beliefs or myths I know of: [list or "suggest common ones"]
Resources to hand out: [pamphlets / none]

TASK:
1. Choose the 3 key messages the audience must remember.
2. Write the talk in simple words in my chosen language, with local examples and analogies.
3. Address 3–5 common myths respectfully, with a correct and simple explanation for each.
4. Include a short demonstration or activity (e.g. FAST for stroke, a foot check).
5. Give 3 clear actions: what to do, where to go, and when to seek help.
6. Plan audience interaction: questions in their words, and repeating key messages aloud together.
7. Write a pamphlet summary of 100 words or fewer.

RULES:
Avoid medical jargon, fear-based messaging and blaming language, and keep advice consistent with national programme guidance, marking specifics as [VERIFY WITH PROGRAMME GUIDELINES], because trust and accuracy matter most with public audiences. Give local helpline or facility details as placeholders only.

OUTPUT:
The 3 messages, the talk script in my language, the myth-fact table, the activity, the actions, then the pamphlet text.

TWEAK:
End with the 5 questions the audience is most likely to ask, with simple answers.
tips: Speak for no more than 15 minutes and leave the rest for questions. Community audiences learn most by asking.
Use objects and demonstrations. A glucometer or a real inhaler teaches more than a slide.
Ask a local health worker (ASHA or ANM) to co-present. It builds trust.

prompts.t: Prepare for a panel discussion (as panellist or moderator)
prompts.use: When you are on a panel, or moderating one, at a conference or CME.
prompts.why: Panels are either the liveliest session of a meeting or the dullest. Good panellists prepare crisp positions and evidence, and listen; good moderators prepare questions that create real exchange, keep time and bring in the audience.
prompts.p:
You are an experienced conference moderator and panellist who has run lively, balanced medical panel discussions for years.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
Panel topic: [paste]
My role: [panellist / moderator]
Other panellists and their expertise: [list]
Duration and format: [e.g. 45 minutes, 4 panellists, audience Q&A]
My position or expertise on the topic: [brief]
Sources: [UPLOAD / LIST]

TASK:
If I am a panellist:
1. Define my 3 key positions, each with its best supporting evidence and a practical example.
2. Prepare a 90-second opening statement.
3. Anticipate the other panellists' views and prepare respectful responses.
4. Prepare answers to 6 likely audience questions.
If I am the moderator:
5. Write the introduction of the topic and the panellists (60 seconds).
6. Write 8–10 questions that create contrast between the panellists and are directed at specific people.
7. Plan the time: openings, discussion, audience Q&A and a summary.
8. Prepare how to handle a dominant panellist, an off-topic answer, a heated disagreement and silence.
9. Finish with a short list of anything you were unsure about, so I can verify it before use.

RULES:
Keep claims evidence-based and attribute positions fairly, marking evidence to confirm as [VERIFY], because panels are recorded and quoted. Declare any conflicts of interest.

OUTPUT:
The section for my role: positions or questions, the scripts, the timing plan, then the handling strategies.

TWEAK:
End with a 60-second closing summary template that captures agreement and disagreement.
tips: As a panellist, answer in under 90 seconds. Short answers get follow-up questions; long ones get interrupted.
As a moderator, speak to the panellists before the session. It prevents surprises.
Invite audience questions early. Panels come alive when the room joins in.

prompts.t: The first 90 seconds of my talk
prompts.use: For any talk, when your current opening is "Good morning, today I will talk about…".
prompts.p:
You are a speaking coach who specialises in strong openings for medical talks.

MY CONTEXT:
Topic, audience and big idea: [brief]
Material I could use (a case, a statistic with its source, a question, an image): [list]
Duration of the whole talk: [minutes]

TASK:
1. Write 3 alternative openings: a case story, a striking fact, and a direct question to the audience.
2. For each, include the transition into the talk's roadmap.
3. Recommend one for my audience, with the reason.
4. Mark the words to deliver slowly and the pauses.

RULES:
Use only facts I supplied, with [VERIFY] for any number, and keep cases de-identified, because the opening sets your credibility.

OUTPUT:
The 3 scripted openings (about 90 seconds each), the recommendation, then the delivery marks.
tips: Memorise your opening word for word. Nerves are highest in the first minute.
prompts.try: A CME talk on deprescribing in elderly patients.

prompts.t: A closing the audience remembers
prompts.use: For the last minute of any talk.
prompts.p:
You are a speaking coach known for powerful, concise endings.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
The big idea and 3 key messages: [paste]
The opening I used: [paste]
Audience: [brief]

TASK:
1. Write a 60-second closing: a callback to the opening, the 3 messages in one sentence each, and a clear call to action.
2. Write a final one-line sentence to end on (not "thank you, any questions?").
3. Suggest what should be on screen during the closing.

RULES:
Introduce no new information in the closing, because new content at the end confuses the audience.

OUTPUT:
The scripted closing, the final line, then the screen suggestion.
tips: End on your strongest sentence, pause, then say "thank you". The pause is where it lands.
prompts.try: A talk on early recognition of sepsis in the wards.

prompts.t: A 5-minute lightning talk
prompts.use: For short-format sessions: lightning talks, flash presentations and 5-minute updates.
prompts.p:
You are a coach for short-format scientific talks.

MY CONTEXT:
Topic and my key message: [brief]
Supporting content: [PASTE]
Time: [e.g. 5 minutes] · slide limit: [e.g. 5 slides]

TASK:
1. Reduce the content to one message and 2 supporting points.
2. Plan the slides (1 per minute), each with a message title and one visual.
3. Write a script of about 650 words for 5 minutes.
4. Mark where to cut if the time is shortened.

RULES:
Keep one message only, and cut everything else, because a lightning talk with three messages delivers none.

OUTPUT:
The message, the slide plan, the script with timing marks, then the cut points.
tips: Rehearse with a strict timer. Lightning sessions often cut the microphone at the time limit.
prompts.try: A 5-minute update on a new antimicrobial stewardship policy for residents.

prompts.t: A PechaKucha-style talk (20 slides × 20 seconds)
prompts.use: When a session uses auto-advancing slides.
prompts.p:
You are an expert in constrained presentation formats.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience or purpose: [brief]
Topic and message: [brief]
Content I want to include: [PASTE]

TASK:
1. Plan 20 slides, each with one striking image or visual and at most 5 words.
2. Write a 20-second script (about 45 words) for each slide.
3. Group the slides into 4–5 story sections.
4. Mark slides where timing is risky, and give simpler scripts for them.

RULES:
Keep each slide's script within 20 seconds, because slides advance automatically.

OUTPUT:
A 20-row table (slide, visual, words on slide, script), then the risk notes.
tips: Rehearse with the slides on auto-advance. It's a completely different experience from clicking.
prompts.try: "The life of an ICU nurse during a pandemic".

prompts.t: Motivational or career talk for students
prompts.use: When invited to speak to MBBS students or interns about careers, exams or life in medicine.
prompts.p:
You are a mentor who gives honest, practical and inspiring talks to medical students.

MY CONTEXT:
Audience and what they're worried about: [e.g. final-year MBBS, NEET-PG pressure]
My own journey and lessons (brief): [PASTE]
Duration: [minutes]

TASK:
1. Identify 3 messages that would genuinely help this audience.
2. Structure the talk with 2–3 personal stories that illustrate them.
3. Include practical advice (specific actions, resources and habits).
4. Address one uncomfortable truth honestly (e.g. burnout, failure, uncertainty).
5. Plan a Q&A segment with likely questions.

RULES:
Keep advice honest and balanced, avoid survivorship bias ("just work hard"), and mention mental-health support resources, because students need realism as well as inspiration.

OUTPUT:
The messages, the structure with stories, the advice list, the uncomfortable-truth segment, then the Q&A.
tips: One honest failure story is worth ten success stories.
prompts.try: A talk for final-year MBBS students on choosing a specialty and preparing for NEET-PG.

prompts.t: Deliver a talk in Hindi or a regional language
prompts.use: When your audience is more comfortable in Hindi or a regional language than in English.
prompts.p:
You are a bilingual medical educator who explains clinical topics fluently in Indian languages.

MY CONTEXT:
Topic and audience: [brief]
Language: [Hindi / Marathi / Bengali / Tamil / other]
My English content or script: [PASTE]

TASK:
1. Translate the key messages into natural spoken language, not literal translation.
2. Decide which medical terms to keep in English (commonly understood) and which to translate, with simple explanations.
3. Suggest local analogies and examples.
4. Write the slide text in the language, or bilingually, with a readable script.

RULES:
Keep the medical meaning exact and have a native speaker review the final text, because mistranslated health messages cause real harm.

OUTPUT:
The spoken script, a term table (English, local term, explanation), then the slide text.
tips: Mixed "Hinglish" is often the most natural register for urban audiences. Match how the audience actually speaks.
prompts.try: A talk on diabetes and diet for a Hindi-speaking community audience.

prompts.t: Using patient stories ethically in talks
prompts.use: When you want to include real patient experiences in a talk.
prompts.p:
You are a clinician-educator who uses patient stories powerfully and ethically.

MY CONTEXT:
The story I want to use (brief, de-identified): [PASTE]
Purpose in the talk: [brief]
Audience and whether the talk will be recorded: [brief]

TASK:
1. Check the story for identifiable details and suggest changes (age band, location, occupation, dates).
2. Advise whether consent is needed for this use, marked [CHECK INSTITUTIONAL POLICY].
3. Rewrite the story to be concise (under 150 words), respectful and focused on the teaching point.
4. Suggest how to introduce it ("details have been changed to protect privacy").

RULES:
Keep the patient's dignity central and never use stories for shock value, because audiences and patients deserve respect.

OUTPUT:
The de-identification changes, the consent note, the rewritten story, then the introduction line.
tips: Composite cases (merging details from several patients) are a safe option for teaching.
prompts.try: A young patient's story of delayed TB diagnosis, for a public-health talk.

prompts.t: Health talk for school students
prompts.use: For school health programmes and awareness events.
prompts.p:
You are a paediatric health educator who engages children and teenagers.

MY CONTEXT:
Topic: [e.g. hand hygiene, tobacco, menstrual health, road safety, mental health]
Age group and school type: [brief]
Language and duration: [brief]

TASK:
1. Choose 3 age-appropriate key messages.
2. Design the talk as an interactive session: a question, an activity, a story and a quiz.
3. Use simple words and relatable examples.
4. Include a take-home activity or pledge.
5. Plan how to handle sensitive questions.

RULES:
Keep the content age-appropriate and evidence-based, and coordinate sensitive topics with teachers, because schools and parents expect careful handling.

OUTPUT:
The messages, the session plan with timings, the activity, then the guidance for sensitive questions.
tips: Children remember what they do, not what they hear. Build in an activity every 5 minutes.
prompts.try: Tobacco and vaping awareness for 13–15-year-olds, in English and Hindi.

prompts.t: Chairing a scientific session
prompts.use: When you are invited to chair a conference or CME session.
prompts.p:
You are an experienced session chair who runs sessions smoothly and fairly.

MY CONTEXT:
The session format, speakers, their titles and time slots: [PASTE]
Co-chair, if any: [name]
Technical set-up: [brief]

TASK:
1. Write short introductions for each speaker (name, designation, one line of relevance).
2. Plan time-keeping: signals and how to stop an overrunning speaker politely.
3. Prepare 1–2 questions per talk in case the audience is silent.
4. Plan the Q&A: how to take and distribute questions fairly.
5. Write a 60-second closing summary template.

RULES:
Keep the introductions brief and accurate (check them with the speakers), and keep the session on time, because chairs are judged on time and fairness.

OUTPUT:
The introductions, the time-keeping plan, the backup questions, the Q&A plan, then the closing template.
tips: Meet the speakers 10 minutes before the session and agree the time signals.
prompts.try: A session with 4 speakers on critical care nephrology, 15 minutes each.

prompts.t: Introduce a guest speaker
prompts.use: When you have to introduce a speaker at a CME, conference or departmental event.
prompts.p:
You are an event host who writes warm, concise speaker introductions.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
The speaker's CV or bio (paste): [PASTE]
Their talk title: [paste]
Event and audience: [brief]

TASK:
1. Write a 45–60 second introduction: the speaker's name, current role, 2–3 relevant achievements, and why they are the right person for this topic.
2. End with the talk title and an invitation to the speaker.
3. Mark names and terms to check pronunciation.

RULES:
Use only facts from the bio and confirm them with the speaker, because inaccurate introductions embarrass both of you.

OUTPUT:
The introduction script with pronunciation notes.
tips: Don't read the whole CV. Choose what connects the speaker to the topic.
prompts.try: Introducing a visiting professor speaking on interventional pulmonology.

prompts.t: A vote of thanks that isn't boring
prompts.use: At the end of a CME, conference or departmental event.
prompts.p:
You are an event host known for gracious, crisp votes of thanks.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience or purpose: [brief]
The event, speakers, chief guests, organisers, sponsors (if any) and volunteers: [LIST]
Duration allowed: [e.g. 2 minutes]

TASK:
1. Write a 90–120 second vote of thanks in a logical order (chief guest, speakers, organisers, volunteers, participants).
2. Include one specific line about each speaker's talk.
3. End warmly and briefly.

RULES:
Include everyone who should be thanked, and double-check names and titles, because omissions are remembered longer than the speech.

OUTPUT:
The script with names marked [CHECK SPELLING / TITLE].
tips: Mentioning one specific point from each talk shows that you actually listened.
prompts.try: The vote of thanks at a state-level CME on diabetes with 5 speakers.

prompts.t: Host a medical webinar
prompts.use: When organising or hosting an online CME or teaching webinar.
prompts.p:
You are an experienced online event host for medical education.

MY CONTEXT:
Platform: [Zoom / Teams / YouTube Live / other]
Topic, speakers and audience size: [brief]
Duration: [minutes]

TASK:
1. Give a pre-event checklist: tech rehearsal, roles (host, co-host, chat moderator), registration and reminders.
2. Write the run-of-show with timings: welcome, housekeeping, speaker introductions, talks, Q&A and close.
3. Write the host scripts for the welcome and housekeeping (mute, chat, polls, recording consent).
4. Plan engagement: polls and chat prompts.
5. Give a backup plan for technical failures.

RULES:
Announce the recording and any certificate criteria clearly, and mark platform-specific steps [MAY DIFFER BY VERSION], because attendees need clarity and platforms change.

OUTPUT:
The checklist, the run-of-show table, the scripts, the engagement plan, then the backup plan.
tips: Assign a co-host to watch the chat. The host can't present and moderate at the same time.
prompts.try: A 60-minute webinar on insulin pumps with 2 speakers and 300 attendees.

prompts.t: Script for a short educational video
prompts.use: For YouTube, Instagram or institutional e-learning videos.
prompts.p:
You are a medical educator who creates short, engaging educational videos.

MY CONTEXT:
Topic and audience (students / doctors / public): [brief]
Video length and platform: [e.g. 3 minutes, YouTube]
Key content: [PASTE]

TASK:
1. Write a hook in the first 5 seconds.
2. Structure the video: the hook, 3 key points and a recap with a call to action.
3. Write the spoken script at about 150 words per minute.
4. Suggest a visual or on-screen text for each segment.
5. Add a short disclaimer line appropriate to the audience.

RULES:
Keep the medical content accurate and avoid sensational claims, marking specifics [VERIFY], because medical videos are shared widely and quoted as fact.

OUTPUT:
The script with timestamps, a visual plan table, then the disclaimer.
tips: Record in short segments. Editing is easier and mistakes cost seconds, not minutes.
prompts.try: A 3-minute YouTube video on how to use an inhaler correctly, for patients.

prompts.t: Rehearsal plan for an important talk
prompts.use: 5–7 days before a significant talk.
prompts.p:
You are a speaking coach who prepares clinicians for high-stakes talks.

MY CONTEXT:
The talk, its duration and its importance: [brief]
Days available: [N]
My main concerns (timing, nerves, questions, content gaps): [list]

TASK:
1. Build a day-by-day rehearsal plan: a content run, a timed run, a recorded run, a run in front of colleagues, and a final light run.
2. Build in specific work on my concerns.
3. Give a checklist for the day before and the day of the talk.
4. Suggest how to collect useful feedback from colleagues.

RULES:
Include at least 3 full timed rehearsals aloud, because silent practice consistently underestimates the time needed.

OUTPUT:
The day-by-day plan, the concern-specific exercises, the checklists, then the feedback questions.
tips: Rehearse standing up, with the clicker, as you will on the day.
prompts.try: A 20-minute invited talk at a national conference, 6 days away.

prompts.t: Manage stage fright before a talk
prompts.use: When nerves are affecting your preparation or delivery.
prompts.p:
You are a performance coach who helps doctors manage public-speaking anxiety.

MY CONTEXT:
What happens to me when I speak (shaking, blanking, rushing): [brief]
The upcoming talk: [brief]

TASK:
1. Explain briefly why anxiety happens and why some of it helps.
2. Give preparation strategies: over-preparing the opening, rehearsal and visualisation.
3. Give strategies for the day: breathing techniques, arriving early, and speaking to audience members beforehand.
4. Give in-the-moment recovery techniques for blanking or rushing.
5. Give a debrief routine after the talk.

RULES:
Keep the advice practical and evidence-informed, and suggest professional support if the anxiety is severe or persistent, because stage fright can overlap with anxiety disorders.

OUTPUT:
Five headed sections of practical techniques.
tips: If you blank, pause, look at your slide title and say it aloud. It restarts your memory.
prompts.try: A first-year resident who freezes during departmental presentations.

prompts.t: Shrink or stretch a talk to a new time slot
prompts.use: When the organisers change your slot, or you reuse a talk for a different event.
prompts.p:
You are a presentation editor who adapts talks to any time slot.

MY CONTEXT:
My current talk outline with its timings: [PASTE]
Original and new durations: [e.g. 45 → 20 minutes]
New audience, if different: [brief]

TASK:
1. Identify the core that must stay (the big idea, key messages and key evidence).
2. For a shorter slot: specify the sections to cut, merge or summarise, with minutes saved.
3. For a longer slot: suggest what to add (a case, interaction, Q&A, depth).
4. Produce the revised outline with timings.

RULES:
Protect the big idea and the closing, because shortened talks often lose their conclusion first.

OUTPUT:
The core list, the changes with minutes, then the revised outline.
tips: Cut whole sections rather than trimming every section. It keeps the pace natural.
prompts.try: Reducing a 45-minute seminar on heart failure to a 15-minute CME talk.

prompts.t: Turn a key paper into a teaching talk
prompts.use: When you want to teach the lessons of an important paper, not appraise it formally.
prompts.p:
You are a clinical teacher who makes landmark studies come alive.

MY CONTEXT:
The paper (upload or paste the key sections): [UPLOAD / PASTE]
Audience and duration: [brief]

TASK:
1. Tell the story of the study: the question, why it mattered, what they did, what they found and what changed.
2. Extract 3 teaching lessons (clinical and methodological).
3. Build a 10–15 minute talk outline with visuals.
4. Link it to current practice and guidelines, with [VERIFY].

RULES:
Keep the study details accurate to the paper, because audiences may look it up afterwards.

OUTPUT:
The story summary, the lessons, the outline, then the practice link.
tips: Start with what doctors did before the study. It makes the result feel important.
prompts.try: A landmark trial on low tidal volume ventilation in ARDS.

prompts.t: Proposal and abstract for an invited talk
prompts.use: When organisers ask for a talk abstract, title and learning objectives.
prompts.p:
You are an experienced speaker who writes clear, attractive talk proposals.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Proposed topic and my angle: [brief]
Audience: [brief]
Required format (word limit, objectives, bio): [paste]

TASK:
1. Write 3 talk titles.
2. Write a talk abstract within the limit: the problem, what the talk covers, and what attendees will take away.
3. Write 3 learning objectives with Bloom's verbs.
4. Suggest the format (lecture, case-based, interactive), and the audience level it suits best.

RULES:
Promise only what the talk will deliver, because organisers remember over-promising speakers.

OUTPUT:
The titles, the abstract, the objectives, then the format note.
tips: Organisers choose talks that solve their audience's problems. Lead with the problem.
prompts.try: A proposal for a talk on AI tools in medical practice for a state medical association.

prompts.t: A short speaker bio
prompts.use: When an event, journal or website asks for a speaker bio.
prompts.p:
You are a professional bio writer for academic clinicians.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
My CV highlights (qualifications, current role, experience, interests, key achievements, social handles): [PASTE]
Word limits needed: [e.g. 50 and 150 words]
Tone: [formal / conversational]

TASK:
1. Write a 50-word bio and a 150-word bio in the third person.
2. Lead with my current role and the relevance to the event.
3. Include 2–3 achievements, without listing everything.
4. Write a one-line version for the host to read aloud.

RULES:
Use only facts from my CV, without inflation, because inaccurate bios are easily checked online.

OUTPUT:
The three versions.
tips: Keep one bio document updated. You'll be asked for it far more often than you expect.
prompts.try: A pulmonologist and co-founder of an AI health-education platform.

prompts.t: Learn from feedback on my talk
prompts.use: After a talk, when you have feedback forms, comments or a recording.
prompts.p:
You are a speaking coach who turns feedback into specific improvements.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Feedback received (ratings and comments): [PASTE]
My own impressions and the recording notes: [brief]

TASK:
1. Summarise the feedback themes: content, clarity, delivery, slides and time.
2. Identify 3 strengths to keep.
3. Identify 3 specific improvements, with an exercise for each.
4. Suggest what to change in the talk before giving it again.

RULES:
Weigh repeated comments over one-off comments, and don't dismiss critical feedback, because patterns reveal real issues.

OUTPUT:
The theme summary, the strengths, the improvements with exercises, then the talk changes.
tips: Watch the recording once with the sound off. Your body language will surprise you.
prompts.try: Feedback from a CME with comments on "too fast" and "excellent cases".

prompts.t: An opening question that hooks the audience
prompts.p: Act as a speaking coach. Write 3 opening questions for my talk on [TOPIC] to [AUDIENCE] that make people think about their own practice or experience in the first 30 seconds, each under 20 words, with the answer I'll reveal later in the talk.
prompts.try: A CME talk on antibiotic overuse in upper respiratory infections.

prompts.t: Organise my talk into three parts
prompts.p: Act as a presentation strategist. Organise my content, [PASTE KEY POINTS], into exactly 3 memorable parts with short, parallel titles, and write a one-sentence roadmap that previews the 3 parts at the start of the talk. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: Points on the recognition, treatment and prevention of heat stroke.

prompts.t: My talk's big idea in one sentence
prompts.p: Act as a speaking coach. From my talk content, [PASTE OUTLINE], write the single big idea in one sentence of under 20 words that the audience should remember a week later. Give 3 options and mark the strongest one. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: A talk on the importance of early mobilisation in hospitalised elderly patients.

prompts.t: Five questions about my audience
prompts.p: Act as a presentation strategist. Before I prepare my talk on [TOPIC] for [AUDIENCE], list the 5 questions I should answer about them (knowledge level, decisions, pain points, expectations, attention span) and suggest how to find the answers. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: A talk for general practitioners in a district town on thyroid disorders.

prompts.t: A safe icebreaker for a medical audience
prompts.p: Act as an experienced medical speaker. Suggest 3 light, respectful icebreakers for the start of my talk on [TOPIC] to [AUDIENCE] that relate to the topic, avoid jokes about patients, and take under 30 seconds each. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: An after-lunch CME talk on hypertension management.

prompts.t: Tell a story in 60 seconds
prompts.p: Act as a medical storyteller. Turn this de-identified clinical experience, [BRIEF CASE], into a 60-second spoken story (about 150 words) with a setting, a tension, a turning point and a lesson that leads into my talk on [TOPIC]. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: A patient whose sepsis was recognised late on a busy night shift.

prompts.t: Recap before moving on
prompts.p: Act as a speaking coach. Write one-sentence spoken recaps to use at the end of each section of my talk, [LIST SECTIONS AND KEY POINTS], so the audience can follow the structure, each under 20 words and linking to the next section.
prompts.try: Sections on the causes, diagnosis and management of iron-deficiency anaemia.

prompts.t: A clear call to action
prompts.p: Act as a public-health communicator. Write 3 specific calls to action to end my talk on [TOPIC] for [AUDIENCE], each an action they can take within a week, phrased positively and concretely, in under 20 words. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: A talk to ward nurses on hand hygiene compliance.

prompts.t: A title for my invited talk
prompts.p: Act as a conference programme editor. Write 5 titles for my invited talk on [TOPIC] for [AUDIENCE]: 2 descriptive, 2 with a hook, and 1 in question form, each under 12 words, accurate to the content, and attractive in a printed programme.
prompts.try: A talk on how AI tools can help practising doctors.

prompts.t: Clean filler words out of my script
prompts.p: Act as a speaking coach. Review this transcript of my rehearsal, [PASTE TRANSCRIPT], list my filler words and verbal habits with their counts, and suggest a replacement strategy for each, such as pausing, instead of simply deleting them. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: A transcript full of "basically", "actually" and "so, uh".

prompts.t: A better way to open the Q&A
prompts.p: Act as a speaking coach. Instead of "any questions?", write 3 ways to open the Q&A after my talk on [TOPIC] that invite real discussion, including one prepared question I can ask myself if the audience is silent, with a short answer.
prompts.try: A talk on non-invasive ventilation in COPD.

prompts.t: Clinical protocol poster for a ward or ICU
prompts.use: When your unit adopts a protocol (sepsis bundle, hypoglycaemia, anaphylaxis, blood transfusion) and staff need it at a glance.
prompts.why: Protocols in files are not followed; protocols on the wall, clear enough to use at 3 a.m., are. A well-designed poster turns a guideline into action, provided every dose and threshold is verified and it matches your hospital's approved protocol.
prompts.p:
You are a clinical quality-improvement lead and medical illustrator who designs bedside protocol posters that nurses and doctors actually use in emergencies.

MY CONTEXT:
Protocol topic: [e.g. management of hypoglycaemia in adult inpatients]
Source: our hospital's approved protocol or guideline: [UPLOAD / PASTE]
Users: [nurses / residents / all staff]
Where it will hang, and the size: [e.g. nursing station, A3]
Language(s): [English / Hindi / bilingual]
Drugs and equipment available locally: [list]

TASK:
1. Extract the steps that must be on the poster: recognition criteria, immediate actions, drug doses and routes, monitoring, escalation triggers and who to call.
2. Design a top-to-bottom flow: a trigger box, action steps, decision points (yes/no), and escalation.
3. Write the text for each box in under 12 words, using action verbs.
4. Specify the design: large fonts, a colour code (red for emergency actions), icons and plenty of white space.
5. Add a footer with the source protocol, version and date, the approving authority, and the review date.
6. Write a 5-minute staff briefing to launch the poster.

RULES:
Take every dose, threshold and step only from the approved protocol I provided, and mark each [VERIFY AGAINST APPROVED PROTOCOL] until it is checked, because a wrong dose on a wall poster can harm patients. Match the local drug formulation and route. Get sign-off from the unit in-charge before printing.

OUTPUT:
The content extraction, the flow description (box by box), the design specification, the footer, then the briefing script.

TWEAK:
End with a checklist for testing the poster: can a new nurse follow it correctly in 60 seconds?
tips: Test the poster with 3 staff members before printing. Watch where they hesitate.
Laminate it and put a review date on it. Outdated protocol posters are dangerous.
Put the poster where the action happens, not where there's space.

prompts.t: Comic-style teaching infographic (AI image tools)
prompts.use: When you want a shareable, memorable 5-panel comic on a clinical topic, using ChatGPT image generation, Gemini or similar tools.
