prompts.why: A comic with two recurring characters, one asking and one answering, turns five high-yield facts into a story students remember and share. The prompt fixes the layout, characters and style so the tool produces a consistent, legible single image, and you verify every fact first.
prompts.p:
You are a medical educator and visual designer who writes precise image-generation prompts for educational comics, and who checks every clinical fact before it goes into an image.

MY CONTEXT:
Topic: [e.g. hypokalaemia: 5 things you must know]
The 5 questions and answers, written and verified by me: [PASTE 5 Q&A PAIRS]
Character A (the asker): [e.g. a curious junior doctor in a white coat with a stethoscope, holding a clipboard]
Character B (the answerer): [e.g. a calm, confident senior physician in scrubs]
Brand colours and handle: [e.g. black and orange, @yourhandle]
Image tool: [ChatGPT image / Gemini / other]

TASK:
1. Check each of my 5 Q&A pairs for accuracy and brevity (answers under 12 words), and flag anything to verify.
2. Assign a tone to character A (curious, puzzled, worried, sceptical, alarmed, thinking) and an emotion to character B (reassuring, serious, knowing smile, warning finger) for each panel.
3. Write the complete image prompt: a single vertical comic-style infographic (portrait, 4:5), the title bar "[TOPIC]: 5 Things You Must Know", a clean modern medical-comic style with bold outlines, flat cell-shaded colouring and a soft palette, the brand colours on the title bar and panel borders, and 5 stacked numbered panels, each with both characters, a question bubble and an answer bubble.
4. Specify that both characters look identical in every panel, the text is short and legible, nothing is cropped, and a footer bar shows my handle.
5. Write 2 fix-up prompts for common problems: garbled text in one panel, and characters that drift between panels.

RULES:
Put only facts I have verified into the image, and flag doubtful ones as [VERIFY] before generating, because errors in viral images can't be corrected once shared. Keep each bubble's text short, because image tools garble long text.

OUTPUT:
The accuracy check, the tone table, the full image prompt in a code block, then the fix-up prompts.

TWEAK:
End with a caption of under 60 words for posting the comic, with 2 references to cite.
tips: Fix one panel at a time: "Fix the spelling in panel 3 only, keep everything else."
Keep answers under 12 words. Longer text is where image tools make spelling errors.
Read the generated image letter by letter before posting. Image tools still misspell medical terms.

prompts.t: Handwritten-style revision notes image
prompts.aud: MBBS Student / PG Resident / Medical educator
prompts.use: When you want an attractive A4 handwritten-style revision sheet on a topic, generated with an AI image tool.
prompts.why: Students love revising from colour-coded handwritten notes, and a consistent design system (paper, handwriting, colour-coded boxes, highlights and sketches) makes every topic look like a page from the same notebook. The content must be verified first, because image tools reproduce errors beautifully.
prompts.p:
You are a medical educator and designer who creates handwritten-style study sheets with AI image tools, and who checks every fact before generating.

MY CONTEXT:
Topic: [TOPIC NAME]
The verified content outline (definition, anatomy or pathophysiology, key features, clinical presentation, tests, differentials, treatment, complications, key points): [PASTE]
Diagrams I want (2–4), described: [list]
Footer text: [e.g. "1 / 1 | @yourhandle"]
Image tool: [ChatGPT image / Gemini / other]

TASK:
1. Check my outline for accuracy and trim it so it fits one A4 page.
2. Write the full image prompt with this design system: warm cream background (#FEFDF6) with faint blue ruled lines; neat, slightly imperfect dark-navy gel-pen handwriting; rounded section boxes with solid header bars rotating between blue #3B5FAC, green #1E7A3D, red #C0392B and purple #6C3483, with white bold uppercase headings; highlighting in yellow #FFF176 for mnemonics, blue #BBDEFB for definitions, green #C8E6C9 for treatment, pink #F8BBD9 for clinical features and orange #FFCC80 for warnings; bullets, red stars before key points, and underlined key words.
3. Specify 2–4 small pen-and-ink labelled sketches with captions.
4. Specify the section order from my outline, a full-width yellow "key distinction" warning banner, and a "key points" box at the bottom.
5. Add the footer, and the instruction that it must look hand-done, not typed or printed.
6. Write 2 fix-up prompts: overcrowded text, and a misspelled term.

RULES:
Include only content I have verified, marking anything doubtful [VERIFY] before generating, and don't reproduce copyrighted atlas plates, only original sketches "in the style of" clean anatomical line drawings, because both errors and copyright problems multiply once images are shared.

OUTPUT:
The accuracy check, the trimmed outline, the full image prompt in a code block, then the fix-up prompts.

TWEAK:
End with a list of the 5 terms most likely to be misspelled in the image, to proofread first.
tips: One topic per page. If the outline is long, split it into two sheets.
Proofread every word of the generated image. Handwriting styles hide spelling errors.
Keep the design system identical across topics. It makes a recognisable series.

prompts.t: Awareness poster series for a health day
prompts.use: For World TB Day, World Diabetes Day, Breastfeeding Week and similar campaigns in the hospital, community or social media.
prompts.why: Awareness posters often say too much, scare people, or repeat the same slogan everywhere. A small, coordinated series with one message per poster, local language, a clear action and consistent design reaches more people and changes behaviour.
prompts.p:
You are a public-health communication specialist who designs health-awareness campaigns for Indian audiences in hospitals, communities and online.

MY CONTEXT:
Health day or theme: [e.g. World TB Day]
Official theme for the year, if any: [paste or "check"]
Audiences: [patients in OPD / community / students / social media followers]
Languages: [list]
Where the posters will be used: [OPD walls / health camp / Instagram / WhatsApp]
Key programme information (free services, helplines, facilities) from official sources: [PASTE]

TASK:
1. Define 4–5 key messages, one per poster, each with a single action (e.g. "Cough for more than 2 weeks? Get tested free at [facility].").
2. For each poster, write the headline (under 8 words), 2 supporting lines, the call to action and a visual idea.
3. Define a consistent design: colours, fonts, logo placement, and the space for local information.
4. Adapt the messages to each language, simply, not literally.
5. Adapt the formats: A3 print, a 1:1 social post and a WhatsApp status.
6. Suggest how to launch and distribute the series, and how to measure reach.

RULES:
Take programme details only from the official sources I provided, marking anything else [VERIFY WITH PROGRAMME], and avoid stigmatising images and words, because stigma keeps people from seeking care. Follow the official campaign's branding rules if it has any.

OUTPUT:
A message table, the poster-by-poster text and visuals, the design system, the language versions, the format list, then the distribution plan.

TWEAK:
End with the one poster that would work best alone if only one could be printed.
tips: Show people like your audience in the visuals. People respond to posters that look like them.
Always include where to go and that services are free, if they are. That's the action people need.
Test the headline with 3 people from the audience. If they can't repeat it back, simplify it.

prompts.t: A medical infographic for teaching or social media
prompts.use: When you want to summarise a topic visually for students, colleagues or the public.
prompts.p:
You are a medical infographic designer who balances accuracy and visual simplicity.

MY CONTEXT:
Topic and audience: [brief]
Verified key facts or data to include: [PASTE]
Format: [A4 portrait / 1:1 Instagram / 4:5 / slide]
Tool: [Canva / PowerPoint / AI image tool]

TASK:
1. Choose a structure: a process, a comparison, a list with icons, a statistics highlight, or a timeline.
2. Write a headline, 5–7 content blocks (under 15 words each) and a source line.
3. Suggest icons and a colour scheme.
4. Suggest the reading flow and hierarchy.

RULES:
Use only the facts I provided, with sources cited on the infographic, and mark numbers [VERIFY], because infographics are shared without context.

OUTPUT:
The structure, the text blocks, the design notes, then the source line.
tips: One infographic, one message. If it needs a second message, make a second infographic.
prompts.try: "5 signs of sepsis every nurse should know", 4:5 for Instagram.

prompts.t: A patient-education leaflet
prompts.use: For patients to take home after a diagnosis, procedure or discharge.
prompts.p:
You are a patient-education specialist who writes clear leaflets at a low reading level.

MY CONTEXT:
Topic: [e.g. living with heart failure / preparing for colonoscopy]
Patient group and language: [brief]
Our hospital's advice and contact details (placeholders are fine): [PASTE]

TASK:
1. Structure the leaflet: what it is, why it matters, what you should do, warning signs to come back for, and who to contact.
2. Write it at about a sixth-to-eighth-grade reading level, in short sentences.
3. Suggest simple pictures or icons.
4. Make a version in [LANGUAGE] if requested.
5. Keep it to one or two sides of A4.

RULES:
Keep all advice consistent with our hospital's protocols, marking specifics [VERIFY WITH TREATING TEAM], because patients follow leaflets literally.

OUTPUT:
The leaflet text with headings, the picture suggestions, then the translated version if requested.
tips: Test the leaflet on a patient's relative. If they can't tell you the warning signs afterwards, rewrite them.
prompts.try: A discharge leaflet on inhaler use and COPD warning signs, in Hindi and English.

prompts.t: Pocket quick-reference card
prompts.use: For a pocket card or phone-wallpaper reference on something you need often at the bedside.
prompts.p:
You are a clinical educator who designs dense but readable quick-reference cards.

MY CONTEXT:
Topic: [e.g. ABG interpretation steps / common emergency drug doses / GCS]
Verified content from source: [PASTE WITH SOURCE]
Size: [ID card / half A5 / phone screen]

TASK:
1. Select the essential information that fits.
2. Organise it into a clear layout (sections, tables, a mnemonic).
3. Suggest a front and back design.
4. Add the source and version date in small print.

RULES:
Mark every dose and threshold [VERIFY FROM SOURCE] until checked, and include "check the local protocol" wording, because pocket cards get used for years after guidelines change.

OUTPUT:
The card content by side, the layout, then the source line.
tips: Put the date on the card, and replace it when the guideline updates.
prompts.try: An emergency drug-dose card for adult cardiac arrest.

prompts.t: A concept map for a complex topic
prompts.use: For teaching or revising topics with many connected ideas.
prompts.p:
You are a medical educator who uses concept maps to show how knowledge connects.

MY CONTEXT:
Topic: [TOPIC]
Level: [brief]
Key concepts I want included: [list or "suggest"]

TASK:
1. Identify the central concept and 12–20 linked concepts.
2. Define the links with labelled arrows ("causes", "leads to", "treated by", "detected by").
3. Organise them into clusters (e.g. mechanisms, features, tests, treatment).
4. Describe the layout for drawing by hand or in a tool (e.g. draw.io, Miro).
5. Suggest 3 questions to test understanding using the map.

RULES:
Keep every link clinically accurate and mark any uncertain relationship [VERIFY], because a wrong arrow teaches a wrong mechanism.

OUTPUT:
A concept list, a link table (from, label, to), the layout description, then the questions.
tips: Ask students to build the map themselves first, then compare it with yours. That's where the learning happens.
prompts.try: Topic: heart failure (causes, mechanisms, features, investigations and drug classes).

prompts.t: Plan a chalk-and-talk or whiteboard session
prompts.use: For bedside teaching, tutorials or rooms without projectors.
prompts.p:
You are a master chalk-and-talk teacher.

MY CONTEXT:
Topic and duration: [brief]
Audience and group size: [brief]
Board size: [small whiteboard / large blackboard]

TASK:
1. Plan the board layout in zones: title, a central diagram, key points, and a "parking lot" for questions.
2. Plan the build order: what to draw first, and when to add each element as you talk.
3. Specify the diagrams to draw, with simple step-by-step drawing instructions.
4. Suggest colour use (if markers are available).
5. Plan a final summary that the finished board shows.

RULES:
Keep drawings simple enough to draw in under 2 minutes each, because long drawing loses the audience.

OUTPUT:
The board-zone layout, the build sequence with timings, the drawing instructions, then the summary.
tips: Practise the diagram twice beforehand. Confident drawing looks expert; hesitant drawing looks unprepared.
prompts.try: A 20-minute tutorial on the brachial plexus for MBBS students.

prompts.t: Sketchnote summary of a topic
prompts.use: For visual notes during or after a lecture, or as a teaching handout.
prompts.p:
You are a visual-thinking coach who teaches sketchnoting to medical students.

MY CONTEXT:
Topic or lecture content: [PASTE]
Audience: [self / students]

TASK:
1. Identify the central idea and 5–7 supporting ideas.
2. Suggest a simple icon or doodle for each idea.
3. Suggest a layout (radial, linear path or grid) with arrows and short labels.
4. Suggest one memorable example to draw.
5. If an AI image tool will be used, write a prompt with a text fallback.

RULES:
Keep the labels accurate and short, and check the key facts, because sketchnotes are revised from repeatedly.

OUTPUT:
The ideas, the icons, the layout, then the image prompt.
tips: Simple shapes and arrows are enough. Sketchnoting isn't about drawing talent.
prompts.try: A sketchnote of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.

prompts.t: Educational poster for a student competition
prompts.use: For poster competitions at college festivals, health days or academic events.
prompts.p:
You are a judge of educational poster competitions.

MY CONTEXT:
Theme and rules (size, format, judging criteria): [PASTE]
My topic idea: [brief]
Audience: [brief]

TASK:
1. Sharpen the topic into one clear message that fits the theme.
2. Plan the poster: headline, 3–5 content blocks, visuals and a call to action.
3. Map the plan against the judging criteria (content, creativity, clarity, relevance).
4. Suggest how to present the poster to the judges in 90 seconds.

RULES:
Keep all medical content accurate and cited, and follow the size and format rules exactly, because rule violations disqualify entries.

OUTPUT:
The message, the poster plan, the criteria map, then the pitch.
tips: Judges walk past dozens of posters. A striking headline and one strong visual decide who stops.
prompts.try: A theme on antimicrobial resistance for a college health festival.

prompts.t: Patient-facing poster for the OPD waiting area
prompts.use: For waiting areas, where patients have a few minutes and a real need.
prompts.p:
You are a patient-communication designer for Indian hospitals.

MY CONTEXT:
Message topic: [e.g. how to use an inhaler / diabetic foot care / when to come back]
Patient languages and literacy: [brief]
Poster size and location: [brief]

TASK:
1. Choose one message with one action.
2. Write a headline (under 7 words) and 3–4 picture-supported steps.
3. Suggest pictograms for low-literacy readers.
4. Produce versions in the required languages.
5. Suggest placement (eye level, near the relevant clinic).

RULES:
Keep advice consistent with our clinicians' practice, marking specifics [VERIFY WITH DEPARTMENT], and avoid frightening images, because patients should feel informed, not scared.

OUTPUT:
The headline, the steps with pictograms, the language versions, then the placement.
tips: Pictures of hands doing each step work better than any text for inhaler technique.
prompts.try: "How to use your inhaler" for a chest-clinic waiting area, in Hindi and English.

prompts.t: Pictorial medication schedule for patients
prompts.use: For patients who struggle with complex medication schedules, especially elderly or low-literacy patients.
prompts.p:
You are a clinical pharmacist experienced in designing pictorial medication aids.

MY CONTEXT:
The patient's medication list with timings (de-identified): [PASTE]
Patient literacy and language: [brief]

TASK:
1. Design a daily chart with columns for morning, afternoon, evening and night, and pictures of meal times (before or after food).
2. Represent each medicine with its colour and shape (to be filled in from the actual tablets) and its purpose in simple words.
3. Add key warnings (e.g. do not stop suddenly).
4. Add a tick box for each dose.

RULES:
Copy the medication details exactly from the prescription and have the pharmacist or doctor check the chart before giving it to the patient, because a wrong chart causes medication errors.

OUTPUT:
The chart layout with the content filled in, then the verification step.
tips: Use actual photos of the patient's tablets if possible. Generic pill icons confuse people.
prompts.try: An elderly patient on 7 medicines, including insulin, with limited literacy.

prompts.t: Brief for a medical illustration
prompts.use: When you need an accurate diagram for a talk, poster or paper and will draw it or commission it.
prompts.p:
You are a medical illustrator who writes precise illustration briefs.

MY CONTEXT:
What the illustration must show: [brief]
Where it will be used and the size: [brief]
Style: [line drawing / colour / schematic]
Reference sources (textbook, atlas, published figure): [LIST]

TASK:
1. Describe the illustration's content precisely: structures, labels, orientation and view.
2. Specify the labels (terminology) and leader-line placement.
3. Specify the style, colours and level of detail.
4. List accuracy checkpoints for the finished illustration.

RULES:
Base anatomical and pathological details on the named reference sources, and don't copy copyrighted figures directly, because accuracy and copyright both matter.

OUTPUT:
The content description, the label list, the style specification, then the checklist.
tips: Ask for a draft sketch before the final version. Anatomical errors are easier to fix early.
prompts.try: A labelled diagram of the bronchopulmonary segments for a seminar.

prompts.t: Prompt an AI image tool for medical visuals
prompts.use: When generating illustrations for slides or posters with ChatGPT, Gemini or other image tools.
prompts.p:
You are a prompt engineer for AI image generation in medical education.

MY CONTEXT:
What I need (concept, diagram or scene): [brief]
Where it will be used: [slide / poster / social post]
Tool: [name]

TASK:
1. Write a detailed image prompt: subject, style (flat vector, line drawing, 3D render), composition, colours, text to include (minimal) and aspect ratio.
2. Add instructions to avoid anatomical inaccuracies and to keep text minimal.
3. Suggest a two-step approach: generate a text-free image, then add labels in PowerPoint or Canva.
4. Write a checklist for reviewing the generated image.

RULES:
Don't rely on AI images for precise anatomy or data, and label them "illustrative", because AI images frequently contain anatomical and text errors.

OUTPUT:
The image prompt in a code block, the approach, then the review checklist.
tips: Add labels yourself afterwards. AI-generated text inside images is the most error-prone part.
prompts.try: A friendly illustration of a doctor explaining an inhaler to an elderly patient, for a slide.

prompts.t: Educational carousel for Instagram or LinkedIn
prompts.use: When sharing medical education on social media in a swipeable format.
prompts.p:
You are a medical educator and social-media content strategist.

MY CONTEXT:
Topic and audience: [e.g. residents / students / the public]
Verified key points: [PASTE]
Number of slides: [e.g. 7–10]
Brand style: [brief]

TASK:
1. Write a hook for slide 1 (under 10 words).
2. Write the slide-by-slide text: one idea per slide, under 30 words each.
3. Write the final slide: a summary and a call to action (save, share, follow).
4. Suggest visuals for each slide.
5. Write a caption with sources.

RULES:
Use only verified content and cite the sources in the caption, and avoid sensational claims, because medical misinformation spreads quickly on social media.

OUTPUT:
The slide-by-slide text table, the visual notes, then the caption.
tips: A strong first slide decides everything. If it doesn't stop the scroll, the rest won't be seen.
prompts.try: "7 ECG patterns every intern must recognise", 9 slides.

prompts.t: Low-cost teaching model or demonstration
prompts.use: When a physical model would teach better than a slide.
prompts.p:
You are a creative medical educator who builds low-cost teaching models.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
The concept to demonstrate: [brief]
Audience: [brief]
Materials and budget available: [brief]

TASK:
1. Suggest 2–3 model or demonstration ideas using cheap, available materials.
2. Give build instructions for the best one.
3. Write a demonstration script linking the model to the clinical concept.
4. Note the model's limitations (where the analogy breaks down).

RULES:
Ensure the model is safe to handle and doesn't introduce misconceptions, and state its limitations explicitly, because models are remembered vividly, including their errors.

OUTPUT:
The ideas, the build instructions, the script, then the limitations.
tips: A balloon in a jar teaches lung compliance better than any animation.
prompts.try: Demonstrating pneumothorax and chest-drain function for nursing students.

prompts.t: Step-by-step procedure wall chart
prompts.use: For procedures done often on a ward: central-line care, catheterisation, nebulisation, NG-tube insertion.
prompts.p:
You are a clinical skills educator who designs procedure charts.

MY CONTEXT:
Procedure: [name]
Our hospital's approved procedure steps: [PASTE / UPLOAD]
Users: [brief]

TASK:
1. Break the procedure into 8–12 numbered steps with action verbs.
2. Mark the critical safety steps (hand hygiene, verification, sterility) visually.
3. Suggest a picture or icon for each step.
4. Add a checklist box format for audits.
5. Add the source, version and review date.

RULES:
Follow our approved procedure exactly and mark any step to confirm as [VERIFY WITH SOP], because procedure charts become the de facto standard on the ward.

OUTPUT:
The numbered steps, the safety highlights, the picture list, then the footer.
tips: Put the chart where the procedure is prepared, such as the dressing trolley or the clean utility room.
prompts.try: Steps for central-line dressing change in the ICU.

prompts.t: Adapt a poster into several Indian languages
prompts.use: When a poster or leaflet must reach patients who speak different languages.
prompts.p:
You are a health-communication translator experienced in Indian languages.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
The English poster text: [PASTE]
Target languages: [list]
Audience literacy: [brief]

TASK:
1. Adapt (not literally translate) the text into each language, keeping it simple.
2. Keep familiar medical words (e.g. "sugar", "BP") where patients use them.
3. Check the text length fits the layout, and suggest cuts if not.
4. Recommend a review by a native speaker from the target community.

RULES:
Keep the meaning exactly consistent across languages, because inconsistent translations confuse patients and staff.

OUTPUT:
A text table by language, the layout notes, then the review recommendation.
tips: Back-translate the key warning line into English to check it survived translation intact.
prompts.try: A "warning signs of dengue" poster in Hindi, Bengali and Odia.

prompts.t: Critique my poster or infographic
prompts.use: Before printing or posting any visual aid.
prompts.p:
You are a senior medical educator and design critic.

MY CONTEXT:
My poster or infographic text and a description (or upload the image): [PASTE / UPLOAD]
Purpose and audience: [brief]

TASK:
1. Check accuracy: flag any claim, number or dose to verify.
2. Check clarity: the single message, reading order and text amount.
3. Check the design: contrast, font size, hierarchy and clutter.
4. Check accessibility: language, literacy and colour-blind safety.
5. Give the top 5 fixes.

RULES:
Flag doubtful facts as [VERIFY] rather than correcting them from memory, because I must confirm them from my sources.

OUTPUT:
A review table by criterion, then the top 5 fixes.
tips: Look at your poster from across the room for 5 seconds. What you remember is its real message.
prompts.try: An A3 poster on hand hygiene with 180 words and 6 colours.

prompts.t: Print specifications for posters and charts
prompts.use: Before sending posters, charts or leaflets to print.
prompts.p:
You are a print-production specialist.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Item, size and quantity: [brief]
Where it will be used (wall, bedside, outdoors, handout): [brief]
File source: [Canva / PowerPoint / other]

TASK:
1. Recommend the file format (PDF), resolution (300 dpi), colour mode and bleed.
2. Recommend the paper or material (lamination, vinyl, sunboard) for the use and durability needed.
3. Recommend minimum font sizes for the viewing distance.
4. Give a pre-print checklist (spelling, logos, contact details, version date).

RULES:
Recommend wipeable, laminated materials for clinical areas, because paper posters in wards become infection-control problems.

OUTPUT:
The specification table, then the checklist.
tips: Print one proof copy and look at it on the actual wall before printing the full batch.
prompts.try: 20 laminated A3 sepsis-protocol posters for medical wards.

prompts.t: Poster with QR codes to videos and resources
prompts.use: When a poster should lead people to videos, forms or detailed resources.
prompts.p:
You are a digital-health educator who connects print and online resources.

MY CONTEXT:
Poster topic: [brief]
Resources to link (videos, PDFs, forms): [list]
Audience and their phones or data access: [brief]

TASK:
1. Choose what the QR code should link to, and why.
2. Write the call to action beside the QR code.
3. Suggest QR code size and placement for scanning distance.
4. Suggest a stable link strategy (a link you control and can update).
5. Suggest how to track scans.

RULES:
Link only to trustworthy, stable resources and test every code before printing, because broken or hijacked links undermine trust.

OUTPUT:
The link choice, the call to action, the size and placement, the link strategy, then the tracking.
tips: Use a URL you can redirect later. Printed posters outlive most links.
prompts.try: A poster in the physiotherapy department linking to home-exercise videos.

prompts.t: Emergency algorithm card for the crash cart
prompts.use: For emergencies where seconds matter: anaphylaxis, cardiac arrest, status epilepticus, hyperkalaemia, massive haemorrhage.
prompts.p:
You are a resuscitation-training instructor who designs algorithm cards for crash carts and emergency rooms.

MY CONTEXT:
Emergency: [name]
Source: our hospital protocol or the current resuscitation guideline: [UPLOAD / PASTE]
Drugs and equipment on our crash cart: [list]
Card size: [A5 / A4, laminated]

TASK:
1. Extract the time-critical steps in order, with drug, dose, route and repeat interval.
2. Design a one-page flow that can be read in under 10 seconds per step.
3. Colour-code the actions (e.g. red for immediate, amber for next, green for monitor).
4. Add a "call for help" box with placeholders for local numbers.
5. Add the source, version date and review date.

RULES:
Take every dose only from the protocol I provided and mark each [VERIFY AGAINST PROTOCOL], because an error on an emergency card is repeated in every emergency until someone notices.

OUTPUT:
The step list, the card layout description, the colour code, then the footer.
tips: Run a mock drill with the card. Where people hesitate, the card needs simplifying.
prompts.try: An anaphylaxis card for the emergency department, adults.

prompts.t: A visual mnemonic poster
prompts.use: When a list must be memorised and a picture could anchor it.
prompts.p:
You are a medical educator skilled in visual memory techniques.

MY CONTEXT:
The list to remember: [LIST]
Audience: [brief]
Format: [poster / slide / flashcard]

TASK:
1. Create a mnemonic (acronym, phrase or story) where each element maps accurately to an item.
2. Design a visual scene or image that links the mnemonic to the items.
3. Write a caption explaining each element.
4. Suggest an image prompt or drawing instructions.

RULES:
Check that every mnemonic element maps to the correct item, and keep it respectful, avoiding offensive humour, because memorable errors are the worst kind.

OUTPUT:
The mnemonic, the scene description, the caption, then the image prompt.
tips: Absurd, vivid images are easiest to remember, as long as they stay professional.
prompts.try: Causes of clubbing, as a visual poster for final-year MBBS students.

prompts.t: Headline for my poster
prompts.p: Act as a health-communication copywriter. Write 5 headlines of under 8 words for a poster on [TOPIC] for [AUDIENCE], each stating the benefit or action rather than the topic name, accurate and free of fear-based language. Mark your favourite. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: A poster encouraging TB testing for anyone with a cough of more than 2 weeks.

prompts.t: Short slogans for a health campaign
prompts.p: Act as a public-health campaign writer. Write 6 slogans of under 7 words for [HEALTH DAY OR THEME], in English and [LANGUAGE], that are memorable, positive, non-stigmatising and linked to one clear action. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: World Diabetes Day, English and Hindi.

prompts.t: Icons for my visual aid
prompts.p: Act as a graphic designer for health materials. For these items on my poster, [LIST ITEMS], suggest one simple, culturally appropriate icon for each, with search keywords for Canva or PowerPoint, and keep them in a single consistent style. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: Items: wash hands, wear mask, cover cough, see a doctor, take full treatment.

prompts.t: Colours for a patient-facing poster
prompts.p: Act as a health-communication designer. Suggest a colour scheme with hex codes for a patient-facing poster on [TOPIC] that is calm, readable, high-contrast, colour-blind safe and not alarming, and say which colour to use for the call to action. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: A poster on diabetes foot care for an OPD waiting area.

prompts.t: Check the reading level of my text
prompts.p: Act as a plain-language editor. Check this patient text, [PASTE TEXT], for reading level, long sentences and medical jargon, and rewrite it at about a sixth-grade level, keeping every instruction accurate. List the words you replaced. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: Discharge instructions after a heart attack, written by a resident.

prompts.t: Pictogram instructions for low literacy
prompts.p: Act as a patient-education designer. Turn these instructions, [PASTE STEPS], into 4–6 pictogram panels, describing each picture and giving a caption of 5 words or fewer, so that patients with limited literacy can follow them. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: How to use an insulin pen.

prompts.t: Caption for my infographic post
prompts.p: Act as a medical social-media writer. Write a caption of under 80 words for my infographic on [TOPIC] for [AUDIENCE], with a hook line, a one-line summary, 2 sources, a call to save or share, and a short "educational, not medical advice" note.
prompts.try: An infographic on the warning signs of stroke (BE-FAST).

prompts.t: Poster size and font sizes
prompts.p: Act as a print designer. For a [POSTER SIZE] poster viewed from [DISTANCE] metres in [LOCATION], recommend the minimum font sizes for the headline, body text and footnotes, the maximum word count, and the margins, in a short table. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: An A3 poster viewed from 2 metres in a ward corridor.

prompts.t: Fix a garbled AI image
prompts.p: Act as an AI image-prompt expert. My generated image has these problems: [DESCRIBE PROBLEMS, e.g. misspelled words, a drifting character, cropped text]. Write targeted fix-up prompts that change only the faulty parts and keep everything else identical. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: Panel 3 says "hypokalmia" and character B's face has changed.

prompts.t: Description for a visual post
prompts.p: Act as an accessibility writer. Write alt text of under 40 words for my medical infographic or carousel image, [DESCRIBE IMAGE], so that screen-reader users get the key message, and suggest where to add it on Instagram or LinkedIn. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: A carousel slide showing the 5 steps of an ABG interpretation.

prompts.t: Call to action for an awareness poster
prompts.p: Act as a public-health communicator. Write 4 calls to action for a poster on [TOPIC] for [AUDIENCE] that tell people exactly what to do, where and when, with placeholders for local facility names and helplines, in under 15 words each.
prompts.try: A poster on early cancer screening for women in a district town.

prompts.t: Departmental case presentation, start to finish
prompts.use: When you present a case at a departmental case discussion or clinical meeting.
prompts.why: Case presentations are where residents show clinical reasoning. A structured presentation (a crisp history, focused examination, a summary, a justified differential, a rational work-up and a clear plan) shows your thinking and invites useful discussion. A disorganised one invites interruption.
prompts.p:
You are a senior physician and clinical teacher who has trained generations of residents in case presentation. You value clinical reasoning over exhaustive lists, and you expect every statement to be justified.

MY CONTEXT:
Specialty and my level: [e.g. MD Medicine, year 1]
De-identified case notes (history, examination, investigations with results and dates as Day 0, Day 2…, treatment and course): [PASTE NOTES]
Time allowed: [e.g. 15 minutes + 15 minutes discussion]
Format: [bedside / slides / verbal]
The discussion point my unit wants: [diagnostic dilemma / management decision / teaching]

TASK:
1. Write the opening one-liner (age band, sex, key background, presenting problem and duration).
2. Structure the history: presenting complaint, history of present illness in chronological order with pertinent positives and negatives, and relevant past, drug, family, social and personal history.
3. Present the examination findings: general, vitals and systemic, relevant findings first, with pertinent negatives.
4. Write a 3–4 line summary that frames the problem.
5. Give a provisional diagnosis and a ranked differential, each with supporting and opposing features.
6. Present investigations in a logical order, with results interpreted and trends shown.
7. Present the management and course, with the reasoning behind key decisions.
8. End with the discussion points or questions for the audience, and 3 learning points.

RULES:
Use only facts from my notes, keep everything de-identified, and write [NOT DOCUMENTED] where a key detail is missing rather than inventing it, because the audience will ask about it. Reason step by step when justifying the differential. This is for learning, not a substitute for the treating team's judgement.

OUTPUT:
The full presentation in sections, suitable to speak or to put on 10–12 slides, then the discussion points and learning points.

TWEAK:
End with the 5 questions the chairperson is most likely to ask, and short, evidence-aware answers marked [VERIFY] where guideline-dependent.
tips: Present in the order the information became available. It lets the audience reason along with you.
Pertinent negatives are as important as positives. They show you considered the differential.
Rehearse the summary until you can say it without notes. It's the part everyone remembers.

prompts.t: Grand rounds presentation
prompts.use: When you present at hospital or departmental grand rounds.
prompts.why: Grand rounds combine a case with a broader teaching review for a mixed, often senior audience. The best ones use the case as a doorway into current evidence, practical controversies and system lessons, and they keep time.
prompts.p:
You are an academic physician who has presented and chaired grand rounds for many years. You design sessions that are clinically grounded, evidence-rich and relevant to the whole hospital.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
The case (de-identified summary): [PASTE]
The broader topic the case illustrates: [e.g. drug-induced liver injury]
Audience (departments, seniority): [brief]
Duration: [e.g. 45 minutes]
Sources for the review part (guidelines, key papers): [UPLOAD / LIST]
Guest discussants, if any: [brief]

TASK:
1. Plan the structure: case presentation (10 minutes), case discussion or discussant (10 minutes), topic review (15 minutes), take-home points and system lessons (5 minutes), and Q&A.
2. Condense the case into a presentation with a clear clinical question.
3. Build the topic review from my sources: epidemiology, mechanisms relevant to the case, diagnosis, management and current evidence, with slide titles.
4. Identify system or quality lessons for the hospital, if any.
5. Write briefing questions for the discussant.
6. Write the take-home points.
7. Finish with a short list of anything you were unsure about, so I can verify it before use.

RULES:
Base the review on my sources and mark guideline or trial specifics [VERIFY], because grand-rounds audiences include experts in the topic. Keep the case de-identified and blame-free.

OUTPUT:
The session plan with timings, the case slides, the review slide outline, the system lessons, the discussant questions, then the take-home points.

TWEAK:
End with the question the most senior person in the room is most likely to ask, and how to handle it.
tips: Invite a discussant from another department. It broadens the discussion and the audience.
Keep the review focused on what the case raised. Grand rounds aren't a textbook chapter.
Circulate the take-home points afterwards. They extend the reach beyond the room.

prompts.t: Morbidity and mortality (M&M) presentation
prompts.use: When presenting an adverse outcome, complication or death at an M&M or death-audit meeting.
prompts.why: M&M meetings exist to learn and prevent recurrence, not to blame. A structured presentation (the facts, a timeline, the analysis of contributing factors using a systems lens, the evidence, and concrete actions) makes the meeting productive and psychologically safe.
prompts.p:
You are a patient-safety physician who runs M&M meetings using a systems approach and a just culture. You are factual, balanced and focused on learning.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
The case, de-identified, with a timeline of events: [PASTE]
The outcome (complication or death): [brief]
Local protocols relevant to the case: [list]
Institutional M&M format, if any: [paste]

TASK:
1. Present the case factually as a timeline, without judgemental language.
2. Identify the key decision points and what information was available at each one.
3. Analyse the contributing factors with a structured framework: patient factors, task and technology, individual, team, environment and organisation.
4. Classify the event (e.g. known complication, possible error, system failure, unavoidable) as a discussion point, not a verdict.
5. Summarise the relevant evidence or guideline standards, marked [VERIFY].
6. Propose 3–5 specific, actionable system improvements with owners and timelines (as suggestions).
7. Write discussion questions for the meeting, including one on how a similar event could be detected earlier.
8. Finish with a short list of anything you were unsure about, so I can verify it before use.

RULES:
Use neutral, non-blaming language and no names or identifiers, because psychological safety is what makes M&M work. Use only facts from my timeline, and mark unknowns [NOT KNOWN].

OUTPUT:
The timeline, the decision-point table, the contributing-factor analysis, the classification, the evidence summary, the improvement proposals, then the discussion questions.

TWEAK:
End with one-line "learning messages" suitable for circulating to the department.
tips: Ask "what made sense to the team at that time?" rather than "who made the mistake?".
Track your action items. An M&M without follow-up changes nothing.
Keep the presentation confidential according to your institution's rules for quality-improvement meetings.

prompts.t: Short "interesting case" presentation with teaching
prompts.use: For 10-minute "interesting case" or "case of the week" slots.
prompts.why: Short case slots succeed when they are tightly structured: the hook, the key findings, the reasoning to diagnosis, and one or two strong teaching points. Presenters who try to include everything run over and teach nothing.
prompts.p:
You are a clinical teacher who coaches residents to present interesting cases in 10 minutes with maximum teaching value.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
The case (de-identified notes): [PASTE]
What makes it interesting: [rare diagnosis / atypical presentation / diagnostic twist / management lesson]
Time: [e.g. 10 minutes]
Audience: [brief]
The key image or result that cracked the case: [describe]
What the treating team would do differently next time: [brief]

TASK:
1. Write a hook for the first 30 seconds.
2. Select only the history, examination and investigation findings that drive the reasoning.
3. Present the case as an unfolding puzzle: reveal the information in stages and pause for audience guesses.
4. Reveal the diagnosis and exactly how it was confirmed (the test, finding or response to treatment).
5. Deliver 2 teaching points with brief evidence, marked [VERIFY].
6. Add a 30-second "what we would do differently" reflection.
7. Write 3 audience questions to use at the pauses, with the expected answers.
8. Plan 6–8 slides with timings that fit the slot exactly.
7. Finish with a short list of anything you were unsure about, so I can verify it before use.

RULES:
Keep it fully de-identified and include only facts from my notes, because interesting cases are often recognisable to colleagues.

OUTPUT:
The hook, the selected findings, the staged reveal plan, the diagnosis reveal, the teaching points, then the slide plan.

TWEAK:
End with one "take-home pearl" for the audience to remember.
tips: The pause before revealing the diagnosis is where the audience learns. Don't rush it.
Show one key image or result, large, at the turning point.
Finish with what you would do differently next time. It's the most useful sentence in the talk.

prompts.t: Presenting at a multidisciplinary team meeting or tumour board
prompts.use: When presenting a patient at an MDT, tumour board, or joint medical-surgical meeting.
prompts.why: MDTs make major decisions in minutes. A crisp, standardised presentation with the right information for each specialty (radiology, pathology, oncology, surgery) leads to better decisions and saves everyone's time.
prompts.p:
You are an MDT coordinator and senior clinician who has run tumour boards and multidisciplinary meetings for years.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
Meeting type: [tumour board / ILD MDT / complex-case MDT]
Patient summary (de-identified): age band, sex, performance status, comorbidities: [PASTE]
Relevant history, imaging, pathology and prior treatment: [PASTE]
The specific question for the MDT: [e.g. surgery versus chemoradiotherapy?]
Patient's preferences, if known: [brief]

TASK:
1. Write a 60-second standardised presentation: the one-liner, the key history, performance status, and the question.
2. Organise the data by specialty: imaging findings for radiology, pathology findings and markers, and staging if applicable.
3. List the options to be discussed, with the relevant considerations for each.
4. Prepare a template for documenting the MDT outcome.
5. Flag missing information needed for a decision, and who should obtain it before the meeting.
6. Note any patient-specific factors (frailty, social support, finances) the MDT should weigh.
6. Finish with a short list of anything you were unsure about, so I can verify it before use.

RULES:
State staging and markers exactly as in the reports, marking any staging version as [VERIFY EDITION], and include the patient's preferences where known, because MDT decisions must be accurate and patient-centred.

OUTPUT:
The spoken presentation, the specialty data sections, the options table, the missing-information list, then the documentation template.

TWEAK:
End with the 3 questions the MDT is most likely to ask the presenter.
tips: State the question for the MDT first, not last. It focuses everyone's attention.
Have the images and pathology slides ready to display. MDTs stall while people search for them.
Document the decision and the rationale before leaving the room.

prompts.t: A three-line case summary
prompts.use: For the summary statement after history and examination, or at the start of rounds.
prompts.p:
You are a clinical teacher who values concise, reasoning-rich summaries.

MY CONTEXT:
Audience or purpose: [brief]
Case details (de-identified): [PASTE]
Specialty: [brief]

TASK:
1. Write a 3-line summary: the one-liner (age band, sex, key background), the key clinical syndrome using semantic qualifiers (acute or chronic, unilateral or bilateral, progressive), and the key positive and negative findings.
2. Write an alternative 1-line version for handovers.
3. Explain which words carry the diagnostic reasoning.

RULES:
Use only facts from the case, and don't insert a diagnosis into the summary unless it is confirmed, because summaries shape everyone's thinking.

OUTPUT:
The 3-line summary, the 1-line version, then the reasoning note.
tips: Semantic qualifiers ("acute, painful, unilateral") turn a summary into a diagnostic tool.
prompts.try: Notes on a 45-year-old man with 3 weeks of fever, weight loss and a right-sided pleural effusion.

prompts.t: Organise a messy history for presentation
prompts.use: When your clerking notes are complete but disorganised.
prompts.p:
You are a clinical examiner who knows what a well-presented history sounds like.

MY CONTEXT:
My clerking notes (de-identified): [PASTE]
Specialty and presenting problem: [brief]

TASK:
1. Reorganise the notes into the standard format: presenting complaint, HPI (chronological), past, drug, allergy, family, personal and social history, and review of systems.
2. Move the pertinent positives and negatives into the HPI.
3. Flag the gaps in the history that the audience will ask about.
4. Write the spoken version (about 2 minutes).

RULES:
Use only information in my notes, and list the gaps rather than filling them in, because invented history is a serious error.

OUTPUT:
The organised history, the gap list, then the spoken version.
tips: For each symptom, cover onset, duration, progression and associated features. Examiners listen for them.
prompts.try: Notes on an elderly woman with breathlessness, leg swelling and reduced urine output.

prompts.t: Present examination findings clearly
prompts.use: When presenting examination findings on rounds or in a case discussion.
prompts.p:
You are a clinical examiner who values focused, organised findings.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience or purpose: [brief]
Examination findings (de-identified): [PASTE]
Presenting problem: [brief]

TASK:
1. Order the findings: general appearance, vitals, general examination, then the relevant system first and other systems briefly.
2. Highlight the findings that support or oppose the leading diagnoses.
3. Include pertinent negatives.
4. Write the spoken version (about 90 seconds).

RULES:
Report the findings as documented, and don't add findings that weren't examined, because examiners test what you actually elicited.

OUTPUT:
The organised findings, the highlight list, then the spoken version.
tips: Say the relevant negatives aloud: "no clubbing, no lymphadenopathy". They show a targeted examination.
prompts.try: Findings in a patient with suspected infective endocarditis.

prompts.t: Justify a differential diagnosis for a case
prompts.use: For the differential-diagnosis part of a case presentation.
prompts.p:
You are a diagnostician who teaches structured differential reasoning.

MY CONTEXT:
Case summary with key findings: [PASTE]
My provisional diagnosis and differentials: [list]

TASK:
1. Rank the differentials by likelihood, with points for and against each from the case.
2. Identify the can't-miss diagnoses and whether they have been excluded.
3. Suggest the discriminating investigation for the top 2.
4. Write the spoken justification (about 2 minutes).

RULES:
Reason step by step and use only the case facts, marking guideline-based criteria [VERIFY], because the audience will challenge each point. This supports learning, not the treating team's decisions.

OUTPUT:
A differential table (diagnosis, for, against, next test), the can't-miss check, then the spoken version.
tips: A short, well-justified differential beats a long, unranked list.
prompts.try: A young woman with fever, arthralgia, rash and pancytopenia.

prompts.t: Present and justify the investigations
prompts.use: When presenting what tests were done and why.
prompts.p:
You are a senior clinician who expects every test to answer a question.

MY CONTEXT:
Investigations done with results and dates: [PASTE]
Differential diagnosis: [list]

TASK:
1. Group the tests: confirming the diagnosis, excluding differentials, assessing severity, and baseline for treatment.
2. For each important test, state the question it answered.
3. Present the abnormal results with trends in a compact table.
4. Identify any test that wasn't needed, or one that is still pending.

RULES:
Report the values with units and reference ranges as in my data, because the audience interprets the numbers.

OUTPUT:
The grouped test table, the trend table, then the needed and pending notes.
tips: Present trends, not single values: "creatinine 1.2 → 2.8 → 1.6 over 5 days".
prompts.try: Investigations in a patient with suspected tuberculous meningitis.

prompts.t: Present the management plan and its reasoning
prompts.use: For the management part of a case presentation or rounds.
prompts.p:
You are a senior clinician who teaches management reasoning.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Diagnosis, current status and management given: [PASTE]
Guidelines or protocols followed: [list]

TASK:
1. Present the management by problem (a problem-based list).
2. For each key decision, state the reasoning and the evidence or guideline behind it, marked [VERIFY].
3. State the monitoring plan and the escalation criteria.
4. State the discharge or follow-up plan.

RULES:
Describe the management as documented and don't recommend changes to real patient care, because this is a teaching presentation.

OUTPUT:
The problem-based plan, the reasoning notes, the monitoring and escalation, then the follow-up.
tips: A problem list (e.g. "1. Septic shock 2. AKI 3. Hyperglycaemia") keeps management presentations organised.
prompts.try: Management of a patient with diabetic ketoacidosis and pneumonia.

prompts.t: ISBAR handover for a patient
prompts.use: For shift handovers and inter-team transfers.
prompts.p:
You are a patient-safety educator who teaches structured handover.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience or purpose: [brief]
Patient details (de-identified), current status and pending issues: [PASTE]
Receiving team: [brief]

TASK:
1. Write the handover in ISBAR format: Identify, Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation.
2. Highlight pending results, tasks and "watch for" items.
3. Include escalation criteria (if X, then do Y).
4. Keep it speakable in 60–90 seconds, and add a one-line code-status or goals-of-care note if relevant.

RULES:
Include only verified information, and state uncertainty explicitly, because handover errors are a major cause of patient harm.

OUTPUT:
The ISBAR handover, then the pending-task checklist.
tips: Ask the receiving doctor to read back the key tasks. Read-back catches errors.
prompts.try: Night handover of a post-operative patient with falling urine output.

prompts.t: Ward-round presentation (SOAP)
prompts.use: For presenting your patients on daily ward rounds.
prompts.p:
You are a consultant who likes concise, organised ward-round presentations.

MY CONTEXT:
Patient's data for today (de-identified): overnight events, symptoms, vitals, examination, new results and current treatment: [PASTE]

TASK:
1. Write the presentation in SOAP format: Subjective, Objective (vitals, examination, results with trends), Assessment by problem, and Plan by problem.
2. Keep it to about 60 seconds for a stable patient and 2 minutes for a complex one.
3. Put the questions for the consultant at the end.

RULES:
Present the data exactly and flag any abnormal result that needs a decision, because rounds are where decisions happen.

OUTPUT:
The SOAP presentation, then the questions for the consultant.
tips: Start with overnight events and anything urgent. Consultants want to know what's changed first.
prompts.try: Day 3 of admission for community-acquired pneumonia with new-onset atrial fibrillation.

prompts.t: Systems-based ICU rounds presentation
prompts.use: For presenting critically ill patients on ICU rounds.
prompts.p:
You are an intensivist who expects systematic, concise ICU presentations.

MY CONTEXT:
Patient's ICU data (de-identified), system by system: [PASTE]
Day of ICU stay and the admitting diagnosis: [brief]

TASK:
1. Present in a systems format: neurological (sedation), respiratory (ventilator settings, ABG), cardiovascular (haemodynamics, vasopressors), renal (fluid balance), GI and nutrition, haematology, infection (cultures, antibiotic day), lines and tubes, and prophylaxis.
2. Close with a problem list and today's goals.
3. Include a daily checklist (e.g. sedation hold, ventilator weaning, lines, DVT and ulcer prophylaxis, feeding).

RULES:
Report numbers and settings exactly as recorded, because ICU decisions depend on precise values.

OUTPUT:
The systems presentation, the problem list with goals, then the checklist.
tips: Always state the antibiotic day and the culture results. It's the most frequently asked ICU rounds question.
prompts.try: Day 4 of septic shock from a urinary source, ventilated, on noradrenaline.

prompts.t: Present a case to a senior on the phone
prompts.use: When calling a senior or another department about a patient, especially at night.
prompts.p:
You are a senior resident who receives dozens of phone referrals and knows what a good one sounds like.

MY CONTEXT:
Patient details (de-identified), the concern and the relevant data: [PASTE]
Who I'm calling and what I need: [advice / review / transfer]

TASK:
1. Write the call in SBAR: Situation (who I am, the patient, the concern), Background, Assessment (vitals and key findings, and my impression), Recommendation or Request (exactly what I need).
2. Keep it under 60 seconds.
3. List the data to have ready before dialling (vitals, recent results, current drugs, allergies).

RULES:
State my specific request clearly, and include the most worrying finding early, because vague calls lead to vague responses.

OUTPUT:
The SBAR script, then the "have ready" checklist.
tips: Start with the request if it's urgent: "I need you to see a patient with a falling GCS now."
prompts.try: Calling a surgical resident about a ward patient with suspected acute abdomen.

prompts.t: Case presentation built around images
prompts.use: When your case hinges on imaging, ECGs, fundoscopy, skin findings or histology.
prompts.p:
You are a clinician-educator who uses images to teach reasoning.

MY CONTEXT:
The case summary and the key images (described or uploaded, de-identified): [PASTE / UPLOAD]
Audience: [brief]

TASK:
1. Place each image at the point in the story where it changed thinking.
2. For each, write "what do you see?" prompts and the systematic description.
3. Plan annotated versions with arrows and labels.
4. Link the image findings to the differential.

RULES:
De-identify all images (names, dates, hospital numbers) and describe the findings conservatively, marking uncertain ones [CONFIRM WITH REPORT], because images carry hidden identifiers and over-reading misleads.

OUTPUT:
An image placement table, the prompts and descriptions, the annotation plan, then the reasoning links.
tips: Show the image first without comment. Let the audience look before you speak.
prompts.try: A case of miliary tuberculosis with serial chest X-rays and a CT.

prompts.t: Teaching points from a case
prompts.use: To close any case presentation.
prompts.p:
You are a clinical educator who distils cases into memorable lessons.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Case summary and outcome: [PASTE]
What went well, and what was difficult: [brief]

TASK:
1. Write 3–5 teaching points, each one sentence, specific and actionable.
2. Classify them: diagnostic, management, systems or communication.
3. Link each to evidence or a guideline where relevant, marked [VERIFY].
4. Suggest one question to test the audience on each point.

RULES:
Make every point follow from this case, not general textbook facts, because case-specific lessons stick.

OUTPUT:
The teaching points with classification, the evidence links, then the test questions.
tips: The best teaching point is often "what I would do differently".
prompts.try: A case of hyponatraemia that worsened with normal saline (SIADH).

prompts.t: A brief literature review for my case
prompts.use: When your case discussion needs 2–3 slides on what the literature says.
prompts.p:
You are an academic clinician who summarises literature quickly and accurately.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
The case's key question (diagnosis, management or rarity): [brief]
Sources I found (uploaded or with details): [UPLOAD / LIST]

TASK:
1. Summarise what the sources say about the key question.
2. Compare the case with published cases or series, if available.
3. Summarise the current guideline position, marked [VERIFY].
4. Write 2–3 slides with speaker notes.

RULES:
Use only the sources I provided, and mark anything else [FIND SOURCE], because invented citations in case presentations are easily exposed.

OUTPUT:
The summary, the comparison, the guideline note, then the slides.
tips: A search limited to case reports in PubMed often finds similar cases quickly.
prompts.try: A case of isoniazid-induced pellagra.

prompts.t: A 10–12 slide case-presentation deck
prompts.use: When your case presentation needs slides.
prompts.p:
You are a presentation coach for clinical meetings.

MY CONTEXT:
My structured case presentation: [PASTE]
Time: [minutes]
Images and tables available: [list]

TASK:
1. Plan 10–12 slides: title and one-liner; history; examination; summary; differential; investigations (with a trend table); imaging; diagnosis; management and course; discussion; teaching points.
2. Write a message title and brief content for each slide.
3. Suggest where the reveals and pauses should be.
4. Check that the timing fits.

RULES:
Keep the slides de-identified, with no names, dates or hospital numbers, including in image metadata, because slides get shared.

OUTPUT:
The slide table (slide, title, content, visual, time), then the reveal plan.
tips: Use a lab-trend table rather than pasting lab reports. It's readable and shows the trajectory.
prompts.try: A case of severe falciparum malaria with AKI.

prompts.t: Case discussion on a management controversy
prompts.use: When a case raises a genuine management dilemma worth debating.
prompts.p:
You are a senior clinician who moderates balanced case-based debates.

MY CONTEXT:
The case and the decision point: [PASTE]
The options considered, and what was chosen: [brief]
Sources for each option: [UPLOAD / LIST]

TASK:
1. Frame the dilemma as a clear question.
2. Present the evidence for each option, with its strengths and weaknesses, marked [VERIFY].
3. Consider patient factors, preferences and resources.
4. Explain what was done and why, and the outcome.
5. Write the discussion questions for the audience.

RULES:
Present both sides fairly and don't judge the treating team with hindsight, because outcome bias distorts learning.

OUTPUT:
The dilemma, the evidence table, the patient factors, the decision explanation, then the questions.
tips: Ask the audience to vote before and after the discussion. Changed votes show learning.
prompts.try: Anticoagulation in a patient with a recent GI bleed and new pulmonary embolism.

prompts.t: Present a case with an ethical dilemma
prompts.use: For cases involving consent, capacity, end-of-life care, resource allocation or confidentiality.
prompts.p:
You are a clinical ethicist who facilitates case discussions using principled frameworks.

MY CONTEXT:
The case (de-identified) and the ethical question: [PASTE]
Relevant Indian law or guidelines I'm aware of: [list]

TASK:
1. State the ethical question clearly.
2. Analyse it using a framework (e.g. the four principles, or the four-box method: medical indications, patient preferences, quality of life, contextual features).
3. Identify the stakeholders and their perspectives.
4. Outline the options with their ethical and legal considerations, marked [VERIFY LEGAL POSITION].
5. Write the discussion questions.

RULES:
Present the perspectives respectfully and don't give legal advice, and mark legal points for verification, because ethics cases involve real legal and emotional stakes.

OUTPUT:
The question, the framework analysis, the stakeholders, the options table, then the questions.
tips: Invite a nurse, social worker or ethicist to the discussion. Ethics cases benefit from several perspectives.
prompts.try: A family requesting withdrawal of ventilation for an elderly patient without a documented advance directive.

prompts.t: Present a rare diagnosis without losing the audience
prompts.use: When your case is a rare disease that most of the audience hasn't seen.
prompts.p:
You are a clinical teacher who makes rare cases relevant to everyday practice.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
The case (de-identified) and the rare diagnosis: [PASTE]
Audience: [brief]

TASK:
1. Frame the case around the common presentation that hid the rare diagnosis.
2. Explain the diagnostic clues that pointed to it.
3. Give a brief overview of the condition (5 bullets), marked [VERIFY].
4. Draw lessons that apply to common practice (e.g. when to think beyond the common).

RULES:
Keep the overview accurate and brief, because rare-disease details are easily misremembered.

OUTPUT:
The framing, the clues, the overview, then the lessons.
tips: "When the common diagnosis doesn't fit, look again" is the universal lesson of rare cases.
prompts.try: Adult-onset Still's disease presenting as fever of unknown origin.

prompts.t: Learning from a delayed or missed diagnosis
prompts.use: For teaching sessions on diagnostic error, using a de-identified case.
prompts.p:
You are a diagnostic-reasoning expert who teaches cognitive bias without blame.

MY CONTEXT:
The case timeline and the eventual diagnosis: [PASTE]
The points where the diagnosis could have been made: [brief]

TASK:
1. Map the diagnostic journey on a timeline.
2. Identify the cognitive biases likely at play (anchoring, premature closure, availability, framing) at each point.
3. Identify the system factors (workload, handover, test delays).
4. Suggest de-biasing strategies and system fixes.
5. Write the teaching points.

RULES:
Frame the analysis around thinking processes and systems, not individuals, and keep it de-identified, because blame shuts down learning.

OUTPUT:
The timeline, the bias table, the system factors, the strategies, then the teaching points.
tips: A "diagnostic time-out" (asking "what else could this be?") is a simple, teachable de-biasing tool.
prompts.try: A pulmonary embolism initially treated as pneumonia for 3 days.

prompts.t: The questions the head of department will ask
prompts.use: The day before presenting a case to your unit head or at a departmental meeting.
prompts.p:
You are a senior professor known for incisive case-discussion questions.

MY CONTEXT:
My case presentation: [PASTE]
My specialty and year: [brief]

TASK:
1. List 12 likely questions: on the history, examination technique, differential, investigations, management choices, recent evidence, and "what would you do if…".
2. Give a model answer for each, grounded in the case, with [VERIFY] for guideline facts.
3. Mark the 3 hardest questions and suggest how to prepare for them.

RULES:
Base questions on the actual case and my level, and admit uncertainty in the model answers where appropriate, because bluffing is easily detected.

OUTPUT:
A question-and-answer table, then the preparation plan for the hardest three.
tips: "I don't know, but I would find out by…" is a respectable answer. Guessing isn't.
prompts.try: A presentation of a young patient with a first episode of status epilepticus.

prompts.t: Root-cause analysis for an M&M case
prompts.use: When preparing the analysis part of an M&M or quality-improvement meeting.
prompts.p:
You are a patient-safety specialist trained in root-cause analysis.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
The event timeline (de-identified): [PASTE]
Initial thoughts on contributing factors: [brief]

TASK:
1. Build a fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram description with categories: people, processes, equipment, environment, communication and policies.
2. Apply "5 whys" to the 2 most important contributing factors.
3. Distinguish root causes from contributing factors.
4. Propose SMART corrective actions.

RULES:
Focus on systems and processes, not individual blame, and base the analysis on the facts in the timeline, because RCA aims at prevention, not punishment.

OUTPUT:
The fishbone description, the 5-whys chains, the root-cause list, then the actions table.
tips: If your "root cause" is "human error", ask "why" at least twice more.
prompts.try: A delayed administration of antibiotics to a septic patient in the emergency department.

prompts.t: Present a follow-up update on a previous case
prompts.use: When the department wants to hear how a previously presented patient did.
prompts.p:
You are a clinical teacher who closes the loop on cases.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
The original presentation summary: [PASTE]
The follow-up course and outcome: [PASTE]

TASK:
1. Remind the audience of the case in 2 lines.
2. Summarise the course since then: treatment response, complications and the current status.
3. Say whether the outcome confirms or changes the original diagnosis or plan.
4. Draw updated lessons.

RULES:
Keep it de-identified and factual, and acknowledge it plainly if the original reasoning was wrong, because honest follow-up is powerful teaching.

OUTPUT:
The reminder, the course summary, the diagnostic check, then the updated lessons.
tips: Follow-up presentations teach humility and the natural history of disease. Do more of them.
prompts.try: A 6-month follow-up of a patient with autoimmune encephalitis.

prompts.t: Turn a case into a teaching session for MBBS students
prompts.use: When teaching undergraduates using a real ward case.
prompts.p:
You are a clinical tutor for MBBS students.

MY CONTEXT:
The case (de-identified): [PASTE]
Students' year and what they have learned so far: [brief]
Time: [minutes]

TASK:
1. Choose 3 learning objectives appropriate for the students' level.
2. Plan a Socratic session: questions at each stage of the case.
3. Include one clinical skill to practise (e.g. eliciting a sign) if possible.
4. Link the case to their exam topics (e.g. NEET-PG and university exams).
5. Write 5 check questions.

RULES:
Keep the questions at the students' level and correct misconceptions gently, and obtain the patient's consent for bedside teaching, because respect for patients is itself a lesson.

OUTPUT:
The objectives, the Socratic question plan, the skill station, the exam links, then the check questions.
tips: Ask students to commit to an answer before you reveal it. Commitment drives learning.
prompts.try: A patient with mitral stenosis for third-year MBBS students.

prompts.t: Link a case to a recent paper
prompts.use: When a case presentation would be stronger with one recent, relevant study.
prompts.p:
You are an academic clinician who connects bedside cases to current evidence.

MY CONTEXT:
The case summary and its key clinical question: [PASTE]
The recent paper I found (upload or paste the abstract): [UPLOAD / PASTE]
Audience: [brief]

TASK:
1. Summarise the paper in 3 lines (design, population, key result).
2. Explain how it applies, or doesn't apply, to this patient.
3. Note the paper's main limitation for this context.
4. Write one slide connecting the case and the paper.

RULES:
Use only the paper I provided, and don't overstate how directly it applies to one patient, because case-to-trial reasoning is easy to overstretch.

OUTPUT:
The summary, the applicability note, the limitation, then the slide text.
tips: One well-chosen recent paper makes a case discussion feel current and evidence-based.
prompts.try: A patient with severe community-acquired pneumonia and a recent trial of corticosteroids.

prompts.t: Opening one-liner for my case
prompts.p: Act as a clinical teacher. Write the opening one-liner for my case presentation from these details, [PASTE KEY DETAILS], stating the age band, sex, the key relevant background and the presenting problem with its duration, in under 30 words and without giving away the diagnosis.
prompts.try: A 58-year-old diabetic woman with 5 days of fever and right upper-quadrant pain.

prompts.t: Summarise my case in three lines
prompts.p: Act as a senior physician. Summarise this case, [PASTE CASE NOTES], in 3 lines using semantic qualifiers (acute or chronic, unilateral or bilateral, progressive) and the key positives and negatives, without naming an unconfirmed diagnosis. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: Notes on a teenager with fever, sore throat, rash and joint pains.

prompts.t: Which negatives matter?
prompts.p: Act as a clinical examiner. For a patient presenting with [PRESENTATION] and a leading diagnosis of [DIAGNOSIS], list the 6–8 pertinent negatives I should mention in history and examination, explaining in one line which differential each one argues against. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: Presentation: acute chest pain. Leading diagnosis: aortic dissection.

prompts.t: Why is this case worth presenting?
prompts.p: Act as a case-meeting coordinator. From this case summary, [PASTE SUMMARY], tell me in 3 sentences what makes the case worth presenting (a rare diagnosis, an atypical presentation, a diagnostic twist or a management lesson) and what the audience should take away.
prompts.try: A patient with hypokalaemic paralysis who turned out to have thyrotoxicosis.

prompts.t: Build the problem list
prompts.p: Act as a physician on rounds. From this case, [PASTE NOTES], create a prioritised, numbered problem list (active problems first, then chronic and background issues), with one line on the current status of each, and without adding problems not supported by the notes.
prompts.try: An elderly patient with pneumonia, AKI, hyponatraemia, diabetes and delirium.

prompts.t: Describe the vitals trend
prompts.p: Act as a clinical teacher. Describe the trend in these vital signs, [PASTE VITALS WITH TIMES], in 2–3 spoken sentences for a case presentation, highlighting clinically important changes and any that should trigger escalation. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.

prompts.t: Present the lab results concisely
prompts.p: Act as a senior resident. Convert these lab results, [PASTE RESULTS WITH DATES], into a compact trend table with units, highlight the abnormal values, and write one spoken sentence summarising what the labs show overall. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: Five days of creatinine, potassium, sodium, haemoglobin and platelet counts.

prompts.t: Hospital course as a timeline
prompts.p: Act as a clinical documentation expert. Turn this hospital course, [PASTE NOTES], into a day-by-day timeline of key events, investigations, treatment changes and responses, using relative days (Day 0, Day 1…) and removing identifiers, for one slide. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: A 10-day admission for dengue with warning signs and plasma leakage.

prompts.t: The final diagnosis statement
prompts.p: Act as a senior physician. Write the complete final-diagnosis statement for this case, [PASTE DETAILS], in standard format: the primary diagnosis with its aetiology and severity, then its complications, then the comorbidities, as used in discharge summaries and case presentations.
prompts.try: A patient with community-acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock and AKI, with diabetes.

prompts.t: One learning point from my case
prompts.p: Act as a clinical educator. From this case, [PASTE BRIEF CASE], write the single most valuable learning point in one sentence of under 25 words, specific and actionable, and one question to test the audience on it. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: A patient whose hypoglycaemia was caused by a sulphonylurea in renal failure.

prompts.t: SBAR script for a phone call
prompts.p: Act as a patient-safety trainer. Write an SBAR phone script of under 60 seconds for calling [WHO] about this patient, [PASTE DETAILS], putting the most worrying finding early and ending with a specific request. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: Calling the ICU resident about a ward patient with a falling GCS and rising respiratory rate.

prompts.t: A title for my case presentation
prompts.p: Act as a case-meeting coordinator. Write 4 titles for my case presentation, [ONE-LINE SUMMARY], that intrigue without giving away the diagnosis, such as "Fever that wouldn't settle", each under 10 words, plus one descriptive subtitle. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: A case of infective endocarditis presenting as a stroke in a young adult.

prompts.t: Plan a small-group teaching session
prompts.use: When you teach interns, students or juniors in a tutorial, skills lab or classroom.
prompts.why: Most clinical teaching is a mini-lecture with no plan. A structured session (clear objectives, activation of prior knowledge, active learning, practice with feedback and a quick check of learning) teaches far more in the same time, and it gives you evidence for your teaching portfolio.
prompts.p:
You are a medical educator trained in instructional design who designs short, active small-group sessions for clinical learners, and you are known for making every minute count.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
Topic: [TOPIC]
Learners: [e.g. 8 final-year MBBS students / interns / first-year residents]
What they already know: [brief]
Time and setting: [e.g. 45 minutes, seminar room with a whiteboard]
Resources available: [projector, mannequin, cases, handouts]

TASK:
1. Write 3 learning objectives with Bloom's verbs.
2. Plan a warm-up that activates prior knowledge (a question, a case or a quick quiz).
3. Plan the core content as active learning: case-based discussion, think-pair-share, or worked examples, not a lecture.
4. Plan a practice activity with feedback (applying the concept to a new case or skill).
5. Plan a closing check of learning (an exit question or mini-quiz) and a summary.
6. Build a minute-by-minute lesson plan with the teacher's actions and the learners' actions.
7. Suggest adaptations for a stronger and a weaker group.
8. Suggest how to collect feedback on the session.

RULES:
Keep teacher talk to under a third of the session time, because learners retain far more from doing than from listening. Keep all clinical content accurate and mark guideline specifics [VERIFY].

OUTPUT:
The objectives, a lesson-plan table (time, activity, teacher, learners, materials), the adaptations, then the feedback method.

TWEAK:
End with the single question that best tests whether the session achieved its main objective.
tips: Start with a question, not a slide. It shows you what the group already knows.
Plan less content than you think. Active learning takes more time, and teaches more.
Keep your lesson plans. Over a year they become a reusable teaching library.

prompts.t: Structured bedside teaching session
prompts.use: When teaching at the bedside on rounds or in a dedicated teaching session.
prompts.why: The bedside is the richest place to teach clinical skills and reasoning, and the easiest place to embarrass a patient or bore a learner. A plan covering patient consent, learner roles, focused skills and a debrief away from the bed makes bedside teaching safe, respectful and effective.
prompts.p:
You are a senior clinical teacher known for respectful, high-yield bedside teaching, who uses frameworks such as SNAPPS and the one-minute preceptor.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
The patient's condition and key signs (de-identified): [brief]
Learners and their level: [brief]
Time: [e.g. 20 minutes]
Skill or concept to teach: [e.g. examining for a pleural effusion]

TASK:
1. Plan the pre-briefing away from the bed: objectives, roles and etiquette.
2. Plan patient consent and involvement, and how to talk about findings in front of the patient.
3. Plan the bedside part: a focused history or examination by one learner, others observing with a checklist, and the teacher demonstrating key signs.
4. Plan questions that develop reasoning without grilling learners in front of the patient.
