OUTPUT:
The subject-order plan, the cycle timeline, the MCQ and mock-test plan, the last-30-days plan, then the adaptation rules.

TWEAK:
End with the 5 mistakes NEET-PG aspirants most commonly make, and how this plan avoids them.
tips: Analysing a grand test for as long as it took to write it is where the marks come from.
Fewer resources, revised more times, beats more resources read once.
Protect sleep in the final month. Tired recall is poor recall.

prompts.t: Plan for the MD / MS / DNB final exam
prompts.use: 6–9 months before your residency final exam (theory, practical and viva).
prompts.why: Residency finals test depth, clinical skills and presentation, all while you're working full duties and finishing a thesis. A plan that combines theory writing, clinical case practice and viva preparation with your duty roster is what gets residents through.
prompts.p:
You are a senior faculty member and examiner for MD, MS and DNB examinations who mentors final-year residents.

MY CONTEXT:
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
Specialty and exam type: [e.g. MD General Medicine university exam / DNB final]
Months until the theory and practical exams: [N / N]
Duty pattern (calls, OPD, ICU postings): [brief]
Thesis status: [submitted / pending]
Weak areas: [list]
Exam format as I understand it (papers, long and short cases, viva, OSCE, spotters): [brief, marked "to confirm"]

TASK:
1. Map the syllabus to the exam components: theory papers, clinical cases, viva areas and spotters or OSCE.
2. Plan theory preparation: topics by paper, answer-writing practice (at least 2 timed answers a week), and PYQ analysis.
3. Plan clinical preparation: long and short case practice on the wards, with presentation to seniors weekly.
4. Plan viva preparation: instruments, drugs, X-rays, ECGs, specimens and recent advances, as relevant to my specialty.
5. Fit everything around my duties, with realistic weekly targets.
6. Plan mock exams with seniors or faculty.
7. Plan the last month and the exam week.

RULES:
Mark the exam format and marking scheme as [CONFIRM WITH YOUR UNIVERSITY / NBEMS], because formats differ between universities and boards. Keep the plan realistic for a working resident.

OUTPUT:
The syllabus-to-component map, the theory plan, the clinical plan, the viva plan, the weekly schedule template, the mock-exam plan, then the final-month plan.

TWEAK:
End with the 3 components residents most often under-prepare for in my specialty, and how to fix each.
tips: Present a case to a senior every week. Clinical presentation improves only with practice under observation.
Write timed answers from month one. Knowing isn't the same as writing well in 15 minutes.
Ask recent passers about their examiners' style. Local exam culture matters.

prompts.t: UPSC CMS preparation strategy
prompts.aud: MBBS graduate / Intern / UPSC CMS aspirant
prompts.use: When preparing for the UPSC Combined Medical Services examination.
prompts.why: UPSC CMS has its own pattern and emphasis, including a heavy weight on community medicine and on general medicine, paediatrics, surgery and obstetrics as its notification defines, and a personality test. Preparing with a NEET-PG plan alone leaves gaps. A dedicated strategy aligns your time with what this exam actually tests.
prompts.p:
You are a mentor for UPSC CMS aspirants who knows how its pattern and emphasis differ from NEET-PG, and who always checks the current official notification.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
Months until the exam: [N]
Also preparing for NEET-PG?: [yes / no]
Daily hours available: [number]
Strong and weak subjects: [lists]
Previous attempt, if any: [brief]

TASK:
1. Summarise the exam structure as I should verify it: papers, subjects covered and the interview or personality test, all marked [VERIFY WITH THE CURRENT UPSC NOTIFICATION].
2. Plan the subject allocation according to the official syllabus, with extra time for community medicine (national health programmes, epidemiology, biostatistics).
3. Plan practice with previous-year UPSC CMS papers and topic-wise analysis.
4. Plan the overlap and differences if preparing for NEET-PG in parallel.
5. Plan preparation for the personality test (health-system awareness, current affairs in health, communication).
6. Build a month-by-month timeline with revision cycles.
7. Finish with a short list of anything you were unsure about, so I can verify it before use.

RULES:
Base all pattern and syllabus statements on the official notification only, marking them [VERIFY WITH THE CURRENT UPSC NOTIFICATION], because the exam structure is revised and unofficial summaries are often wrong.

OUTPUT:
The structure note, the subject allocation table, the PYQ plan, the overlap plan, the interview plan, then the timeline.

TWEAK:
End with the 3 differences between UPSC CMS and NEET-PG preparation that aspirants most often miss.
tips: Download the official notification and syllabus first. Plan from it, not from coaching summaries.
Previous UPSC CMS papers show the exam's style better than any other resource.
Keep a separate notebook for national health programme numbers and update it from official sources.

prompts.t: A spaced-repetition revision schedule
prompts.use: After first coverage of a subject, so that you don't forget it.
prompts.p:
You are a learning-science coach who applies spaced repetition to medical exams.

MY CONTEXT:
Topics I've completed, with the dates: [LIST]
Exam date: [date]
Daily time available for revision: [minutes]

TASK:
1. Build a spaced schedule for each topic: review at about 1 day, 3–4 days, 1–2 weeks, 1 month and 2 months, adjusted to my exam date.
2. Show a daily revision list for the next 2 weeks.
3. Explain what to do in each review (active recall, not re-reading).
4. Suggest how to use Anki or a simple spreadsheet to track it.

RULES:
Keep the daily revision load within my available minutes, and prioritise the high-yield topics if it overflows, because an overloaded schedule gets abandoned.

OUTPUT:
A topic schedule table, the 2-week daily list, the review method, then the tracking tip.
tips: A 10-minute active-recall review beats an hour of re-reading.

prompts.t: The last 30 days before the exam
prompts.use: One month before the exam.
prompts.p:
You are an exam strategist who has coached many students through the final month.

MY CONTEXT:
Exam: [brief]
Subjects and my confidence in each (1–5): [LIST]
Mock-test scores so far: [brief]
Hours available per day: [number]

TASK:
1. Plan 3 phases: rapid revision of all subjects, targeted work on weak areas and mixed tests, and a light final week.
2. Build a day-by-day plan.
3. Plan mock tests and their analysis.
4. Plan sleep, food and exercise.
5. Say what not to start new in this phase.

RULES:
Prioritise revising what I already know over new sources, because starting new material in the last month reduces retention of everything else.

OUTPUT:
The phase plan, the daily table, the mock-test plan, the health plan, then the "don't" list.
tips: The last month is for consolidation, not expansion.
prompts.try: NEET-PG in 30 days, with low confidence in pharmacology and microbiology.

prompts.t: The last 7 days before the exam
prompts.use: In the final week.
prompts.p:
You are a calm exam coach who prevents last-week panic.

MY CONTEXT:
Exam and date: [brief]
Topics I still feel shaky on: [list]
My usual exam-week problems (anxiety, insomnia, cramming): [brief]

TASK:
1. Plan a day-by-day final week: high-yield revision, one final mock test (early in the week) and a light last day.
2. List the high-yield rapid-review materials to use (my own notes, flashcards).
3. Give a sleep and stress plan.
4. Give a checklist for the day before (admit card, ID, route, timing).

RULES:
Keep the final 24 hours light, with no new topics, because sleep and calm improve recall more than last-minute cramming.

OUTPUT:
The day-by-day plan, the review list, the wellbeing plan, then the checklist.
tips: Stop studying by early evening the day before. Rest is part of preparation.

prompts.t: I've fallen behind: recover my plan
prompts.use: When you are weeks behind schedule and feel overwhelmed.
prompts.p:
You are a supportive but realistic study coach who rescues derailed plans.

MY CONTEXT:
Original plan and where I am now: [brief]
Days left: [N]
Reasons I fell behind: [brief]
Hours now available: [number]

TASK:
1. Assess honestly what can still be achieved.
2. Triage the remaining syllabus: must do, should do, and skip or skim.
3. Build a revised plan that fits my real hours.
4. Address the reasons I fell behind with practical fixes.
5. Set small daily wins to rebuild momentum.

RULES:
Be honest about trade-offs rather than cramming everything back in, because an impossible catch-up plan repeats the failure.

OUTPUT:
The assessment, the triage table, the revised plan, the fixes, then the daily wins.
tips: A revised plan you finish beats a perfect plan you abandon again.
prompts.try: 5 weeks behind in NEET-PG preparation, 3 months left, internship duties heavy.

prompts.t: Weekly study review
prompts.use: Every Sunday (or your weekly off-day), to review and adjust.
prompts.p:
You are an accountability coach for exam preparation.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
This week's plan and what I actually did: [brief]
Test scores this week: [brief]
Energy, sleep and mood this week: [brief]

TASK:
1. Compare planned and actual, and calculate the completion rate.
2. Identify what worked and what didn't.
3. Adjust next week's plan (move topics, change timings, adjust targets).
4. Set 3 specific goals for next week.

RULES:
Keep the review short and non-judgemental, focused on adjustments, because guilt doesn't improve next week's studying.

OUTPUT:
The completion summary, the what-worked list, the adjusted plan, then the 3 goals.
tips: 20 minutes of weekly review saves hours of wasted effort.

prompts.t: Which subject should I study first?
prompts.use: When deciding the order of subjects for a long preparation.
prompts.p:
You are an exam strategist who sequences subjects for maximum retention and momentum.

Exam: [brief]
Subjects remaining: [list]
Strong and weak subjects: [lists]
Months available: [N]

TASK:
1. Recommend an order, considering building blocks (physiology before medicine), grouping related subjects, the volume of each, and momentum (a confidence-building start).
2. Estimate the time for each subject.
3. Suggest pairing a heavy subject with a light one each week.
4. Place revision checkpoints.

Justify the order with reasoning rather than tradition, and mark claims about exam weightage [VERIFY WITH PYQs], because weightage varies between years.

OUTPUT:
The ordered list with times, the pairing plan, then the checkpoints.
tips: Studying related subjects together (pathology with medicine) saves time and deepens understanding.

prompts.t: Study around internship or residency duties
prompts.use: When duties are heavy and study time is fragmented.
prompts.p:
You are a productivity coach who works with busy clinicians.

MY CONTEXT:
My duty roster pattern (days, calls, post-call days): [brief]
Commute and free pockets of time: [brief]
Study goals: [brief]

TASK:
1. Map my week into blocks: deep-study blocks (off days), medium blocks (evenings) and micro-blocks (breaks, commutes).
2. Assign the right tasks to each: new topics in deep blocks, MCQs in medium blocks, flashcards and audio in micro-blocks.
3. Plan post-call days realistically (light revision or rest).
4. Suggest tools for micro-learning.

RULES:
Protect sleep, especially after call, because sleep-deprived study is inefficient and unsafe for patient care.

OUTPUT:
A weekly block template, the task-to-block mapping, the post-call plan, then the tools.
tips: Twenty-five minutes of flashcards in duty breaks adds up to 10 hours a month.

prompts.t: Plan revision cycles (R1, R2, R3)
prompts.use: After first coverage, to plan repeated revisions.
prompts.p:
You are an exam strategist who designs efficient revision cycles.

MY CONTEXT:
Subjects and the time available after first coverage: [brief]
My notes format: [own notes / printed notes / annotated books]

TASK:
1. Plan 3 cycles of decreasing length (e.g. R1 at about 50% of the coverage time, R2 at about 25%, R3 at about 10%).
2. Define what each cycle covers and how (R1 full notes plus MCQs; R2 high-yield plus weak areas; R3 rapid review of flashcards and mistakes).
3. Build the calendar.
4. Explain how to mark notes during each cycle to speed up the next one.

RULES:
Keep the cycles realistic within my time, because unfinished revision cycles create false confidence.

OUTPUT:
The cycle plan, the calendar, then the note-marking method.
tips: Highlight what you got wrong in R1. R3 should be mostly those highlights.
prompts.try: 8 months after first coverage for NEET-PG, with my own handwritten notes.

prompts.t: Analyse a mock or grand test properly
prompts.use: After every mock test or grand test.
prompts.p:
You are a performance analyst for competitive medical exams.

MY CONTEXT:
Score, rank or percentile, and the time taken: [brief]
Subject-wise results: [PASTE]
The questions I got wrong or guessed (topics or question text): [PASTE]

TASK:
1. Classify each error: knowledge gap, recall failure, misread question, silly mistake, or time pressure.
2. Identify patterns by subject and error type.
3. Build a 1-week fix plan targeting the top patterns.
4. Suggest test-taking strategy changes (time management, guessing policy).
5. Track the trend against my previous tests.

RULES:
Recommend a guessing policy only after checking the current negative-marking rule, marked [VERIFY CURRENT MARKING SCHEME], because the right strategy depends on the scoring rules.

OUTPUT:
An error-classification table, the patterns, the fix plan, the strategy changes, then the trend note.
tips: Guessed-but-right answers are gaps too. Review them as if you'd got them wrong.
prompts.try: A grand test with 142 wrong answers, many in medicine and pharmacology.

prompts.t: Rescue my weakest subject
prompts.use: When one subject keeps pulling your scores down.
prompts.p:
You are a subject-rescue coach who turns weak subjects into scoring ones.

MY CONTEXT:
Subject: [name]
Why I find it hard: [brief]
Time available for it: [hours per week, weeks]
Recent test performance in it: [brief]

TASK:
1. Diagnose the problem: foundations, volume, memory or application.
2. Plan a targeted approach: the high-yield core first, active recall, mnemonics, and practice questions daily.
3. Set weekly milestones with measurable targets.
4. Suggest how to make it interesting (clinical links, cases).

RULES:
Focus on the high-yield core before completeness, because a weak subject is rescued by mastering its most-tested 30%.

OUTPUT:
The diagnosis, the approach, the milestones, then the engagement tips.
tips: Do 20 questions in your weakest subject every day. Familiarity reduces fear.
prompts.try: Microbiology, where I forget organisms within a week.

prompts.t: Am I heading for burnout?
prompts.use: When studying feels exhausting, pointless or overwhelming.

You are a supportive physician-mentor familiar with student burnout and mental health.

MY CONTEXT:
How I've been feeling (energy, sleep, mood, motivation, concentration): [brief]
Study hours and duties: [brief]
Support I have (friends, family, mentors): [brief]

TASK:
1. Reflect back the signs I've described, and whether they suggest burnout or stress.
2. Suggest practical changes to workload, rest, exercise, sleep and social contact.
3. Suggest how to adjust the study plan without giving up.
4. Tell me clearly when and where to seek professional help.

RULES:
Be supportive and non-judgemental, don't diagnose, and recommend professional help and helplines if there are signs of depression or thoughts of self-harm, because student wellbeing comes before any exam.

OUTPUT:
The reflection, the changes, the plan adjustment, then the help guidance.
tips: Rest is not a reward for finishing work. It's part of the work.

You are a productivity coach who applies focus techniques to medical study.

My distractions (phone, social media, noise, fatigue): [list]
Study environment: [hostel / library / home]
Daily study hours: [number]

TASK:
1. Design a session structure (e.g. 50 minutes of focus and 10 of break, or 25/5), with a clear goal per session.
2. Suggest environment changes and phone rules.
3. Suggest how to start a session quickly (a 2-minute starter task).
4. Suggest how to track sessions completed, rather than hours "spent".

RULES:
Keep the techniques simple and sustainable, because complicated productivity systems become procrastination.

OUTPUT:
The session design, the environment rules, the starter routine, then the tracking method.
tips: Put your phone in another room. It's the single most effective focus technique.

prompts.use: When studying with friends for exams.
prompts.p:
You are a peer-learning coach.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience or purpose: [brief]
Group size and members' strengths: [brief]
Exam and meeting frequency: [brief]

TASK:
1. Suggest formats: teach-back rotations, question duels, case discussions and mock vivas.
2. Build a weekly schedule with roles.
3. Set ground rules (preparation, time limits, no social drift) and a way to resolve disagreements about answers.
4. Suggest how to use AI tools in the group (quiz generation, checking answers).

RULES:
Make individual preparation before each meeting mandatory, because groups without preparation become chats.

OUTPUT:
The formats, the schedule, the ground rules, then the AI tips.
tips: Teaching a topic to your group is the fastest way to find out whether you really know it.

You are a mentor who helps students simplify their resources.

Resources I currently use or own: [list]
Exam and time left: [brief]

2. Recommend one primary resource per role, and what to drop.
3. Explain how to integrate the chosen resources (e.g. annotate one set of notes).
4. Set a rule for adding any new resource.

RULES:
Recommend fewer, well-used resources, and don't endorse specific commercial products as superior, because the best resource is the one you revise repeatedly.

OUTPUT:
The resource assessment table, the final set, the integration method, then the rule.
tips: One source revised five times beats five sources read once.

prompts.t: The night before and the exam day
prompts.use: 1–2 days before any major exam.
prompts.p:
You are an exam coach who helps students perform at their best on the day.

MY CONTEXT:
Exam type (computer-based, written, practical or viva), timing and venue: [brief]
My exam-day worries: [list]

TASK:
1. Plan the day before: light revision, logistics check, meals and sleep time.
2. Plan the morning: wake-up time, breakfast, travel buffer and what to carry.
3. Plan the in-exam strategy: time allocation, handling hard questions, and breaks.
4. Plan how to manage anxiety in the hall.
5. Plan between papers, if there are several.

RULES:
Include only practical, safe advice, and remind me to verify exam-specific rules (documents, items allowed) from the official instructions, because rules differ by exam.

OUTPUT:
Timelines for the day before and the exam day, the in-exam strategy, the anxiety plan, then the between-papers plan.
tips: Don't discuss answers between papers. It only adds anxiety.

prompts.t: Sleep, memory and study performance

prompts.p:
You are a sleep-medicine physician who advises students.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
My current sleep pattern and study schedule: [brief]
Duties or night shifts: [brief]

TASK:
1. Explain briefly how sleep affects memory consolidation.
2. Assess my current pattern.
3. Suggest a realistic sleep schedule that fits my study.
4. Suggest strategies for shift workers and post-call days.
5. Suggest habits for better sleep quality.

RULES:
Keep the advice evidence-based and practical, and recommend medical review for persistent insomnia, because chronic sleep problems need proper assessment.

OUTPUT:
The explanation, the assessment, the schedule, the shift strategies, then the habits.
tips: Reviewing flashcards before sleep and again on waking uses sleep to strengthen memory.

prompts.t: Build a simple accountability tracker
prompts.use: When you want to stay consistent over months of preparation.
prompts.p:
You are an accountability coach who designs simple tracking systems.

My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience or purpose: [brief]

Tools: [paper / Google Sheets / Notion / app]

TASK:
1. Design a tracker with daily inputs (topics done, MCQs attempted, accuracy, hours, sleep).
2. Add weekly summary formulas or sections.
3. Add a visual progress indicator.
4. Suggest a weekly reflection prompt.

RULES:
Keep the daily input under 2 minutes, because trackers that take longer are abandoned.

OUTPUT:
The tracker layout (columns and formulas), the weekly summary, then the reflection prompt.
tips: Track the process (MCQs done, topics revised), not just the hours. The process is what you control.

Plan my study day for [EXAM], with the topics [TOPICS], including one active-recall block, one question-practice block, breaks and a 15-minute review at the end. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.

prompts.t: Exam-pattern MCQs with full explanations
prompts.aud: MBBS Student / NEET-PG / UPSC CMS aspirant
prompts.use: When you want high-quality practice questions on a topic you have just studied.
prompts.why: Random question banks don't target the topic you've just finished. Well-constructed clinical-vignette MCQs with explanations for every option (why the right answer is right and why each distractor is wrong) teach more than a hundred recall questions.
prompts.p:
You are an experienced MCQ writer for Indian postgraduate entrance and licensing exams. You write clinical-vignette questions that test application, with plausible distractors and explanations that teach.

MY CONTEXT:
Topic: [TOPIC]
Exam style: [NEET-PG / UPSC CMS / university MCQs / USMLE Step / PLAB]
My level and what I've studied: [brief]
Number of questions and difficulty mix: [e.g. 20: 6 easy, 10 moderate, 4 hard]
My standard textbook or source (to stay consistent with): [name]

TASK:
1. Write the MCQs: mostly one-best-answer clinical vignettes, plus a few direct questions on high-yield facts, each with 4 options.
2. Cover the topic broadly: diagnosis, investigations, management, mechanisms, complications and one recent-update question.
3. Show the questions first without answers, so I can attempt them.
4. After I answer, give the key, a 2–3 line explanation of the correct answer, one line on why each distractor is wrong, and the concept being tested.
5. Score my attempt and list the concepts I got wrong.
6. Give 3 follow-up questions targeting my mistakes.

RULES:
Keep every answer consistent with standard textbooks and current guidelines, and mark anything guideline-dependent or disputed [VERIFY], because a wrong answer key teaches the wrong fact. Avoid "all of the above" and trick questions without a teaching purpose. Don't claim the questions are actual past exam questions.

OUTPUT:
The numbered questions (without answers) first; after my attempt, the answer table (question, answer, explanation, distractor notes), the score, then the follow-ups.

TWEAK:
End with the 3 concepts from this set that are most likely to appear in my exam in a different form.
tips: Attempt all the questions before reading any explanation. That makes it retrieval practice.
Write down every concept you got wrong in your mistake notebook.
Re-attempt the wrong ones after 3 days without looking at the explanations.

prompts.t: Solve a question and learn the logic
prompts.aud: MBBS Student / NEET-PG / UPSC CMS aspirant
prompts.use: When a question stumps you and you want to understand the reasoning, not just the answer.
prompts.why: Knowing the answer to one question helps with one question. Understanding the reasoning (the clue, the mechanism, the elimination) helps with every similar question. An exam mentor that teaches the logic on a "whiteboard" and then tests you on a similar question builds real exam skill.
prompts.p:
You are an exam mentor for Indian medical entrance exams who teaches like a teacher at a whiteboard: step by step, from the clue to the answer, then testing whether the student can do it alone.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
The question with its options: [PASTE QUESTION]
My answer and why I chose it: [brief]
Subject and exam: [brief]

TASK:
1. Don't give the final answer immediately. First identify the key clue or clues in the stem.
2. Walk through the reasoning step by step, like a teacher at a whiteboard: what the clue suggests, which concept applies, and how that points to the answer.
3. Eliminate each wrong option with a reason.
4. Explain where my reasoning went wrong, if it did.
5. State the general rule or concept this question tests.
6. Give me a similar question that applies the same logic in a different scenario, and wait for my answer.
7. Tell me whether my answer and reasoning are correct.

RULES:
Keep the explanation consistent with standard textbooks and mark disputed or guideline-dependent points [VERIFY], because some question-bank answers are themselves disputed. Wait for my answer to the similar question before explaining it.

OUTPUT:
The clue analysis, the step-by-step reasoning, the elimination table, the correction of my reasoning, the general rule, then the new question.

TWEAK:
End with a one-line "rule to remember" for my mistake notebook.
tips: Always write down why you chose your answer before checking it. It reveals your reasoning errors.
If you got it right for the wrong reason, treat it as wrong.
The similar question is the real test. Don't skip it.

prompts.t: Analyse previous-year questions for patterns
prompts.aud: MBBS Student / NEET-PG / UPSC CMS aspirant / PG Resident
prompts.use: At the start of preparation, and again midway, using real previous-year papers.
prompts.why: Previous-year questions are the most reliable guide to what an exam values. Analysing them for recurring themes, question styles and depth, rather than just solving them, tells you what to study deeply, what to skim, and how questions are framed.
prompts.p:
You are an exam analyst who studies previous-year papers to guide preparation, and who reports only what the actual papers show.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
Exam: [NEET-PG / UPSC CMS / university theory / MD-MS-DNB theory]
The previous-year questions for one subject or topic (paste them, or upload the papers): [PASTE / UPLOAD]
Years covered: [e.g. 5 years]

TASK:
1. Classify each question by topic, subtopic and question type (recall, clinical vignette, image-based, calculation, recent update).
2. Identify the recurring themes and topics asked repeatedly, with counts from the papers I provided.
3. Identify the depth: which details were asked (e.g. drug of choice, a specific sign or criterion).
4. Identify trends over the years (e.g. more clinical vignettes, more image-based questions).
5. Build a "must-master" topic list for this subject, based on the analysis.
6. Suggest how to practise for each question type.
7. Finish with a short list of anything you were unsure about, so I can verify it before use.

RULES:
Base every count and pattern only on the questions I provided, and don't claim frequencies beyond them, because extrapolated "important topics" from memory are unreliable. Say where the sample is too small for conclusions.

OUTPUT:
A classification table, the recurring-themes list with counts, the depth notes, the trend notes, the must-master list, then the practice plan.

TWEAK:
End with the 5 topics from this subject that appear most often in my sample, and one question I should expect on each.
tips: Analyse by subject, 5 or more years at a time. Patterns only show up across years.
Mark previous-year topics in your notes. Revise those pages more often.
For university theory exams, repeated questions are common. Prepare model answers for them.

prompts.t: Rapid-fire MCQ and viva grilling
prompts.aud: MBBS Student / NEET-PG aspirant / PG Resident
prompts.use: For quick daily practice, especially in the final months.
prompts.why: Rapid-fire questioning builds speed and instant recall, the two things that separate good scores from great ones under time pressure. A drill that keeps going, corrects instantly and highlights the traps keeps you sharp without long explanations.
prompts.p:
You are a strict, energetic examiner who runs rapid-fire question drills for NEET-PG, UPSC CMS and residency exam aspirants.

MY CONTEXT:
Deadline or time I have for this: [brief]
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
Today's topic or subject: [TOPIC]
Exam: [NEET-PG / UPSC CMS / MD-MS-DNB viva / university exam]
Mode: [MCQ-style / one-line viva answers / mixed]
Number of questions: [e.g. 25]

TASK:
1. Ask me rapid-fire questions one at a time: a mix of MCQ-style and short case-scenario questions.
2. After each answer, say "correct" or "wrong", give the correct answer in one line, and name the one trap to remember.
3. Move straight to the next question without long explanations or summaries.
4. Gradually increase the difficulty, and mix in one question from a related topic every 5 questions.
5. After the set, give my score and list my wrong answers with the correct ones.
6. Suggest the 3 topics to review based on my errors.
7. Finish with a short list of anything you were unsure about, so I can verify it before use.

RULES:
Keep answers accurate to standard sources and mark disputed facts [VERIFY], and keep the pace fast, because the drill trains speed as well as knowledge. Don't summarise between questions; just keep grilling.

OUTPUT:
One question per turn with a one-line correction, then the final score, the wrong-answer list and the review topics.

TWEAK:
End with the single fact I should say aloud 5 times today.
tips: Answer within 10 seconds. If you can't, that topic isn't recall-ready yet.
Do a drill on the topic you studied yesterday. It's spaced retrieval in disguise.
Use it on your commute with voice mode, if your tool supports it.

prompts.t: A mistake notebook that raises scores
prompts.aud: MBBS Student / NEET-PG / UPSC CMS aspirant
prompts.use: Set it up now, and feed it after every test or question session.
prompts.why: Most aspirants repeat the same mistakes because they read the explanation and move on. A structured mistake notebook, classified by error type and converted into one-line rules and flashcards, turns every wrong answer into a future right answer.
prompts.p:
You are a performance coach for competitive medical exams who builds systems for learning from errors.

MY CONTEXT:
Deadline or time I have for this: [brief]
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
My wrong or guessed questions from recent sessions (question, my answer, correct answer, explanation): [PASTE]
Exam and time left: [brief]
Tools I use: [paper notebook / Google Sheets / Notion / Anki]

TASK:
1. Design the journal format: date, subject, topic, error type (knowledge gap, recall failure, misread, silly mistake, time pressure), the correct concept, a one-line rule, and a review date.
2. Process my pasted mistakes into this format.
3. Convert each mistake into a flashcard (question on the front, rule on the back).
4. Identify the patterns in my errors, by subject and error type.
5. Set a review schedule (e.g. every 3 days, then weekly).
6. Suggest how to use the journal in the last month, and how much time to give it each week.
7. Finish with a short list of anything you were unsure about, so I can verify it before use.

RULES:
Base the correct concepts on standard sources and mark disputed answers [VERIFY], because a wrong rule in the journal gets reinforced with every review.

OUTPUT:
The journal template, my processed mistakes as a table, the flashcards, the patterns, the review schedule, then the last-month plan.

TWEAK:
End with my top 3 recurring error types and one habit to fix each.
tips: Write the rule in your own words. Copying the explanation doesn't build memory.
Review the journal before every mock test.
"Silly mistakes" repeated three times aren't silly. They're a pattern to fix.

prompts.t: Practise image-based questions
prompts.use: When preparing for image-based questions: X-rays, ECGs, instruments, specimens and clinical photographs.
prompts.why: Image-based questions are a recurring part of modern exams and a common weak area, because students read about images but don't look at enough of them. Structured practice (a systematic look, the key features, and a differential of look-alikes) builds pattern recognition.
prompts.p:
You are a medical educator who trains students for image-based exam questions across radiology, ECGs, clinical photographs, instruments and pathology specimens.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
Image category to practise: [chest X-ray / ECG / clinical signs / instruments / gross specimens / fundus]
Exam: [NEET-PG / UPSC CMS / university spotters]
Image source: [I will upload images / describe images in text / suggest verified sources]

TASK:
1. Teach the systematic approach for this image category in 5–7 steps.
2. List the 20 most commonly tested diagnoses or items in this category, with the key visual feature of each and the look-alike it's confused with.
3. If I upload images, ask me for my interpretation first, then give feedback using the systematic approach.
4. If I describe images, quiz me with text descriptions of classic images.
5. Give 10 practice questions in exam style.
6. Suggest verified sources for real images (standard atlases, radiology education websites, textbook image banks).
7. Finish with a short list of anything you were unsure about, so I can verify it before use.

RULES:
Describe findings conservatively and don't over-interpret uploaded images, marking uncertain findings [CONFIRM WITH A STANDARD ATLAS], because AI image interpretation can be wrong and I'm learning pattern recognition. Use only de-identified images.

OUTPUT:
The approach, the top-20 table (item, key feature, look-alike), the interactive practice, then the source suggestions.

TWEAK:
End with the 5 image pairs students most often confuse in this category.
tips: Look at 10 real images a day for 3 weeks. Recognition becomes automatic.
Always describe the image before naming it. It's how you avoid being fooled by look-alikes.
Keep a folder of the images you got wrong and review it weekly.

prompts.t: Why was my answer wrong?
prompts.aud: MBBS Student / NEET-PG / UPSC CMS aspirant
prompts.use: Immediately after getting a question wrong.
prompts.p:
You are a patient MCQ tutor who diagnoses reasoning errors.

MY CONTEXT:
The question and options: [PASTE]
My answer and my reasoning: [brief]
The correct answer given: [answer]

TASK:
1. Explain why the correct answer is correct.
2. Explain exactly where my reasoning went wrong: a knowledge gap, a misread clue, a trap, or overthinking.
3. Point out the clue I missed.
4. Give a one-line rule for my mistake notebook.
5. Give one similar question to test the fix.

RULES:
If the given answer key seems disputed, say so and explain both views with [VERIFY], because question banks occasionally contain errors.

OUTPUT:
The explanation, the diagnosis of my error, the missed clue, the rule, then the similar question.
tips: The missed clue is usually one word in the stem: "painless", "sudden", "elderly". Train your eye for it.
prompts.try: A question on the drug of choice for absence seizures, where I chose a different anticonvulsant.

prompts.t: Learn from the distractors
prompts.use: After solving a question, to squeeze every concept out of it.
prompts.p:
You are an MCQ writer who teaches students to learn from every option.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
The question with its 4 options and the answer: [PASTE]

TASK:
1. For each wrong option, write the scenario in which it would be the correct answer.
2. Explain the distinguishing feature between each distractor and the right answer.
3. Turn the four options into a mini comparison table.

RULES:
Keep every alternative scenario accurate to standard sources, because this turns one question into four learned facts.

OUTPUT:
A distractor table (option, when it would be right, distinguishing feature), then the comparison.
tips: One question analysed this way is worth four questions merely solved.
prompts.try: A question on the causes of a raised anion gap with 4 plausible options.

prompts.t: Eliminate options when I'm unsure
prompts.aud: MBBS Student / NEET-PG / UPSC CMS aspirant
prompts.use: To improve on questions where you're only partly sure.
prompts.p:
You are an exam-technique coach.

MY CONTEXT:
A question I was unsure about: [PASTE]
What I knew and what I didn't: [brief]

TASK:
1. Demonstrate elimination step by step: absolute words, options that contradict the stem, options that are true but don't answer the question, and "two similar options".
2. Show how to reason from partial knowledge to the most likely answer.
3. Give 5 general elimination rules with examples.
4. Explain when to stop and mark the question for review.

RULES:
Present elimination as a strategy for partial knowledge, not a replacement for learning, and remind me to check the negative-marking rules, marked [VERIFY CURRENT SCHEME], because guessing strategy depends on scoring.

prompts.p: Act as an exam mentor. Here is a question, [PASTE QUESTION], my chosen answer, [ANSWER], and my reasoning, [REASONING]. Tell me whether the reasoning is sound, even if the answer is right, and correct any flawed step. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: A question on the first-line investigation in suspected pulmonary embolism.

prompts.t: Which option is most likely?
prompts.p: Act as an exam coach. For this question, [PASTE QUESTION], I've narrowed it to options [X and Y]. Explain which is more likely and why, using the clues in the stem, and give a rule for similar "two good options" situations.
prompts.try: The best initial test versus the gold-standard test, in a question on myasthenia gravis.

prompts.t: Solve an EXCEPT question safely
prompts.p: Act as an exam-technique coach. Solve this EXCEPT or NOT question, [PASTE QUESTION], by marking each option true or false with a one-line reason, and then name the odd one out as the answer, showing the method clearly. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: "All of the following cause a raised JVP EXCEPT…"

prompts.t: Numbers I must remember for this topic
prompts.p: Act as a revision expert. List the numbers that MCQs commonly test for [TOPIC] (cut-offs, durations, doses, percentages), each with one line of context, all marked [VERIFY FROM STANDARD SOURCE] because numbers differ between editions. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: Topic: diabetes mellitus diagnostic criteria and targets.

prompts.t: Formula recall drill
prompts.aud: MBBS Student / NEET-PG / UPSC CMS aspirant
prompts.p: Act as a biostatistics quizmaster. Ask me for the formulas of [LIST OF MEASURES] one at a time, check each of my answers, correct mistakes with a one-line example calculation, and finish with my score. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: Incidence, prevalence, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV and NNT.

prompts.t: Twenty last-minute facts
prompts.p: Act as a revision expert. Give me 20 last-minute, high-yield facts for [SUBJECT] for [EXAM], each under 12 words, grouped by topic, marking numbers and guideline-dependent facts [VERIFY], for a final 10-minute revision. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: Subject: pharmacology, the day before NEET-PG.

prompts.t: Model long answer (10–15 marks)
prompts.use: For long-answer questions in university theory exams and residency theory papers.
prompts.why: Long answers are marked quickly against a mental checklist of key points, structure and diagrams. A model answer that is well structured, with headings, a diagram, a flowchart or table and a focused conclusion, shows you exactly what earns full marks, and trains you to reproduce it in 15–20 minutes.
prompts.p:
You are a senior university examiner in [SUBJECT] who has marked thousands of theory scripts and knows what earns full marks. You write model answers that are complete, well structured and realistic to write in the time allowed.

MY CONTEXT:
The question (exactly as asked): [PASTE QUESTION]
Marks and the time available for it: [e.g. 15 marks, 20 minutes]
Exam: [MBBS university / MD-MS-DNB theory / other]
Standard textbook for this subject: [name and edition]
My current knowledge of the topic: [brief]

TASK:
1. Interpret the question: the directive word (discuss, describe, enumerate, compare), its scope, and the marks split implied.
2. Give an answer skeleton with headings in the right order.
3. Write the model answer: a 2–3 line introduction or definition, structured headings with points, at least one labelled diagram (described so I can draw it), a flowchart or table where it helps, and a brief conclusion.
4. Keep the length realistic for the time (about 600–800 words for a long answer).
5. Mark the "examiner's key points": 5–8 non-negotiable facts that must appear.
6. Suggest what to underline or highlight.
7. Give a 2-minute planning version (the skeleton only) for rapid practice.

RULES:
Keep the content consistent with the standard textbook and mark doses, cut-offs and guideline-dependent statements [VERIFY FROM TEXTBOOK / GUIDELINE], because examiners mark against the standard source. Don't pad with irrelevant material; examiners penalise it.

OUTPUT:
The interpretation, the skeleton, the model answer with the diagram description, the key-points box, the underlining guide, then the 2-minute version.

TWEAK:
End with the 3 common mistakes students make on this question, and how to avoid them.
tips: Practise writing the answer by hand in the time allowed. Knowing and writing are different skills.
Draw the diagram first in practice. If it takes too long, simplify it.
Keep a file of model answers for repeated questions. It's your final-month revision.

prompts.t: Model answers for previous-year questions
prompts.use: With past papers, one question at a time, weeks before the exam.
prompts.why: University theory papers repeat themes and often whole questions. Model answers for previous-year questions, written to the right length and format with the non-negotiable points highlighted, are the highest-yield preparation for theory exams.
prompts.p:
You are an expert examiner and teacher in [SUBJECT] who writes model university exam answers exactly as a strong student would in the exam hall.

MY CONTEXT:
Deadline or time I have for this: [brief]
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
The previous-year question (paste exactly): [PASTE QUESTION]
Question type and marks: [long answer / short note / brief answer; marks]
University or exam: [brief]
Standard textbook: [name]

TASK:
1. Write a model answer as a student would write it in the exam: subheadings, a brief introduction (2–3 lines), and structured points.
2. Include a labelled diagram description or a text schematic where relevant.
3. Match the length to the marks: about 600–800 words for a long answer and 200–250 for a short answer, or as appropriate.
4. End with an "Examiner's expected key points" box listing the 5 non-negotiable facts that must appear.
5. Note any repeated variants of this question and how the answer would change for each.
6. Suggest a 1-minute recall checklist for the day before the exam.

RULES:
Keep facts consistent with the standard textbook and mark doses and guideline details [VERIFY FROM TEXTBOOK], because model answers are memorised and reproduced. Avoid content beyond what the question asks.

OUTPUT:
The model answer with its diagram description, the key-points box, the variants note, then the recall checklist.

TWEAK:
End with the question's likely marking breakdown (which section earns how much), marked as an estimate.
tips: Paste questions directly from past papers. The theory, clinical and short-note formats all work.
Build a bank of model answers for questions repeated across 3 or more years.
Rewrite each model answer once in your own words and handwriting. That's what you'll reproduce.

prompts.t: Examiner evaluation of my written answer
prompts.use: After writing a practice answer by hand (type it or upload a photo).
prompts.why: You can't improve answer writing without feedback, and teachers rarely have time to mark practice answers. An examiner-style evaluation with marks, missed key points, structure and presentation feedback, and a rewritten section shows you exactly how to gain marks.
prompts.p:
You are a strict but fair university examiner in [SUBJECT] who marks answers against a key-point checklist and gives specific, actionable feedback.

MY CONTEXT:
Deadline or time I have for this: [brief]
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
The question and its marks: [PASTE]
My answer (typed, or a photo of my handwritten answer): [PASTE / UPLOAD]
Time I took: [minutes]
Exam: [brief]

TASK:
1. Build the marking scheme: the key points and their approximate marks, and the credit for structure and diagrams.
2. Mark my answer against it, with a total out of the maximum.
3. List the key points I covered, missed, or got wrong.
4. Give feedback on structure, headings, the diagram, legibility and presentation (from the photo, if uploaded), and length versus time.
5. Rewrite the weakest section of my answer as an example.
6. Give 3 specific changes for my next practice answer.
7. Finish with a short list of anything you were unsure about, so I can verify it before use.

RULES:
Base the marking on standard textbook content and mark disputed points [VERIFY], and be honest about the marks, because generous marking in practice leads to surprises in the exam. If handwriting in a photo is unreadable, say which parts couldn't be read.

OUTPUT:
The marking scheme, the mark awarded, the points table (covered, missed, wrong), the presentation feedback, the rewritten section, then the 3 changes.

TWEAK:
End with the mark I could realistically reach with the 3 changes.
tips: Write under timed conditions before asking for evaluation. Untimed answers give false confidence.
Re-write the same answer after the feedback and have it evaluated again.
Track your marks across practice answers. Improvement is motivating.

prompts.t: MD / MS / DNB theory essay with depth
prompts.use: For residency theory papers, where depth, recent evidence and a critical perspective are expected.
prompts.why: Residency theory answers are expected to go beyond MBBS level: current guidelines, landmark evidence, recent advances and a critical view, all written clearly in limited time. A model built to that standard shows the difference between a pass and a distinction.
prompts.p:
You are a senior examiner for MD, MS and DNB theory papers who expects postgraduate-level depth, current evidence and clear structure.

MY CONTEXT:
Deadline or time I have for this: [brief]
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
Specialty and paper: [e.g. MD General Medicine, Paper 3]
The question: [PASTE QUESTION]
Marks and time: [e.g. 10 marks, 15 minutes]
Guidelines and key sources I know for this topic: [LIST]

TASK:
1. Interpret the question and plan the structure.
2. Write the model answer: definition and classification, pathophysiology relevant to management, diagnostic approach (criteria, scores, investigations), management with current guideline recommendations, recent advances or trials, controversies, and a conclusion.
3. Include a flowchart or algorithm and a table where they help.
4. Cite guidelines and trials by name and year where appropriate, each marked [VERIFY], without a full reference list.
5. Keep the length realistic for the time.
6. Mark the points that distinguish a postgraduate-level answer from an MBBS-level one.
7. Finish with a short list of anything you were unsure about, so I can verify it before use.

RULES:
Name guidelines and trials only from my list or with [VERIFY], because examiners notice misattributed trials. Keep the content current, and flag anything that may have changed recently.

OUTPUT:
The plan, the model answer, the flowchart and table descriptions, then the "postgraduate-level" markers.

TWEAK:
End with the recent advance or controversy most likely to impress the examiner on this topic, and how to write it in 3 lines.
tips: One recent trial or guideline change, correctly cited, lifts an answer above the average.
Practise writing algorithms quickly. They save words and show clarity of thought.
Read the question twice: postgraduate questions often ask for "critical appraisal" or "recent advances" specifically.

prompts.t: Short note (5 marks)
prompts.use: For short notes and brief-answer questions.
prompts.p:
You are a university examiner who knows what a 5-mark short note must contain.

MY CONTEXT:
Topic: [TOPIC]
Marks and time: [e.g. 5 marks, 7 minutes]
Exam: [brief]

TASK:
1. Write a short note of about 200–250 words: a one-line definition, then 4–6 headed points, and a small diagram or table if relevant.
2. Highlight the 5 must-have points.
3. Give a 1-minute skeleton version.

RULES:
Keep it within the length a student can write in the time, and consistent with the standard textbook, marking specifics [VERIFY], because short notes are marked on key points, not volume.

OUTPUT:
The short note, the must-have points, then the skeleton.
tips: Headings and a small table make a short note look complete at a glance.
prompts.try: Short note on Horner's syndrome.

prompts.t: Plan any answer in 2 minutes
prompts.use: In practice, to train fast planning before writing.
prompts.p:
You are an exam-writing coach.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience or purpose: [brief]
The question and its marks: [PASTE]
Subject: [brief]

TASK:
1. Give a 2-minute planning method: underline the directive word, list the headings, choose one diagram, and note the key facts per heading.
2. Apply it to my question and produce the skeleton.
3. Allocate words or space per heading according to the marks.

RULES:
Keep the skeleton aligned with what the question actually asks, because off-topic sections earn nothing.

OUTPUT:
The planning method, the skeleton, then the allocation. Keep it concise, and list anything you were unsure about at the end so I can check it.
tips: A 2-minute plan saves 5 minutes of rambling and earns more marks.
prompts.try: "Discuss the aetiology, clinical features and management of acute pancreatitis."

prompts.t: A diagram that earns marks
prompts.use: When an answer needs a diagram and you're unsure what to draw.
prompts.p:
You are an examiner who values clear, relevant diagrams.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
The question or topic: [brief]
Time I can give the diagram: [e.g. 3 minutes]

TASK:
1. Choose the best diagram (anatomical, flowchart, graph or schematic) for this answer.
2. Describe how to draw it step by step, with its labels.
3. Suggest a simpler 1-minute version.
4. Say where to place it in the answer.

RULES:
Keep the diagram accurate and relevant to the question, because irrelevant diagrams waste time without adding marks.

OUTPUT:
The diagram choice, the drawing steps with labels, the simple version, then the placement.
tips: Practise each important diagram three times before the exam. Speed comes from repetition.
prompts.try: A diagram for "pathophysiology of septic shock".

prompts.t: Put a flowchart in my answer
prompts.use: For management, approach and pathophysiology questions.
prompts.p:
You are an examiner who rewards clear flowcharts.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience or purpose: [brief]
The question and the content to convert: [PASTE]

TASK:
1. Convert the content into a compact flowchart (6–10 boxes) with arrows and decision points.
2. Suggest the box labels (under 6 words each).
3. Say which paragraphs of the answer the flowchart can replace, to save time.

RULES:
Keep the clinical logic accurate and mark thresholds [VERIFY], because flowcharts are marked as content, not decoration.

OUTPUT:
The flowchart in text form, the labels, then the time-saving note. Keep it concise, and list anything you were unsure about at the end so I can check it.
tips: A flowchart for "management" questions shows examiners you think in steps.
prompts.try: Management of an acute exacerbation of asthma.

prompts.t: A comparison table in my answer
prompts.use: For "compare", "differentiate" and "classify" questions.
prompts.p:
You are an examiner who values well-designed tables.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience or purpose: [brief]
The question and the items to compare: [brief]

TASK:
1. Choose 6–8 comparison features that matter most.
2. Build the table with concise entries.
3. Add a one-line conclusion under the table.
4. Suggest how to draw it quickly by hand.

RULES:
Keep the entries accurate and parallel, because tables are scanned quickly for correctness.

OUTPUT:
The table, the conclusion, then the drawing tip. Keep it concise, and list anything you were unsure about at the end so I can check it.
tips: Tables let examiners see 8 points at a glance. They're the fastest way to show breadth.
prompts.try: Differentiate nephritic from nephrotic syndrome.

prompts.t: Strong introductions and conclusions
prompts.use: When your answers start and end weakly.
prompts.p:
You are an examiner who notices first and last impressions.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
The question: [PASTE]
My current introduction and conclusion: [PASTE]

TASK:
1. Write a 2–3 line introduction: a definition, and why the topic matters (importance or burden, with [VERIFY] for numbers).
2. Write a 2–3 line conclusion: a summary, a key principle, or a recent direction.
3. Give 3 reusable introduction patterns and 3 conclusion patterns.

RULES:
Keep them brief and factual, because long introductions steal time from the points that earn marks.

OUTPUT:
The rewritten introduction and conclusion, then the reusable patterns.
tips: A precise definition as the first line signals competence immediately.
prompts.try: "Describe the clinical features and management of rheumatic heart disease."

prompts.t: Time allocation for a theory paper
prompts.use: Before practice papers and the real exam.
prompts.p:
You are an exam strategist for theory papers.

MY CONTEXT:
Paper duration and the question pattern (number, types, marks): [brief]
My usual problem (running out of time, long first answers): [brief]

TASK:
1. Calculate the time per question by marks, with reading and review time.
2. Recommend the order (e.g. strongest questions first, or in paper order).
3. Set checkpoints for the paper.
4. Plan what to do when time runs out (bullet-point the remaining answers).

RULES:
Base the allocation on my paper's actual pattern, because patterns differ between universities and papers.

OUTPUT:
The time table, the order recommendation, the checkpoints, then the emergency plan.
tips: Never exceed a question's time by more than 20%. The next question's marks are easier to earn.
prompts.try: A 3-hour paper with 2 long answers of 15 marks and 10 short notes of 5 marks.

prompts.t: Answer "compare and contrast" questions
prompts.use: For comparison questions.
prompts.p:
You are an examiner who marks comparison questions.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience or purpose: [brief]
The question: [PASTE]
Marks: [number]

TASK:
1. Write a brief introduction defining both items.
2. Build a comparison table (the core of the answer).
3. Add a short paragraph on the key distinguishing points and their clinical relevance.
4. Add a diagram if relevant.

RULES:
Keep the comparisons parallel and accurate, and mark specifics [VERIFY], because comparison answers are checked point by point.

OUTPUT:
The introduction, the table, the paragraph, then the diagram suggestion. Keep it concise, and list anything you were unsure about at the end so I can check it.
tips: Include "similarities" briefly. Many students forget, and examiners notice.
prompts.try: Compare type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus.

prompts.t: What does the question word really ask?
prompts.use: When you're unsure how to approach "discuss", "describe", "enumerate", "outline" or "critically evaluate".
prompts.p:
You are an examiner who explains question directives.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience or purpose: [brief]
The directive words in my exam papers: [list]
Example questions: [PASTE 2–3]

TASK:
1. Define each directive word and what it expects: depth, format and length.
2. Show how the same topic changes with different directives.
3. Rewrite the approach to my example questions.

RULES:
Keep the definitions consistent with common university conventions, and suggest checking local expectations, because institutions differ slightly.

OUTPUT:
A directive table (word, meaning, expected format), the same-topic examples, then my question approaches. Keep it concise, and list anything you were unsure about at the end so I can check it.
tips: "Enumerate" means a list, not an essay. Answering the directive saves time and earns marks.
prompts.try: "Enumerate the causes of haemoptysis" versus "discuss the approach to haemoptysis".

prompts.t: A "recent advances" paragraph
prompts.use: When a question asks about recent advances, or an answer would benefit from one.
prompts.p:
You are an academic clinician who writes accurate recent-advances sections.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience or purpose: [brief]
Topic: [TOPIC]
Recent developments I know of, with sources: [LIST]
Exam: [brief]

TASK:
1. Write a recent-advances paragraph or bullet list (5–7 points) from my sources.
2. Include the year and source for each, marked [VERIFY].
3. Indicate which are established, and which are emerging.

RULES:
Use only the developments I listed or mark new suggestions [VERIFY — FIND SOURCE], because "recent advances" copied from old notes are often outdated.

OUTPUT:
The paragraph or list with sources and status.
tips: Two correct, recent, well-cited points beat seven vague ones.
prompts.try: Recent advances in the management of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.

prompts.t: A stepwise management answer
prompts.use: For "discuss the management of…" questions.
prompts.p:
You are an examiner who expects structured management answers.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
The condition and the question wording: [PASTE]
Marks: [number]

TASK:
1. Structure the answer: general measures, specific treatment (first line, then second line), management of complications, monitoring, prevention and follow-up.
2. Add a management flowchart.
3. Mark drug doses and durations [VERIFY].
4. Add special situations (pregnancy, renal failure, children) if relevant.

RULES:
Keep the recommendations consistent with standard textbooks and current guidelines, and mark every dose [VERIFY], because dosing errors lose marks and credibility.

OUTPUT:
The structured answer, then the flowchart description.
tips: "General measures" first shows examiners you think of the whole patient.
prompts.try: Management of acute severe ulcerative colitis.

prompts.t: Answer a case-based theory question
prompts.use: When a theory question starts with a clinical scenario.
prompts.p:
You are an examiner who writes case-based questions.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
The question with its scenario and sub-questions: [PASTE]
Marks: [number]

TASK:
1. Identify the diagnosis from the scenario and justify it briefly.
2. Answer each sub-question in order, with headings matching the sub-questions.
3. Keep each part proportional to its marks.
4. Link the answers to the scenario details.

RULES:
Reason step by step from the scenario, and keep facts accurate with [VERIFY] for specifics, because case-based questions reward reasoning.

OUTPUT:
The diagnosis with its justification, then the headed answers to each part.
tips: Quote the scenario's clues in your answer ("the history of X suggests…"). It shows your reasoning.
prompts.try: A scenario of a young woman with fever, a malar rash and arthralgia, with questions on diagnosis, investigations and management.

prompts.t: Make my answers look complete at a glance
prompts.use: When your content is good but your marks are average.
prompts.p:
You are an examiner who knows how presentation affects marks.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience or purpose: [brief]
A photo or description of a recent answer I wrote: [UPLOAD / DESCRIBE]

TASK:
1. Assess the presentation: headings, spacing, underlining, point format, diagrams, legibility and margins.
2. Give 8 specific presentation rules.
3. Show a before-and-after layout of one page.

RULES:
Focus on presentation techniques allowed in the exam (pen colours, underlining), and remind me to check my university's rules, because some restrict colours or formats.

OUTPUT:
The assessment, the rules, then the before-and-after layout. Keep it concise, and list anything you were unsure about at the end so I can check it.
tips: Headings underlined, points numbered and one diagram per page make an answer look complete before it is even read.
prompts.try: A photo of a handwritten 15-mark answer that is one continuous paragraph.

prompts.t: Build a bank of repeated questions
prompts.use: With past papers from 5–10 years.
prompts.p:
You are an exam analyst for university theory papers.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Past questions for my subject (paste them): [PASTE]
Years covered: [range]

TASK:
1. Group the questions by topic and identify the repeats and near-repeats.
2. Rank the topics by how often they recur.
3. Create a list of model answers to prepare, in priority order.
4. Suggest a schedule to write them.

RULES:
Base the counts only on the questions I pasted, because claims about "frequently asked" topics beyond my papers are guesses.

OUTPUT:
The grouped table with counts, the priority list, then the schedule.
tips: Questions repeated 3 or more times deserve a memorised model answer.
prompts.try: 8 years of MBBS pathology theory papers.

prompts.t: Model answers from a textbook chapter
prompts.use: After studying a chapter, to prepare answer-ready material.
prompts.p:
You are an examiner who converts chapters into exam answers.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
The chapter (upload or paste the key sections): [UPLOAD]
Exam: [brief]

TASK:
1. Identify the 3–5 most likely long and short questions from this chapter.
2. Write a model skeleton for each (headings, key points and a diagram).
3. Write one full model answer for the most likely long question.

RULES:
Use only the chapter's content, and mark details to check [VERIFY IN CHAPTER], because answers must match the source.

OUTPUT:
The likely questions, the skeletons, then the full model answer.
tips: Skeletons are enough for revision. Write the full answers only for high-priority questions.
prompts.try: A chapter on tuberculosis in a medicine textbook.

prompts.t: Improve my writing speed
prompts.use: When you know the answers but can't finish the paper.
prompts.p:
You are an exam coach who trains writing speed and efficiency.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and level: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
My current speed (e.g. words per 10 minutes) and my handwriting issues: [brief]
Weeks until the exam: [N]

TASK:
1. Give techniques: planning first, bullet points instead of prose, standard abbreviations (defined once), and quick diagrams.
2. Plan a weekly practice routine with timed writing.
3. Set speed targets with measurement.
4. Suggest ergonomic tips (pen, posture, breaks).

RULES:
Keep the abbreviations to standard, recognisable ones, because examiners won't decode private shorthand.

OUTPUT:
The techniques, the routine, the targets, then the ergonomics.
tips: Timed practice twice a week for 6 weeks noticeably improves speed.
prompts.try: I write 250 words in 15 minutes and need 400 or more.

prompts.t: What examiners actually look for
prompts.use: To understand how theory answers are marked.
prompts.p:
You are a senior examiner who explains marking honestly.

MY CONTEXT:
Exam type and subject: [brief]
My typical marks versus my expectations: [brief]

TASK:
1. Explain how examiners typically mark: key points, structure, diagrams, relevance and presentation.
2. Explain what loses marks: irrelevance, missing key points, poor structure and illegibility.
3. Explain how the marks for a 10-mark answer might be split, as an illustrative estimate.
4. Give a checklist to run on every practice answer.

RULES:
Present the marking insights as general practice, not official schemes, because marking varies between examiners and universities.

OUTPUT:
The marking explanation, the mark-losers, the illustrative split, then the checklist.
tips: Examiners often mark tired and fast. Make key points easy to find.
prompts.try: MBBS final-year medicine theory.

prompts.t: A one-line definition to open my answer
prompts.p: Act as a university examiner. Give a precise, textbook-standard one-line definition of [TOPIC] to open a theory answer, plus one line on its clinical importance, marking the source type as [CHECK STANDARD TEXTBOOK]. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: Topic: acute respiratory distress syndrome.

prompts.t: The five points I must not miss
prompts.p: Act as an experienced university examiner. For the question "[QUESTION]", list the 5 non-negotiable points a full-marks answer must contain, each in one line, in the order they should appear. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: "Describe the clinical features of hypothyroidism."

prompts.t: An "enumerate" answer
prompts.p: Act as an examiner. For "Enumerate [TOPIC]", give a numbered, grouped list (grouped by mechanism or category), with no explanations unless one word is needed, so I can write it in under 3 minutes, and mark anything uncertain [VERIFY]. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: "Enumerate the causes of splenomegaly."

prompts.t: Which diagram should I add?
prompts.p: Act as an examiner. For my answer on [TOPIC], suggest the single most valuable diagram to add, describe it in 4–5 drawing steps with labels, and say where in the answer it should go. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: An answer on the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis.

prompts.t: Convert my paragraph into exam points
prompts.p: Act as an exam-writing coach for university theory papers. Convert this paragraph from my answer, [PASTE PARAGRAPH], into a heading with 4–6 concise numbered points, keeping every fact and removing filler words. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: A 150-word paragraph on the complications of diabetes.

prompts.t: Headings for my answer
prompts.p: Act as a university examiner. Give the heading structure (in order) for the question "[QUESTION]" worth [MARKS] marks, with a suggested word allocation for each heading and the place for one diagram. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: "Discuss the approach to a patient with pyrexia of unknown origin" (15 marks).

prompts.t: A 2-mark answer
prompts.p: Act as an examiner. Write a 2-mark answer for [QUESTION] in 40–60 words: the direct answer first, then one supporting point or example, with nothing extra. Mark any number [VERIFY]. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: "What is the Kussmaul sign?"

prompts.t: A reusable template for disease answers
prompts.p: Act as an exam coach. Give me a reusable heading template for long answers on any disease in [SUBJECT] (e.g. definition, aetiology, pathogenesis, clinical features, investigations, management, complications, prognosis), with one line on what to write under each heading. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: Subject: general surgery.

prompts.t: A strong closing line
prompts.p: Act as an examiner. Write 3 possible concluding lines (under 30 words each) for my answer on [TOPIC] (a summary principle, a clinical pearl, and a recent direction marked [VERIFY]), and say which suits a long answer best. Flag anything you are unsure of so I can check it.
prompts.try: An answer on the management of hypertension in pregnancy.

prompts.t: Viva voce simulator, one question at a time
prompts.use: In the weeks before a university viva, a residency practical, or any oral examination.
prompts.why: Vivas punish silence and rambling, not just ignorance. A simulator that presents a clinical scenario, asks one question at a time, waits for your answer, gives feedback and escalates like a real examiner builds the calm, structured answering that examiners reward.
prompts.p:
You are a strict but fair university examiner in [SUBJECT] conducting a viva voce. You start from a clinical scenario, ask one question at a time, give frank feedback, and escalate from basic to advanced questions as a real examiner does.

MY CONTEXT:
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Subject and topic: [e.g. ophthalmology: sudden painless loss of vision]
Exam: [MBBS final practical / MD-MS-DNB practical / other]
My level: [brief]
Weak areas I want to be tested on: [list or "any"]
Number of questions: [e.g. 10]

TASK:
1. Start with a clinical scenario as you would present it in the exam hall.
2. Ask me one question at a time, covering signs, investigations, differentials, management decisions and applied basic science.
3. Wait for my answer each time.
4. After each answer, give feedback: what I got right, what I missed, and a model answer in 3–5 points.
5. Adjust the difficulty according to my answers, as a real examiner would.
6. Include one "why" question and one "what if" twist.
7. After the set, give a performance summary: score, strengths, weak areas and 3 topics to revise.

RULES:
Ask only one question per turn and wait for my answer, because the value is in answering under pressure. Keep the model answers accurate to standard textbooks and mark guideline-dependent facts [VERIFY].

OUTPUT:
Conversational: one question per turn with short structured feedback; then the final performance summary.

TWEAK:
End with the 3 questions I answered worst, rephrased as I would hear them from a different examiner.
tips: Answer aloud before typing. The viva is spoken.
Try topics such as "a patient with sudden painless loss of vision" or "diabetic retinopathy grading".
Repeat the drill with a friend reading the questions for a realistic rehearsal.

prompts.t: Long case: presentation and examiner questions
prompts.use: For long-case practice before university or residency practical exams.
prompts.why: The long case is the centrepiece of most clinical practicals. Examiners judge your history, examination, summary, differential and management, and how you defend them. Structured practice with a realistic examiner discussion prepares you for both the presentation and the grilling.
prompts.p:
You are a senior clinical examiner for MBBS and MD/MS/DNB practical examinations who has examined long cases for 20 years. You expect a structured presentation and probe the reasoning behind every statement.

MY CONTEXT:
Subject and exam: [e.g. MD General Medicine practical]
The case I clerked (de-identified history and examination findings): [PASTE]
Time allowed for presentation: [e.g. 10 minutes]
My provisional diagnosis: [brief]

TASK:
1. Review my history for completeness and organisation, and list the key questions I missed asking the patient.
2. Review my examination findings for completeness, and list the signs I should have looked for.
3. Help me write the presentation: the one-liner, a concise history, the positive and relevant negative findings, and a summary.
4. Build the diagnosis in the format examiners expect (anatomical, pathological, aetiological and functional, where relevant).
5. List the differentials with points for and against each from the case.
6. Plan the investigations and management with their reasoning.
7. Conduct an examiner discussion: ask me 8 questions one at a time about this case, and give feedback after each.

RULES:
Use only the findings I clerked, and flag missing information as [NOT ELICITED] rather than assuming it, because examiners test what you actually found. Mark guideline-dependent management points [VERIFY]. This is exam practice, not a treatment plan for the patient.

OUTPUT:
The history and examination review, the presentation script, the diagnosis statement, the differential table, the investigation and management plan, then the interactive examiner questions.

TWEAK:
End with the 3 questions examiners most often use to test a candidate on this type of case.
tips: Practise presenting in the time allowed with a timer. Examiners stop overrunning candidates.
Always state the diagnosis in the complete format your department expects.
Know why you ordered each investigation. "To rule out X" is a complete answer.

prompts.t: Short cases: examination and spot findings
prompts.use: For short-case practice, where examiners watch you examine and ask quick questions.
prompts.why: Short cases test examination technique, recognition of findings and quick reasoning, all within minutes. Knowing the examination sequence cold, what examiners look for, and the standard follow-up questions for common short cases is what gets you through.
prompts.p:
You are a clinical examiner who conducts short cases in medicine, surgery, paediatrics and other clinical subjects, and who watches technique as closely as answers.

MY CONTEXT:
Deadline or time I have for this: [brief]
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
Subject and exam: [brief]
The system or short-case type: [e.g. cardiovascular system / a neck swelling / hepatosplenomegaly / a peripheral nerve lesion]
My weak points in examination technique: [brief]

TASK:
1. Give the complete examination sequence for this short case, step by step, including inspection, palpation, percussion and auscultation, and the special tests.
2. List what examiners watch for (hand hygiene, introduction, consent, exposure, positioning, technique).
3. Give the 10 most common short cases in this category with their key findings.
4. For each, give the typical examiner questions and short model answers.
5. Give a "presenting your findings" template (in 60 seconds).
6. Run a practice round: describe a case's findings, and ask me for the diagnosis and the next questions.
7. Finish with a short list of anything you were unsure about, so I can verify it before use.

RULES:
Keep the examination technique consistent with standard clinical-methods textbooks, and mark answers that depend on guidelines [VERIFY], because short cases test standard technique.

OUTPUT:
The examination sequence, the examiner checklist, the common cases table, the Q&A, the presentation template, then the practice round.

TWEAK:
End with the 3 technique errors examiners penalise most in this short case.
tips: Practise the examination sequence on friends until you do it without thinking.
Say what you're doing as you examine, if the examiner allows it. It shows your system.
Present findings, then your conclusion: "These findings suggest…".

prompts.t: OSCE station simulator
prompts.aud: MBBS Student / PG Resident / licensing-exam candidate
prompts.use: For OSCE practice: history-taking, communication, examination, procedures and data interpretation stations.
prompts.why: OSCE stations are marked against checklists, often including items candidates forget under time pressure, such as introductions, consent, summarising and safety-netting. Simulated stations with the checklist revealed afterwards train both the content and the process.
prompts.p:
You are an OSCE examiner and simulated-patient trainer who designs realistic stations and marks strictly against checklists.

MY CONTEXT:
Deadline or time I have for this: [brief]
My specialty and year: [e.g. final-year MBBS / MD Medicine, year 2]
Audience and time available: [brief]
What I most want to get out of this: [one line]
Station type: [history-taking / communication / examination / procedure / data interpretation / counselling]
Topic: [e.g. chest pain history / breaking bad news / inhaler counselling]
Exam: [university OSCE / PLAB 2 / OSCE for MD/MS / other]
Station duration: [e.g. 8 minutes]

TASK:
1. Give the candidate instructions exactly as they would appear on the station door.
2. Play the simulated patient or examiner: respond realistically to my questions and actions, revealing information only when asked.
3. Keep track of time and tell me when it's time to close.
4. After I finish, reveal the marking checklist with the items I achieved and missed.
5. Give global feedback on communication, structure and empathy.
6. Give a model performance script for comparison.
7. Finish with a short list of anything you were unsure about, so I can verify it before use.

RULES:
Stay in character during the station, and reveal the checklist only after I finish, because knowing the checklist in advance defeats the practice. Keep the clinical content accurate and mark guideline specifics [VERIFY].

OUTPUT:
The station instructions, then an interactive role-play; afterwards the checklist table (item, achieved yes or no), the global feedback and the model script.

TWEAK:
End with the 3 checklist items candidates most often miss in this type of station.
tips: Always introduce yourself, confirm identity, take consent and summarise. These are easy marks.
Practise with a timer. Running out of time before the summary loses marks.
Rotate station types. Candidates often over-practise history-taking and neglect communication.

prompts.t: Thesis defence viva preparation
prompts.use: Before your thesis defence or the thesis part of the practical exam.
